title: ECG lead theory
sourceFilename: D1-1 ECG lead theory  DipECG amended Mar 2026.pdf
summary: Connect the cardiac activation sequence to the twelve electrical views, and place the recording electrodes accurately.

objectives.title: Explain how cardiac electrical activation produces the ECG
objectives.why: A tracing makes more sense when every component is connected to an electrical event rather than memorised as a shape.
know: The surface ECG records changing potential differences generated by cardiac electrical activity. It does not directly measure the force of contraction, cardiac output or coronary blood flow. A depolarisation wave changes the electrical state of myocardial cells; repolarisation restores their electrical state. The timing and direction of these processes determine the recorded waveform.

In the usual activation sequence, an impulse from the sinus node spreads through the atria, producing the P wave. It then reaches the atrioventricular conduction system, where conduction is delayed before rapid ventricular activation through the His–Purkinje network. Ventricular depolarisation produces the QRS complex. Ventricular repolarisation contributes to the T wave. Atrial repolarisation is usually obscured by the much larger ventricular complex.

The PR interval begins at the onset of P and ends at the onset of QRS. It therefore includes atrial activation and conduction towards the ventricles, rather than representing the AV node alone. The PR segment is the portion after P and before QRS. Electrical and mechanical events are linked but are not identical: electrical activation precedes contraction, and an organised tracing alone does not prove effective mechanical output.

steps.title: Follow the impulse
steps.text: Trace sinus node → atrial myocardium → AV conduction system → His–Purkinje system → ventricular myocardium.

steps.title: Name the signal
steps.text: Associate atrial depolarisation with P, ventricular depolarisation with QRS and ventricular repolarisation with T.

steps.title: Separate electrical from mechanical
steps.text: Describe what is recorded without claiming that the ECG alone demonstrates effective contraction.

example.question: Supplemental example: what electrical process produces the QRS complex?
working: The impulse has reached the ventricular conduction system.
Activation spreads through ventricular myocardium.
The summed changing ventricular potentials generate the QRS complex.
example.answer: Ventricular depolarisation.

pitfalls: Calling the QRS ventricular contraction rather than ventricular depolarisation.
Describing the entire PR interval as AV nodal delay alone.

practice.prompt: Which component primarily represents ventricular repolarisation?
practice.explanation: The T wave represents ventricular repolarisation; QRS represents ventricular depolarisation.
practice.hint: Ask which process follows ventricular activation.

practice.prompt: What can an ECG directly establish?
practice.explanation: An ECG is an electrical recording; mechanical and haemodynamic measurements require additional assessment.
practice.hint: Separate the electrical signal from the circulation.

objectives.mastery: Correctly link P, QRS and T to their electrical events and explain why the ECG is not a direct measure of pumping.

glossary.definition: A change in cellular membrane potential associated with electrical activation.
The electrical recovery process following depolarisation.
The specialised conduction network that normally activates the ventricles rapidly.

deepDive.title: A sequence, not four isolated shapes
deepDive.text: Think of the ECG as a changing view of an activation sequence. Atrial myocardium activates first, the atrioventricular conduction system introduces a delay, ventricular myocardium activates rapidly, and ventricular electrical recovery follows. These processes overlap in the recorded signal: atrial repolarisation is usually hidden by larger ventricular activity. Naming a component is therefore only the first step. A stronger explanation states which tissue process produces it, where its boundaries are, and how its timing relates to the next event. The source conduction-system image and its electrical-event diagram should be studied together rather than treated as separate facts.

deepDive.title: Why a small interval can represent several processes
deepDive.text: The PR interval starts with atrial activation, before the impulse has reached the AV node. Its duration includes atrial conduction and passage through the AV conduction system towards the beginning of ventricular activation. The PR segment excludes the visible P wave, but even it should not be described as a direct recording of AV-node depolarisation. The surface ECG displays summed potential differences; it does not place a recording electrode inside each conduction structure. When an interval changes, describe the observed timing first. Inferring precisely where conduction slowed requires more information than a single surface measurement usually provides.

deepDive.title: Electrical organisation and mechanical function
deepDive.text: An organised P–QRS–T sequence shows electrical organisation, not a measured stroke volume or blood pressure. Electrical activation normally precedes the mechanical contraction associated with it, but the tracing does not directly measure contraction strength, valve movement or coronary flow. This distinction protects your report from an unsupported conclusion. You can say that ventricular activation occurs regularly at a stated rate. You cannot replace a pulse examination or haemodynamic assessment with that statement. In study exercises, practise separating the electrical observation, its likely physiological interpretation and the clinical information still required.

guidedExercise.prompt: A tracing has a P wave, a PR interval of 160 ms, a QRS duration of 80 ms and a T wave after each QRS. Explain what these observations establish, and identify two things they do not measure.
steps: Identify P as atrial depolarisation and QRS as ventricular depolarisation.
Place the PR interval from P onset to QRS onset; do not equate it solely with AV nodal delay.
Identify T as ventricular repolarisation.
Separate observed electrical timing from unmeasured mechanical or circulatory variables.
guidedExercise.answer: An organised atrial-to-ventricular electrical sequence with the stated conduction timings; contraction strength and coronary blood flow have not been measured.
guidedExercise.explanation: The explanation is defensible because it links every visible feature to its electrical meaning while avoiding a claim about pumping effectiveness. The numerical values are a hypothetical teaching example, not a patient record.

objectives.title: Distinguish electrodes from leads and derive the bipolar limb leads
objectives.why: Electrode position is a physical recording choice; a lead is a calculated electrical viewpoint. Confusing them causes acquisition and interpretation errors.
know: An electrode is a physical contact on the skin. A lead is an electrical viewpoint defined by a potential difference. A standard twelve-lead ECG uses ten electrodes: four limb electrodes and six chest electrodes. The three active limb potentials provide six limb leads, so six separate active limb electrodes are not required.

Using RA for right-arm potential, LA for left-arm potential and LL for left-leg potential, lead I is LA − RA, lead II is LL − RA and lead III is LL − LA. These definitions show that lead I + lead III = lead II. At the same instant and with the same calibration, the limb leads therefore obey Einthoven’s relationship. Their values cannot be treated as six independent measurements.

The right-leg electrode contributes to an interference-reduction circuit; it does not create one of the twelve diagnostic viewpoints and should not be described simply as an earth connection. The course uses IEC limb colours: red right arm, yellow left arm, green left leg and black right leg. Colour schemes vary internationally, so identify the printed electrode labels and local protocol rather than relying on colour alone. Standardised placement and correct labelling are prerequisites for interpreting axis and waveform polarity.

steps.title: Count the contacts
steps.text: Identify four limb and six chest electrodes.

steps.title: Define the positive pole
steps.text: For lead I the left arm is positive relative to the right arm; for lead II the left leg is positive relative to the right arm.

steps.title: Check the algebra
steps.text: Add LA − RA to LL − LA; LA cancels and the result is LL − RA.

example.question: Supplemental example: if lead I is +0.4 mV and lead III is +0.6 mV at the same instant, what is lead II?
working: Use II = I + III.
Substitute +0.4 + +0.6 mV.
example.answer: +1.0 mV, provided the readings are simultaneous and comparably calibrated.

pitfalls: Counting twelve leads as twelve skin electrodes.
Mixing IEC and AHA colour conventions.
Repeating the slide’s phrase “other six” limb leads: I and II allow the remaining four limb leads to be derived.

practice.prompt: How many skin electrodes normally produce a standard twelve-lead ECG?
practice.explanation: Four limb electrodes plus six chest electrodes produce twelve leads.
practice.hint: A lead is a viewpoint, not a separate electrode.

practice.prompt: At the same instant, I = +0.3 mV and III = −0.1 mV. Calculate II in mV.
practice.hint: Use Einthoven’s relationship.

objectives.mastery: Explain electrode versus lead and correctly calculate one bipolar limb lead from the other two.

glossary.definition: A physical skin contact used to acquire an electrical potential.
A defined electrical viewpoint formed from a potential difference.
For simultaneous bipolar limb-lead signals, lead II = lead I + lead III.

deepDive.title: Ten contacts, twelve electrical views
deepDive.text: An electrode is a physical contact with the body. A lead is the electrical comparison produced from electrode signals. A standard twelve-lead recording uses ten electrodes because several views can be derived from the same limb signals. The right-leg electrode participates in interference-reduction circuitry; it is not an additional positive diagnostic view and should not be casually described as an earth electrode. This distinction is practical: changing a physical contact can affect several recorded leads, whereas changing which lead you inspect does not move an electrode. Begin troubleshooting by identifying the contacts and connections before interpreting their calculated views.

deepDive.title: Derive the relationship instead of memorising it
deepDive.text: Let RA, LA and LL represent the instantaneous potentials at the right arm, left arm and left leg. Lead I is LA minus RA, lead II is LL minus RA, and lead III is LL minus LA. Adding I and III cancels the LA terms, leaving II. The relationship concerns signals at the same instant; it is not a rule for adding the largest peaks from unrelated moments. Because these limb views are mathematically linked, two independent limb-lead signals are sufficient to derive the other four of the six limb leads. The source wording that says the other six is a counting error, not an extra set of limb leads.

deepDive.title: What the geometry does and does not mean
deepDive.text: Einthoven’s triangle is an explanatory model that organises the limb-lead axes around the heart. It does not mean that the torso is literally an equilateral electrical conductor or that each electrode records one isolated chamber. All the limb leads observe cardiac activity through different potential comparisons in the frontal plane. The augmented leads use one limb against a reference derived from the other two. Treat the six views as related perspectives on a distributed signal. This helps explain why a finding may be large in one lead, small in another and nearly balanced in a third without implying three different cardiac events.

guidedExercise.prompt: At one instant, suppose RA = 0.20 mV, LA = 0.65 mV and LL = 1.05 mV. Calculate I, II and III and verify their relationship.
steps: Check that I + III = 0.85 mV = II.
guidedExercise.answer: I = +0.45 mV, II = +0.85 mV and III = +0.40 mV; I + III = II.
guidedExercise.explanation: These are hypothetical simultaneous electrode potentials. Adding peak heights taken at different times would not be the same calculation. Four remaining limb leads, rather than six, are derived from two independent limb-lead signals.

objectives.title: Explain limb-lead orientation and waveform polarity
objectives.why: The same activation can appear positive in one lead and negative in another because the viewing directions differ.
know: The six limb leads view the heart in the frontal plane, describing right–left and superior–inferior directions. Their positive axes form the hexaxial reference system: I at 0°, II at +60°, III at +120°, aVF at +90°, aVL at −30° and aVR at −150°. These angles refer to the patient’s anatomical directions, not the observer’s right and left.

For a depolarisation vector, a component directed towards a lead’s positive pole tends to generate a positive deflection, whereas a component directed away tends to generate a negative deflection. A vector perpendicular to that lead has little net projection. A complete QRS can contain both positive and negative phases because ventricular activation changes direction over time; its overall balance is used when estimating the mean QRS axis.

The augmented limb leads compare one limb potential with a reference derived from the other two active limbs. They are mathematically related to I, II and III rather than offering six independent sets of limb information. Their value lies in displaying the same electrical activity from several useful directions. Once orientation is understood, opposite-looking complexes no longer need to be memorised as unrelated shapes. Axis interpretation is developed in the later QRS-axis topic.

steps.title: Draw the frontal plane
steps.text: Place lead I horizontally towards the patient’s left and aVF inferiorly.

steps.title: Locate the other axes
steps.text: Add II +60°, III +120°, aVL −30° and aVR −150°.

steps.title: Project a vector
steps.text: Decide whether a depolarisation vector points towards, away from or perpendicular to a lead’s positive direction.

example.question: Supplemental example: a mean ventricular vector points approximately +60°. What is expected in lead II?
working: Lead II’s positive axis is +60°.
The vector is closely aligned with the positive direction.
example.answer: A predominantly positive QRS projection in lead II.

pitfalls: Applying the depolarisation polarity rule uncritically to repolarisation without considering the different process.
Treating one small negative component as proof that the whole QRS is predominantly negative.

practice.prompt: Which lead’s positive axis is +90°?
practice.explanation: aVF views in the inferior direction at +90°.
practice.hint: The F refers to the foot/inferior direction.

practice.prompt: A depolarisation vector perpendicular to a lead’s axis has what net projection?
options: Always a very tall R wave
A measured heart rate of zero
practice.explanation: Perpendicular orientation produces little net projection; a real QRS may appear approximately equiphasic.
practice.hint: Think of the component of the vector along the lead.

objectives.mastery: Place the six limb leads on the hexaxial system and predict the sign of a simple depolarisation projection.

glossary.definition: The plane describing right–left and superior–inferior directions.
The six standard frontal-plane limb-lead axes arranged around the heart.
The component of an electrical vector along a chosen lead axis.

deepDive.title: A lead records a projection
deepDive.text: A cardiac electrical vector has direction and size. A lead records a component of that vector along its own electrical axis, rather than displaying the whole vector unchanged. For a depolarisation vector directed towards a lead’s positive pole, the main projection is positive. If the vector points away, the projection is negative. A vector nearly perpendicular to the lead has little net projection. This is the mechanism behind the polarity rules used later in axis estimation. The same activation event can therefore make a dominant R wave in one lead and a dominant negative complex in another.

deepDive.title: Separate electrode position from axis notation
deepDive.text: The limb-lead axes are conveniently displayed by the hexaxial system: I at 0°, II at +60°, III at +120°, aVF at +90°, aVL at −30° and aVR at −150°. These angles describe electrical viewing directions in the frontal plane. They are not instructions to place an electrode at a certain angle on the chest. Positive and negative poles are essential to the interpretation. A line without its positive direction is ambiguous because the opposite direction on that line has opposite polarity. When sketching an axis diagram, label the positive pole before reasoning from a waveform.

deepDive.title: Balanced does not mean inactive
deepDive.text: An equiphasic QRS has roughly balanced positive and negative contributions in that lead. Ventricular activation has not disappeared; the net projection is small because the changing forces substantially cancel in that view. A broad or multi-component waveform can require consideration of the whole complex rather than its tallest spike. Similarly, a very small complex may be difficult to classify reliably because noise and baseline movement are a large fraction of its amplitude. The direction inferred from one weak lead should be checked against clearer neighbouring views. Learn the underlying projection rule so you can explain uncertainty rather than force a positive or negative label.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical mean ventricular depolarisation vector is +60°. Predict its net polarity in leads I, II, aVF and aVL.
steps: Compare +60° with the positive direction of each lead.
Lead II is aligned with the vector, so its projection is strongly positive.
Lead I is 60° away and aVF is 30° away, so both have positive projections.
aVL at −30° is 90° away, giving an approximately balanced net projection.
guidedExercise.answer: I positive, II positive, aVF positive and aVL approximately equiphasic.
guidedExercise.explanation: The answer follows the angle between the vector and each lead axis, not a separate memorised rule for every lead. Exact amplitudes would also depend on the magnitude and changing sequence of electrical forces.

objectives.title: Locate the precordial electrodes and explain their electrical view
objectives.why: Accurate chest-electrode placement is essential before judging R-wave progression, ST–T changes or possible disease.
know: The six precordial electrodes give complementary views in the horizontal, or transverse, plane. V1 is placed at the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal edge and V2 at the fourth intercostal space at the left sternal edge. V4 is placed at the fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line. V3 is then positioned midway between V2 and V4. Locating V4 before V3 avoids guessing the diagonal spacing.

V5 is level horizontally with V4 at the anterior axillary line, and V6 is level with V4 at the mid-axillary line. Following an intercostal space upwards around the chest is not the same as remaining on that horizontal level. Anatomical landmarks, rather than a drawing’s apparent spacing or the position of clothing, should guide placement.

Each chest electrode acts as the positive exploring electrode relative to Wilson’s central terminal, a reference formed from the active limb electrodes. The sequential views normally help demonstrate changing QRS balance across the chest. Placement error can imitate or conceal abnormal patterns, so a surprising tracing should prompt an acquisition-quality check before a disease label. A conventional printout may show short 2.5-second lead segments and a longer rhythm strip; inspect the actual printed layout rather than assuming all displayed leads are simultaneous throughout.

steps.title: Locate V1 and V2
steps.text: Find the fourth intercostal spaces at the right and left sternal edges.

steps.title: Place V4, then V3
steps.text: Find the fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, then position V3 midway between V2 and V4.

steps.title: Keep V5 and V6 horizontal
steps.text: Use the anterior and mid-axillary lines at V4’s horizontal level.

steps.title: Check the printout
steps.text: Read paper speed, gain and time layout before comparing leads.

example.question: Supplemental example: V5 has been placed one intercostal space above V4. Is this standard?
working: V5 should be horizontal with V4.
Following a higher rib space changes its anatomical view.
example.answer: No. Recheck landmarks and reposition according to the standard acquisition protocol.

pitfalls: Placing V1 and V2 too high.
Placing V3 before accurately finding V4.
Mistaking a 2.5-second lead segment for a ten-second recording.

practice.prompt: Where is V1 placed?
options: Second intercostal space, left sternal edge
Fourth intercostal space, right sternal edge
practice.explanation: V1 belongs in the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal edge.
practice.hint: V1 is on the patient’s right.

practice.prompt: Which statement about V6 is correct?
options: It is above V4 by one intercostal space
It is at the mid-axillary line, level with V4
It records the frontal plane only
practice.explanation: V6 is at the mid-axillary line on the horizontal level of V4.
practice.hint: Keep V4, V5 and V6 on one horizontal level.

objectives.mastery: Identify all six precordial landmarks and explain the difference between frontal and horizontal electrical views.

glossary.definition: The six chest leads V1–V6, which view electrical activity in the horizontal plane.
The reference potential derived from the three active limb electrodes for the chest leads.
An anatomical space between adjacent ribs.

deepDive.title: Placement is part of interpretation
deepDive.text: The chest leads depend on anatomical electrode placement. Locate V1 and V2 at the fourth intercostal spaces on the right and left sternal edges. Locate V4 at the fifth intercostal space on the mid-clavicular line, then place V3 midway between V2 and V4. V5 and V6 remain horizontally level with V4 at the anterior and mid-axillary lines. This order matters because V3 depends on knowing V4, and V5–V6 follow a horizontal reference rather than simply tracing the same numbered intercostal space around a curved chest. Rehearse the anatomical sequence before attaching diagnostic meaning to an unexpected pattern.

deepDive.title: A different plane adds different information
deepDive.text: Limb leads describe frontal-plane views, while the precordial leads add views across the horizontal or transverse plane. Each chest electrode acts as a positive pole against a reference constructed from the limb electrodes, commonly represented by Wilson’s central terminal. A chest lead is therefore not a direct voltage measurement from only the tissue immediately underneath its contact. Its waveform still reflects distributed cardiac electrical activity, projected through its particular comparison. Study how V1 through V6 surround the electrical viewpoint in the source cross-sectional diagram, then connect this changing viewpoint with the usual evolution of the QRS complex.

deepDive.title: Check the display before comparing beats
deepDive.text: A typical printed twelve-lead layout shows short segments in several columns and often a longer rhythm strip. Do not assume that two complexes printed side by side in different columns represent the same instant. Inspect the time scale, rhythm-strip label and display format. Acquisition and display checks come before a claim of beat-to-beat change. If chest-lead progression is surprising, consider placement or connection errors as well as biological causes. A repeat recording with documented correct placement can resolve an apparent change; a strong diagnostic label should not be built on an unexamined technical assumption.

guidedExercise.prompt: A trainee places V4 correctly, then places V5 one intercostal space lower and V6 at the same lower level. What should be corrected before interpreting unusual chest-lead progression?
steps: Use V4 as the established horizontal reference.
Place V5 at the anterior axillary line, horizontally level with V4.
Place V6 at the mid-axillary line, horizontally level with V4.
Reassess the tracing after correct placement rather than interpreting the misplaced recording as definitive anatomy.
guidedExercise.answer: Reposition V5 and V6 horizontally level with V4, using the correct axillary landmarks.
guidedExercise.explanation: The exercise concerns recording quality, not a diagnosis. Correct electrode positions are necessary before the observed sequence can be confidently compared with expected precordial progression.

title: The normal ECG
summary: Measure the tracing accurately, establish sinus rhythm and describe morphology before judging whether a pattern is normal.

objectives.title: Name ECG waves, segments and QRS components correctly
objectives.why: Precise description lets another reader reconstruct what you saw before considering its clinical cause.
know: An ECG description separates individual deflections from the intervals and segments between them. The P wave represents atrial activation. A QRS complex represents ventricular activation; it may contain several positive and negative components, and not every named component has to be present. The T wave reflects ventricular recovery. A U wave may follow T and is usually smaller; its origin and interpretation should not be assumed from a small bump alone.

Within the QRS, a negative deflection before any positive deflection is a Q wave. The first positive deflection is R; a negative deflection after R is S. A subsequent positive deflection is R-prime. If the entire complex is negative, it is described as QS. Thus an initial negative component is not called S simply because it points downwards. Upper- and lower-case letters can indicate relative amplitude in conventional descriptions.

The ST segment runs from the end of QRS, commonly identified by the J point, towards the beginning of T. Segment displacement is judged against an appropriate isoelectric reference after checking the baseline and recording quality. An interval includes named wave boundaries: PR begins at P onset, whereas QT begins at QRS onset. Naming the boundaries before measuring helps prevent systematic error. These descriptions characterise an electrical signal; they do not, by themselves, establish an aetiological diagnosis.

steps.title: Find QRS onset
steps.text: Start at the first ventricular deflection, even if a Q wave is absent.

steps.title: Label the components in sequence
steps.text: Use Q before a positive deflection, R for positive and S after R.

steps.title: Identify the boundaries
steps.text: Separate the ST segment from the QT interval and recognise a possible U wave.

example.question: Supplemental example: a complex begins with a small negative deflection, then a tall positive deflection, then a negative deflection. Name its components.
working: The first negative component occurs before R: q.
The positive component is R.
The final negative component follows R: S.
example.answer: A qRS complex; the case convention can be adjusted to the relative amplitudes.

pitfalls: Starting QT at the R-wave peak rather than QRS onset.
Calling every downward deflection a Q wave.
Including a separate U wave automatically in QT measurement.

practice.prompt: A wholly negative ventricular complex with no positive deflection is called what?
practice.explanation: A QS complex has no positive R component.
practice.hint: Ask whether any R wave is present.

practice.prompt: Which segment follows the end of QRS and precedes T?
practice.explanation: The ST segment extends from QRS termination towards T-wave onset.
practice.hint: It lies between ventricular activation and the visible T wave.

objectives.mastery: Label Q, R, S, T, ST, PR and QT boundaries consistently on an educational tracing.

glossary.definition: A QRS complex that is entirely negative.
The junction between the end of QRS and the ST segment.
A measured period defined by specified waveform boundaries.

deepDive.title: Name QRS components by sequence
deepDive.text: Q, R and S are descriptive names determined by the sequence and direction of deflections. A negative deflection before any positive deflection is Q; a positive deflection is R; a negative deflection after R is S. A subsequent positive component can be labelled R′. If the entire ventricular complex is negative, QS describes the appearance without inventing a missing positive component. These names do not themselves establish infarction, conduction disease or chamber size. Accurate descriptive language lets a reader reconstruct the shape before considering its cause.

deepDive.title: Intervals include boundaries; segments lie between waves
deepDive.text: The PR interval begins at P onset and ends at QRS onset, so it includes the P wave. The PR segment begins after the P wave ends. QRS duration spans all ventricular depolarisation components, even when the final deflection is small. QT begins at QRS onset, whether the first component is called Q or R, and ends when T returns to its baseline. The ST segment lies between QRS completion and T onset. Saying QT is measured from the Q wave is incomplete because a Q wave need not exist in the lead used for measurement.

deepDive.title: Use a coherent baseline and describe uncertainty
deepDive.text: The apparent height of a segment depends on the baseline chosen and the stability of the recording. Drift, overlapping atrial activity and a poorly defined T ending can all obscure boundaries. The source introduces the baseline between T and P and compares ST with the PR segment; in a real tracing, first check whether these regions are identifiable and stable. A U wave, when visible, follows T and is not automatically part of QT. If a component cannot be confidently separated, record the measurement uncertainty rather than assigning a precise boundary by appearance alone.

guidedExercise.prompt: A ventricular complex begins with a small positive deflection, then a deep negative deflection, then another positive deflection. Name its components and state where QRS duration starts and ends.
steps: The first positive component is an r or R deflection, depending on the descriptive amplitude convention.
The following negative component is S.
The next positive component is R′.
Measure from the beginning of the first ventricular deflection to the end of the last ventricular deflection.
guidedExercise.answer: An rSR′-type sequence; QRS duration spans the entire complex rather than only the first positive spike.
guidedExercise.explanation: The component labels are a shape description. They do not identify a bundle-branch-block diagnosis without duration, lead distribution and other supporting information.

objectives.title: Convert ECG paper distances into time and voltage
objectives.why: Every numerical interpretation depends on using the recorded speed and gain rather than an assumed scale.
know: At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, a horizontal distance of one small 1 mm square represents 0.04 seconds, or 40 ms. A large 5 mm square represents 0.20 seconds. Five large squares span one second. The relationship is distance divided by speed: a measured horizontal distance in millimetres divided by millimetres per second gives seconds.

At the usual gain of 10 mm/mV, one vertical millimetre represents 0.1 mV and ten vertical millimetres represent 1 mV. Voltage is therefore vertical distance divided by gain. Time and voltage use different axes; a horizontal millimetre cannot be interpreted as an electrical amplitude. Measure from the relevant baseline and distinguish the height of a single component from the total peak-to-peak range.

These values are conditional on the actual printed settings. At 50 mm/s, one horizontal millimetre is 20 ms, so using the 25 mm/s rule would double the calculated duration. Half-standard gain similarly changes the voltage represented by each vertical square. The source checklist contains a unit inconsistency for a voltage-sum threshold: 35 mm at 10 mm/mV is 3.5 mV, not 35 mV. A reliable report records the settings and conversion before interpreting whether a measurement is unusual.

steps.title: Read the settings
steps.text: Confirm paper speed and gain from the printout or calibration signal.

steps.title: Convert the horizontal measurement
steps.text: At 25 mm/s, multiply small squares by 40 ms.

steps.title: Convert the vertical measurement
steps.text: At 10 mm/mV, divide vertical millimetres by ten to obtain mV.

steps.title: Check units
steps.text: Keep milliseconds, seconds, millimetres and millivolts distinct.

example.question: Supplemental example: a PR interval spans four small squares at 25 mm/s. What is its duration?
working: One small square = 40 ms.
Four × 40 ms = 160 ms.

pitfalls: Using 300 divided by large squares on a tracing recorded at 50 mm/s.
Confusing a 35 mm voltage sum with 35 mV.
Measuring a waveform from a drifting baseline without noting the limitation.

practice.prompt: At 25 mm/s, how many milliseconds are represented by five small squares?
practice.hint: At the standard speed, each small square is 40 ms.

practice.prompt: At 10 mm/mV, a positive deflection is 12 mm above baseline. What is its amplitude in mV?
practice.explanation: 12 mm ÷ 10 mm/mV = 1.2 mV.
practice.hint: Divide height by the gain.

objectives.mastery: Correctly convert a duration and an amplitude, including when the supplied speed or gain differs from standard.

glossary.definition: The horizontal recording scale, usually expressed in mm/s.
The vertical calibration, usually expressed in mm/mV.
A known signal displayed to indicate the recording scale.

deepDive.title: Derive the time scale from the paper speed
deepDive.text: Paper speed tells you how much distance represents one second. At 25 mm/s, one millimetre represents 1/25 s, or 40 ms; a five-millimetre large square represents 200 ms. At 50 mm/s, those times halve to 20 and 100 ms. The familiar square-counting rate formulae therefore depend on speed. Before measuring anything, read the printed speed or calibration label. A screenshot resized on a phone does not preserve physical millimetres on the screen, so use its recorded grid or a time-labelled digital scale rather than a ruler placed against the display.

deepDive.title: Treat voltage independently of time
deepDive.text: Gain specifies vertical distance per millivolt. At 10 mm/mV, one small vertical square is 0.1 mV and a 10 mm calibration height represents 1 mV. Changing gain alters displayed amplitude without changing the underlying voltage in the same proportion that the display appears to change. It does not alter paper speed or interval duration. Keep the two conversions separate in your working: horizontal distance divided by speed gives time, and vertical distance divided by gain gives voltage. Reporting both the measurement and the calibration makes the result reproducible.

deepDive.title: Make the units carry the reasoning
deepDive.text: Write units at each stage rather than applying an unexplained multiplier. For example, 7 mm ÷ 25 mm/s gives 0.28 s because millimetres cancel. A 35 mm summed voltage at 10 mm/mV equals 3.5 mV, not 35 mV. This corrects a unit inconsistency in the source checklist. A useful quality check is to ask whether the converted value would change appropriately if the same signal were printed at a different scale. The true voltage and time should be recovered after the calibration change is taken into account.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical strip is recorded at 50 mm/s and 5 mm/mV. An interval spans eight small squares and a deflection is 7.5 small squares high. Calculate duration and voltage.
steps: Duration = 8 mm ÷ 50 mm/s = 0.16 s.
Convert 0.16 s to 160 ms.
Voltage = 7.5 mm ÷ 5 mm/mV = 1.5 mV.
Check that the faster speed and lower gain were both used instead of the usual 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV defaults.
guidedExercise.answer: Duration 160 ms; voltage 1.5 mV.
guidedExercise.explanation: The two conversions use different calibration settings and different axes. Applying the usual default square values here would produce incorrect results even if the grid had been counted accurately.

objectives.title: Calculate ventricular rate in regular and irregular rhythms
objectives.why: Rate is an objective measurement, and choosing the correct method avoids misleading estimates in irregular recordings.
know: For a regular rhythm recorded at 25 mm/s, heart rate in beats per minute can be calculated as 300 divided by the number of large squares between successive QRS complexes. The equivalent small-square formula is 1500 divided by the number of small squares. These constants come from the distance covered in one minute at the specified paper speed; they are not universal constants for every recording.

Choose two clearly identified adjacent ventricular complexes and measure comparable points, usually consecutive R peaks when the morphology is consistent. Several intervals can be inspected to confirm regularity. If R–R distances vary substantially, one interval is not representative of the average ventricular rate. Count QRS complexes over a longer known duration instead: in a ten-second rhythm strip, multiply the count by six to estimate beats per minute. In a six-second strip, multiply by ten.

A counted-strip estimate has finite precision because only a short time sample is observed. Counting one additional complex in ten seconds changes the estimate by 6 bpm. Record the method and state that an irregular rhythm’s rate is an average over the sampled interval. Atrial and ventricular rates can differ when not every atrial impulse conducts, so explicitly say which rate is being measured. A fast ventricular rate does not establish the rhythm mechanism; P-wave behaviour and regularity must still be assessed.

steps.title: Check speed and duration
steps.text: Confirm 25 mm/s before using 300 or 1500; identify the actual strip duration.

steps.title: Assess regularity
steps.text: Compare several R–R intervals.

steps.title: Select the calculation
steps.text: Use an R–R formula for a regular rhythm and a longer timed count for an irregular one.

steps.title: Report the result
steps.text: Give bpm and describe whether the value is an interval-based rate or timed average.

example.question: Supplemental example: a regular rhythm has four large squares between R waves at 25 mm/s.
working: Use heart rate = 300 ÷ large squares.
example.answer: 75 bpm.

pitfalls: Calculating an irregular rhythm’s average rate from its shortest R–R interval.
Counting P waves while reporting a ventricular rate.
Assuming every printed short lead segment lasts ten seconds.

practice.prompt: A regular rhythm has three large squares between QRS complexes at 25 mm/s. Calculate its rate.
practice.hint: Use 300 divided by large squares.

practice.prompt: There are 13 QRS complexes in a ten-second rhythm strip. Estimate the average ventricular rate.
practice.hint: Scale the ten-second count to one minute.

objectives.mastery: Choose the appropriate method and correctly calculate rate for one regular and one irregular rhythm.

glossary.definition: The time between corresponding points on successive ventricular complexes.
The number of ventricular activations per minute.
A rhythm with approximately consistent successive cycle lengths.

deepDive.title: Decide what rate is being measured
deepDive.text: Ventricular rate is counted from ventricular complexes, whereas atrial rate is counted from atrial events. They are equal only when the observed relationship produces one ventricular response for each atrial event. Calling both simply heart rate can hide an important conduction difference. Start by identifying the event you are counting. In a regular ventricular rhythm, measure between equivalent points on consecutive QRS complexes. If the complexes have variable shapes, choose a consistent landmark and make sure a premature event or artefact has not been missed.

deepDive.title: Choose a calculation appropriate to the timing
deepDive.text: For a regular rhythm, rate equals 60 divided by the RR interval in seconds. At 25 mm/s this produces the familiar 300 divided by the number of large squares or 1500 divided by the number of small squares. These are shortcuts to the same relationship, not independent tests. For an irregular rhythm, one RR interval gives only an instantaneous cycle rate. A timed count over six or ten seconds gives an average ventricular response over that observation window. State the window and recognise that a short sample may not represent a longer recording.

deepDive.title: Explain precision honestly
deepDive.text: Counting seven complexes in six seconds gives an approximate average of 70/min, but the exact position of the strip boundaries affects whether a partly included cycle is counted. A longer suitable recording reduces the influence of one counted event. In a patterned irregular rhythm, describe the pattern as well as the average: an alternating short and long cycle can share an average rate with a completely regular rhythm while representing different timing. A defensible report includes regularity, the measurement method and whether the value is approximate rather than presenting a short-strip count as a perfectly precise long-term rate.

guidedExercise.prompt: A regular hypothetical recording at 25 mm/s has 4.5 large squares between QRS complexes. A second strip has nine QRS complexes in a labelled ten-second window and visibly variable RR intervals. Calculate and describe each rate.
steps: For the regular strip, use 300 ÷ 4.5.
This gives approximately 66.7 ventricular complexes/min.
For the irregular strip, multiply the ten-second count by six.
State that 54/min is an average over the observed window, not the rate of every individual cycle.
guidedExercise.answer: Regular strip: approximately 67/min. Irregular strip: approximately 54/min over the ten-second sample, with variable cycle lengths.
guidedExercise.explanation: Method selection follows timing behaviour. Using the shortest or longest RR interval from the irregular example would produce a cycle-specific number rather than the requested average ventricular response.

objectives.title: Measure PR and QRS intervals and describe their limitations
objectives.why: The conduction intervals locate timing abnormalities more precisely than a label such as “abnormal ECG”.
know: The PR interval starts at the beginning of atrial depolarisation and ends at the beginning of ventricular depolarisation. It is measured from the onset of P to the onset of QRS, not from the P peak or the R peak. The course uses 120–200 ms as the usual adult PR range. A constant PR of 160 ms is therefore within that teaching range, whereas 400 ms is prolonged. A short PR requires interpretation of P morphology and QRS onset rather than an automatic diagnosis of pre-excitation.

QRS duration runs from the earliest onset of ventricular activation to its end. A global measurement may require comparing several leads because onset or offset is clearer in one lead than another. The normal-ECG lecture uses a duration below 110 ms as its normal teaching criterion. This should not be confused with the 120 ms boundary commonly used to classify broad-complex tachycardia or complete bundle-branch block; a single threshold cannot replace morphology and context.

Assess whether the PR interval is constant, changing or not measurable. If P waves are absent, obscured or unrelated to QRS, assigning a neat PR value can be misleading. Distinguish a prolonged but constant interval from progressively changing conduction. Likewise, QRS broadening describes delayed or altered ventricular activation, not its cause. Bundle-branch patterns, ventricular origin, pacing, pre-excitation, drugs and electrolyte abnormalities are considered in later topics. Record measurement uncertainty when waveform boundaries are indistinct.

steps.title: Locate P onset
steps.text: Find the first departure from baseline attributable to P.

steps.title: Locate QRS onset and offset
steps.text: Use the first and last ventricular deflections, comparing leads where helpful.

steps.title: Measure and describe
steps.text: State PR and QRS in ms; say whether PR is constant or variable.

steps.title: Separate timing from diagnosis
steps.text: Use the duration as evidence for the later morphological interpretation.

example.question: Supplemental example: PR is five small squares and QRS is two small squares at 25 mm/s.
example.answer: PR is at the upper boundary of the course’s usual adult range; QRS is narrow.

pitfalls: Treating 110 ms and 120 ms as interchangeable rules for every ECG task.
Measuring PR when the visible atrial deflection does not belong to that QRS.
Assuming that a short PR alone proves an accessory pathway.

practice.prompt: The correct PR measurement boundaries are:
practice.explanation: PR includes the P wave and subsequent conduction until ventricular activation begins.
practice.hint: Start when atrial depolarisation begins.

practice.prompt: A QRS spans 2.5 small squares at 25 mm/s. What is its duration?
practice.hint: Use 40 ms for each small square.

objectives.mastery: Measure PR and QRS correctly and distinguish a timing description from a definitive diagnosis.

glossary.definition: Time from P-wave onset to QRS onset.
Time from the beginning to the end of ventricular depolarisation.
A descriptive term for prolonged ventricular activation, interpreted using the relevant task-specific threshold.

deepDive.title: Locate boundaries before counting squares
deepDive.text: A PR measurement starts at the earliest clearly identifiable beginning of P in the lead being measured and ends at QRS onset. A QRS measurement must include the full ventricular activation waveform, including a low-amplitude terminal component that may be less obvious in one lead than another. Magnification or comparison with another suitable lead can improve boundary identification, but avoid pretending that a blurred or noisy image permits millisecond precision. Record the calibration, chosen boundaries and any uncertainty. Correct counting cannot rescue an incorrectly chosen start or end point.

deepDive.title: Duration is a description before it is a mechanism
deepDive.text: The course uses an adult PR reference of 120–200 ms and a QRS reference below 110 ms in its introductory checklist. Use these as the course’s measurement framework, not as a diagnosis generator. A long PR does not by itself identify the anatomical site or cause of delay. A short PR needs interpretation alongside P-wave origin and ventricular activation; it is not sufficient alone to establish pre-excitation. Similarly, a broad QRS says that ventricular activation is prolonged, but its mechanism requires morphology, lead distribution and rhythm context.

deepDive.title: Relationships across multiple cycles matter
deepDive.text: A single PR value cannot describe a changing conduction pattern. Follow consecutive atrial events and their ventricular responses, including any atrial event without a visible QRS. Distinguish a consistently long interval from progressive prolongation, abrupt changes or varying P-wave timing. If an atrial event is concealed within another waveform, measuring only the most obvious P waves can create a misleading story. The source examples of long, short and varying PR are best used as comparisons in a sequence: identify the timing behaviour first, then state which additional observations are needed to interpret it.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical strip at 25 mm/s has a PR interval of seven small squares and a QRS duration of three small squares. The next three PR intervals appear unchanged. What should you report before assigning a cause?
steps: QRS = 3 × 40 ms = 120 ms.
Describe the PR as prolonged and apparently constant across the measured cycles.
Describe the QRS as broad in the introductory course framework; inspect morphology and the wider record before identifying why.
guidedExercise.answer: Constant prolonged PR of about 280 ms with QRS duration about 120 ms; cause and anatomical mechanism are not established by these measurements alone.
guidedExercise.explanation: The answer distinguishes measured timing from interpretation. The additional description of constancy is useful because the same first PR value could otherwise belong to a changing pattern.

objectives.title: Measure QT and calculate a rate-corrected QT cautiously
objectives.why: QT depends on cycle length; rate correction supports comparison but can introduce errors if treated as an infallible normality test.
know: The QT interval begins at QRS onset and ends at the end of the T wave. It includes both ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation. Identify a lead in which the T-wave end can be recognised, and distinguish a separate U wave from T. Baseline noise, merging waves and an indistinct T-wave end make the measurement less certain. State the measured QT and the associated R–R interval before reporting a corrected value.

The lecture illustrates Bazett correction: QTc = QT / √RR, with RR in seconds. QT may be supplied in milliseconds if the resulting QTc is also reported in milliseconds. For example, QT 400 ms and RR 0.88 s produce QTc approximately 426 ms by calculator; rounding and the underlying measurement precision explain small differences from a printed worked value. The correction is a mathematical estimate, not a direct new measurement.

The source uses 460 ms as a simplified teaching limit. Real assessment depends on the clinical setting, sex, age, heart rate, correction formula and QRS duration. Bazett correction can be misleading at heart rates far from the usual resting range, and a long QT caused partly by a broad QRS is not equivalent to isolated delayed repolarisation. Do not use one number alone to diagnose congenital long-QT syndrome or to make treatment decisions. Later lessons address acquired changes and channelopathies.

steps.title: Measure the raw intervals
steps.text: Record QT from QRS onset to T end and RR in seconds.

steps.title: Keep units consistent
steps.text: Use QT in ms and RR in s for the displayed Bazett calculation.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.text: Divide QT by the square root of RR.

steps.title: Qualify the result
steps.text: Document formula, measurement uncertainty and the setting in which the value is interpreted.

example.question: Supplemental example: QT = 400 ms and RR = 1.00 s. Calculate Bazett QTc.
example.answer: 400 ms. At RR = one second, this correction leaves QT unchanged.

pitfalls: Entering RR = 1000 rather than 1.0 in the seconds-based formula.
Measuring to the end of a separate U wave automatically.
Calling a result “normal” solely because it is below the lecture’s simplified 460 ms boundary.

practice.prompt: QT is 360 ms and RR is 0.81 s. Calculate Bazett QTc, rounded to the nearest millisecond.
practice.hint: Take the square root of RR before dividing.

practice.prompt: Why should QTc be interpreted cautiously when QRS is broad?
options: QT contains ventricular depolarisation as well as repolarisation
Broad QRS always proves congenital long-QT syndrome
practice.explanation: A portion of the prolonged QT may reflect prolonged depolarisation, so the repolarisation component needs contextual interpretation.
practice.hint: Remember where QT starts.

objectives.mastery: Correctly calculate a supplied Bazett example and explain at least two reasons QTc alone does not establish a diagnosis.

glossary.definition: Time from QRS onset to the end of the T wave.
A heart-rate-corrected estimate of QT using a named correction formula.
QTc = QT divided by the square root of RR, with RR in seconds.

deepDive.title: Separate the interval into its components
deepDive.text: QT contains ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation because it begins at QRS onset and ends at T completion. A longer QT can therefore arise partly from a longer QRS, from a longer repolarisation phase or from both. Broad QRS complexes make a simple QTc interpretation less straightforward; they should not be dismissed as automatically harmless. The introductory lesson focuses on recognising this limitation and reporting the measured components. A more specialised assessment may require a method that deals explicitly with the depolarisation contribution.

deepDive.title: Rate correction is an estimate, not a direct measurement
deepDive.text: The measured QT is an observed interval. QTc is a calculated estimate intended to account for rate dependence. Bazett divides QT by the square root of RR; RR must be in seconds. Keeping QT in milliseconds gives QTc in milliseconds after that correction. The source worked example uses QT 400 ms and RR 0.88 s, producing approximately 428 ms. Be able to reproduce the calculation, but do not treat its result as an exact property independent of formula, rate, rhythm and measurement choice. A formula cannot correct a poorly identified T-wave endpoint.

deepDive.title: Make the endpoint defensible
deepDive.text: Choose a lead in which the T wave and its return towards baseline can be identified, and keep a separate U wave out of the QT measurement when it is distinguishable. Overlap, low-amplitude endings and irregular timing make the choice less certain. In a report or exercise, state the measured QT, corresponding RR, formula and uncertainty rather than only a single corrected number. The course’s introductory QTc range is a teaching heuristic. Patient characteristics and recording context matter; this lesson does not convert that range into a universal rule for diagnosing an inherited or acquired syndrome.

guidedExercise.prompt: In a hypothetical example, QT is 420 ms and RR is 0.81 s. Calculate Bazett QTc, then state three pieces of information needed to assess how trustworthy that number is.
steps: Take the square root of RR: √0.81 = 0.9.
Divide 420 ms by 0.9 to obtain approximately 467 ms.
Check that QRS onset and T ending were clearly identified and a separate U wave was excluded.
Record whether the rhythm, QRS duration and the selected QT/RR pair make the formula estimate representative.
guidedExercise.answer: Bazett QTc is approximately 467 ms. Interpretation requires confidence in the endpoint, QRS contribution, rhythm/rate context and the pairing of QT with RR.
guidedExercise.explanation: The arithmetic is correct without proving a clinical diagnosis. The exercise deliberately asks for measurement context so that the calculated result is not treated as a self-sufficient conclusion.

objectives.title: Establish sinus rhythm from atrial and ventricular relationships
objectives.why: A rate in the usual range is not enough: sinus rhythm requires an appropriate atrial activation pattern and its relation to ventricular activation.
know: Sinus rhythm originates from the sinus node and normally activates the atria in a consistent direction. On the surface ECG, P-wave morphology should be compatible with that origin; the lecture emphasises upright P waves in leads I and II. Inspect several cycles rather than accepting one visible P wave. Assess whether the P waves are consistent and whether the atrial rhythm itself is regular or varies.

For uncomplicated normal sinus rhythm in the course framework, each P is followed by a QRS, every QRS has an associated preceding P, the PR is consistent and within the usual adult teaching range, and the ventricular rate is approximately 60–100 bpm. Sinus bradycardia and sinus tachycardia retain sinus origin despite being outside that rate range. Their significance depends on context, so a resting rate cannot be interpreted without considering physiology, symptoms and other findings.

P waves that are very tall, broad or notched merit description and further assessment, but an individual measurement does not directly measure atrial size. A retrograde atrial activation pattern can produce negative inferior P waves and may occur with a junctional rhythm; its timing relative to QRS is important. Conversely, an irregular sinus rhythm can occur with respiratory variation. Distinguish sinus origin, conduction and rate as three related but separate questions. The supraventricular-arrhythmia topic develops these distinctions further.

steps.title: Find and compare P waves
steps.text: Use leads where atrial activity is clearest, including II and V1 when useful.

steps.title: Check the relationship
steps.text: Determine whether each atrial activation is linked to one QRS and whether PR is consistent.

steps.title: Measure rate separately
steps.text: Describe sinus origin and then state whether the rate is usual, slow or fast.

steps.title: Describe morphology
steps.text: Note unusual P shape without substituting a chamber-size diagnosis for an ECG observation.

example.question: Supplemental example: regular upright P waves in I and II precede every narrow QRS with PR 160 ms, at 72 bpm.
working: The P-wave direction is compatible with sinus activation.
The P–QRS relationship is one-to-one with a constant PR.
The rate is within the course’s usual adult range.
example.answer: The supplied features are consistent with normal sinus rhythm; a complete ECG assessment is still needed.

pitfalls: Using a rate of 70 bpm as sufficient evidence of sinus rhythm.
Calling any rhythm with P waves before QRS sinus without inspecting their direction.
Equating irregularity automatically with atrial fibrillation.

practice.prompt: Which is strongest evidence of uncomplicated sinus rhythm?
options: A rate of exactly 70 bpm alone
Compatible P waves consistently preceding QRS with a stable PR
A tall R wave in V5 alone
practice.explanation: The atrial morphology and its consistent relationship to ventricular activation support sinus origin.
practice.hint: Rate and origin are different questions.

practice.prompt: A sinus-origin rhythm at 48 bpm is best described as:
practice.explanation: Bradycardia describes the slow rate; the rhythm can still be sinus in origin.
practice.hint: Keep the origin label while describing the rate.

objectives.mastery: Support a sinus-rhythm description with P-wave direction, P–QRS linkage, PR behaviour and an independently measured rate.

glossary.definition: A rhythm originating from the sinus node, recognised using appropriate atrial activation and timing.
Activation spreading through the atria in a direction opposite to the usual sinus sequence.
A relationship in which each relevant atrial activation is associated with one ventricular activation.

deepDive.title: Begin with atrial identity
deepDive.text: Sinus rhythm is a statement about the origin and sequence of atrial activation, not just a ventricular rate between two numbers. In the course framework, look for consistent P waves with an orientation compatible with sinus activation, particularly upright P waves in I and II. Inspect a lead where the atrial waveform is clear rather than assuming that an inconspicuous P wave is absent. P-wave shape can be affected by the viewing lead, and a short displayed segment may conceal an atrial event within the preceding T wave or ventricular complex.

deepDive.title: Check the relationship in both directions
deepDive.text: Ask whether every visible P wave is followed by a ventricular complex and whether every ventricular complex is preceded by a corresponding P wave. Both questions are needed. Merely finding a P before one QRS does not establish a stable one-to-one relationship across the recording. Follow PP intervals, RR intervals and PR intervals over several cycles. Stable relationships support an organised atrial-to-ventricular sequence; absent responses, extra ventricular events or shifting timing require a different description. Rate and regularity should then be stated as additional properties of the rhythm.

deepDive.title: Do not confuse sinus origin with a completely normal ECG
deepDive.text: A sinus rhythm can be slow, fast or variably timed, and it can coexist with prolonged AV conduction, broad QRS complexes or other abnormalities. Conversely, a junctional-origin rhythm may have retrograde atrial activity before, within or after QRS, so an apparent P–QRS order alone is insufficient. The source comparison with AV nodal rhythm demonstrates why P polarity and timing both matter. A useful report separates origin, atrioventricular relationship and accompanying findings instead of using normal sinus rhythm as a blanket judgement on the whole twelve-lead recording.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical tracing has regular upright P waves in I and II at 55/min, one P before every QRS, one QRS after every P, and a constant PR of 240 ms. Is the entire ECG normal because the sequence is sinus?
steps: Use P-wave orientation and consistent atrial timing to support sinus origin.
Verify the one-to-one P–QRS relationship in both directions.
Describe the slow rate separately from the rhythm origin.
Describe the prolonged PR separately rather than allowing the word sinus to hide it.
guidedExercise.answer: The observations support sinus bradycardia with a consistently prolonged PR interval; they do not justify calling the whole ECG normal.
guidedExercise.explanation: Rhythm origin, rate and conduction are different descriptive dimensions. The example is original teaching material and does not establish a clinical cause of the slow rate or PR prolongation.

objectives.title: Describe normal morphology and recognise the limits of a checklist
objectives.why: A checklist structures observation; it does not make every deviation disease or every passing tracing normal.
know: After rate, rhythm and intervals, examine QRS axis, Q-wave distribution, voltage, R-wave progression and ST–T morphology. Compare anatomically related leads rather than judging an isolated component without its neighbours. In a usual precordial sequence, V1 has a small initial r followed by a deeper S, with increasing R:S balance towards the left-sided leads. Poor progression is a descriptive finding with several possible explanations, including technical factors.

Small septal q waves can be normal in appropriate leads, whereas their duration, depth and distribution can make other Q waves important. Describe these features before attributing them to infarction. Similarly, voltage-sum criteria are screening observations and not direct measurements of ventricular mass. ST position should be assessed from the relevant reference and lead distribution. T-wave direction, amplitude and its relation to QRS require context; the lecture’s numerical teaching rules contain inconsistencies and should not be used as universal diagnostic cut-offs.

Normal variants in the course include isolated Q waves in certain limb leads, early-repolarisation patterns, juvenile anterior T-wave inversion and athletic adaptations. Their labels do not make all similar-looking ECGs benign. Age, symptoms, prior recordings, family history, acquisition quality and the overall pattern can change interpretation. The lecture itself states that a tracing can meet checklist criteria and still be abnormal, or miss a criterion and be normal. Conclude with an evidence-based description and identify uncertainty rather than forcing a binary answer from one measurement.

steps.title: Use a fixed order
steps.text: Review axis → Q waves and voltage → R-wave progression → ST segments → T waves.

steps.title: Compare related leads
steps.text: Look for a coherent regional pattern and check technical quality.

steps.title: Consider a variant carefully
steps.text: Use the relevant demographic and clinical context; do not infer benignity from shape alone.

steps.title: Summarise observations
steps.text: Separate what is seen from the differential explanation and any limitations.

example.question: Supplemental example: an isolated Q wave is visible in lead III, with no corresponding abnormal Q in aVF. What is the defensible first response?
working: Check its dimensions and compare inferior leads.
Review acquisition quality and the rest of the ECG.
Recognise that an isolated lead-III Q can be a normal variant.
example.answer: Describe and contextualise the finding; do not diagnose an old inferior infarction from that isolated observation.

pitfalls: Calling all concave ST elevation benign early repolarisation.
Equating high voltage alone with proven ventricular hypertrophy.
Using the source’s inconsistent T-amplitude rules as absolute diagnostic boundaries.

practice.prompt: What is the best role of a normal-ECG checklist?
options: A structured aid that still requires context
A guarantee that all disease is excluded
A method that diagnoses every abnormality from one lead
practice.explanation: The checklist supports a systematic description but cannot guarantee normality or establish every diagnosis.
practice.hint: Recall the caution printed in the source checklist.

practice.prompt: Poor R-wave progression should initially be treated as:
options: Proof of anterior infarction in every patient
A descriptive finding requiring technical and clinical context
Evidence that a twelve-lead ECG uses twelve electrodes
A direct measurement of left ventricular mass
practice.explanation: Progression can be influenced by lead placement and several clinical processes; the pattern is not uniquely diagnostic.
practice.hint: Describe the signal before naming its cause.

objectives.mastery: Produce a structured morphological description and identify at least three situations where a single criterion is insufficient.

glossary.definition: The changing relative R and S amplitudes across the chest leads.
An ECG pattern that may occur without disease in an appropriate context, but still requires careful assessment.
A relationship in which compared waveform directions are similar; its significance depends on the feature and leads being assessed.

deepDive.title: Use a checklist as a reading order
deepDive.text: The source checklist is useful because it forces a complete survey: rate and rhythm, atrial features, intervals, frontal axis, ventricular morphology and voltage, ST segments, T waves and chest-lead progression. Its role is to organise observation, not replace interpretation. Work through all leads in a reproducible order and record the actual finding whenever a criterion is not met. A report that says only abnormal ECG cannot be defended as well as a report that names the lead distribution, direction and measured size of the abnormalities.

deepDive.title: Normal variation is contextual
deepDive.text: The source demonstrates isolated Q waves in particular limb leads, early-repolarisation patterns, age-related anterior T-wave appearances and athlete-associated changes. These examples teach that an apparently unusual feature is not automatically disease. They do not make every similar-looking tracing benign. Consider whether a finding is isolated or accompanied by other abnormalities, whether the distribution fits the proposed variant, and whether age, training history, symptoms and previous recordings support that interpretation. Neither demographic membership nor a single concave ST shape is a substitute for an integrated assessment.

deepDive.title: Describe multiple findings before combining them
deepDive.text: The source’s final case pairs show original tracings followed by lists of observable abnormalities. Use them to practise assembling a structured description before deciding what the pattern may mean. For example, broad QRS, altered axis, voltage changes and discordant repolarisation should each be recognised before their relationships are discussed. Voltage is affected by recording scale and body-related factors; a voltage sum is not a direct measurement of myocardial mass. Poor R-wave progression also needs technical review rather than automatic attribution to infarction. The introductory numerical criteria contain simplifications and a voltage-unit error, so retain their teaching purpose while keeping interpretation qualified.

guidedExercise.prompt: Create a structured description of a hypothetical ECG with rate 80/min, one-to-one sinus-like atrial activity, QRS 140 ms, an abnormal frontal axis and ST–T changes in several leads. What should be written before choosing a single unifying diagnosis?
steps: State the rhythm evidence and ventricular rate.
Record QRS duration and describe its lead-specific morphology.
State the axis finding and how it was estimated.
Name the leads and direction of ST–T changes, then consider whether they relate to the altered ventricular activation.
guidedExercise.answer: A structured list of the observed rhythm, timing, axis, morphology and repolarisation findings, with technical quality and context considered before a diagnostic synthesis.
guidedExercise.explanation: The exercise tests an interpretation process rather than a disease label. The course checklist can guide the survey, but meeting or failing one checklist item does not by itself determine whether an ECG is clinically normal.

title: QRS axis
sourceFilename: D1-3.  QRS axis DipECG reviewed mar 2026.pdf
summary: Use limb-lead polarity and the hexaxial system to estimate the mean frontal ventricular activation direction.

objectives.title: Explain the mean frontal QRS axis and its categories
objectives.why: Axis summarises ventricular activation direction; knowing what is being averaged prevents it being confused with anatomical heart position.
know: The mean frontal QRS axis is an estimate of the overall direction of ventricular depolarisation in the frontal plane. Individual regions activate in different directions over time, so the mean vector is a summary rather than a claim that all cells activate along one line. The axis describes an electrical direction projected onto the limb leads; it is not a direct measurement of the physical orientation or size of the heart.

The course uses −30° to +90° as the usual adult normal range. Left-axis deviation lies beyond −30° towards −90°; right-axis deviation lies beyond +90° towards +180°. The superior rightward region between −90° and −180° is described as extreme axis. At category boundaries, measurement uncertainty matters: a nearly equiphasic lead may make the exact category uncertain, and a point exactly on a boundary should not be forced into a confident pathological label.

Axis deviation can accompany conduction changes, chamber-loading patterns, congenital anatomy or technical errors. It does not establish a specific disease on its own. The source lists several associations, but those associations are not diagnostic equations. A reliable interpretation combines the calculated direction with rate, rhythm, QRS width, morphology and acquisition quality. Before explaining an unexpected axis physiologically, verify patient identity, lead labels and electrode placement. The following objectives show how the lead projections constrain the possible direction.

steps.title: Define the plane
steps.text: Use the six limb leads for the frontal-plane axis.

steps.title: Locate the usual interval
steps.text: Mark −30° to +90° on the hexaxial circle.

steps.title: Describe deviation
steps.text: Use left, right or extreme only after supporting the relevant angular region.

steps.title: Keep inference separate
steps.text: State the electrical observation before suggesting possible causes.

example.question: Supplemental example: an estimated mean frontal QRS axis is +120°. Classify the direction using the course’s adult framework.
working: The normal upper boundary is +90°.
+120° is more rightward than +90° and remains below +180°.
example.answer: Right-axis deviation; its cause is not established by the angle alone.

pitfalls: Using chest leads to calculate the frontal axis.
Equating left-axis deviation with left ventricular hypertrophy in every patient.
Treating small differences near a boundary as perfectly precise measurements.

practice.prompt: Which statement defines the QRS axis most accurately?
options: The anatomical angle of the whole heart on X-ray
The average frontal-plane direction of ventricular depolarisation
The direction of atrial repolarisation only
The time between successive P waves
practice.explanation: The mean QRS axis summarises ventricular depolarisation projected into the frontal plane.
practice.hint: Focus on QRS and the limb leads.

practice.prompt: Using the course’s adult framework, an axis of −60° is:
practice.explanation: −60° lies beyond the normal leftward boundary of −30°.
practice.hint: Mark the negative angles above lead I on the reference circle.

objectives.mastery: Define the axis, place its main adult categories and distinguish an axis observation from its possible causes.

glossary.definition: The overall frontal-plane direction of ventricular depolarisation.
An axis more leftward than the usual adult −30° boundary.
An axis more rightward than the usual adult +90° boundary.

deepDive.title: The axis is a summary of changing forces
deepDive.text: Ventricular activation produces forces in many directions and at different times. The mean frontal QRS axis summarises their overall direction in the frontal plane. It is not a photograph of the heart’s anatomical position, nor does it mean that every part of the QRS follows the same direction. The source’s resultant-force diagrams explain why a complex activation sequence can still be described by one approximate frontal direction. When the QRS is unusual or has large opposing components, recognise that this summary may be less straightforward to infer from a quick peak-height comparison.

deepDive.title: Use the angle convention consistently
deepDive.text: The conventional reference places lead I at 0°, aVF at +90°, aVL at −30° and aVR at −150°. The source uses an adult reference region from −30° to +90°, with left, right and extreme deviations outside that region. A category boundary is a convention on a continuous circle, not a biological cliff. If a lead is nearly equiphasic at a boundary, small measurement or baseline differences may change the categorical label. State that the axis is approximately at the boundary when the waveform does not justify a more definite classification.

deepDive.title: Category and cause are separate conclusions
deepDive.text: The course lists possible associations of left or right axis deviation, including fascicular conduction patterns, ventricular changes, congenital abnormalities and technical electrode interchange. Such lists are differential possibilities, not automatic diagnoses. The same axis category can occur in different settings, and the underlying cause cannot be established from the angle alone. Describe how you estimated the axis and inspect the rest of the ECG, recording quality and clinical context. This keeps a mathematical direction estimate from becoming an unjustified claim about chamber structure or a specific conduction-system lesion.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical ECG has an estimated frontal QRS axis of −25°. Another estimate from a noisy repeat is −35°. How should the small difference be discussed?
steps: Compare each estimate with the course boundary at −30°.
Recognise that the numerical estimates differ by only 10° near that boundary.
Review the waveform balance, baseline and recording quality rather than treating the category change as a large physiological change.
Use approximate language if the data do not support a precise angle.
guidedExercise.answer: The estimates lie close to the leftward boundary of the course reference range; the apparent category difference may reflect estimation uncertainty and is not, by itself, evidence of a new disease.
guidedExercise.explanation: Axis categories are useful summaries of a continuous direction. A finding near a threshold requires more careful wording, not stronger certainty simply because it crosses the category boundary.
