objectives.title: Use lead I, aVF and lead II to classify an axis region
objectives.why: A fast regional method is useful only if it preserves the distinction between a mildly leftward normal axis and true left-axis deviation.
know: A predominantly positive QRS in lead I means the mean axis lies within 90° of lead I’s positive direction: between −90° and +90°. A predominantly negative QRS places it on the opposite side. Lead aVF then separates inferior from superior directions. I positive and aVF positive places the axis between 0° and +90°, within the usual adult normal range. I negative and aVF positive supports a rightward region.

I positive with aVF negative is not automatically abnormal left-axis deviation. That combination includes both the normal interval from 0° to −30° and the more leftward interval beyond −30°. Lead II, whose positive axis is +60°, resolves this useful distinction. A positive lead II supports an axis on the normal side of −30°; a negative lead II supports an axis more leftward than −30°. An approximately equiphasic lead II suggests proximity to the boundary rather than a precise categorical diagnosis.

Judge the overall positive versus negative balance of QRS, not just whether a small q or S exists. I negative with aVF negative suggests an extreme superior-rightward region. Broad, fragmented or nearly balanced complexes may make a simple sign-based estimate uncertain. Use more leads or the perpendicular method when needed, and report a region instead of inventing a precise angle. The method works because each lead provides a geometrical constraint on the same underlying electrical vector.

steps.title: Assess lead I
steps.text: Classify the QRS as predominantly positive, negative or approximately balanced.

steps.title: Add aVF
steps.text: Separate inferior and superior frontal directions.

steps.title: Use II for a leftward borderline region
steps.text: When I is positive and aVF negative, inspect II before labelling left-axis deviation.

steps.title: State the region
steps.text: Give the supported category and any boundary uncertainty.

example.question: Supplemental example: I is positive, aVF is negative and II is positive. Is this necessarily left-axis deviation?
working: I positive and aVF negative restrict the axis to the superior-leftward quadrant.
Positive II places it on the normal side of −30°.
example.answer: No. The axis can lie between −30° and 0°, within the course’s usual adult normal interval.

pitfalls: Calling every I-positive/aVF-negative tracing left-axis deviation.
Using the tallest single peak without considering negative components.
Reporting an exact degree value from only two sign observations.

practice.prompt: I is positive and aVF is negative. Which lead helps distinguish a mildly leftward normal axis from left-axis deviation?
practice.explanation: Lead II is perpendicular to the −30° boundary: its QRS polarity helps identify which side of that boundary the axis occupies.
practice.hint: Think of the course’s normal leftward boundary.

practice.prompt: I and aVF are both predominantly negative. The supported region is usually:
practice.explanation: The vector points away from both lead I’s leftward and aVF’s inferior directions.
practice.hint: Combine the two negative projections.

objectives.mastery: Classify an axis region from three supplied limb-lead polarities and recognise the lead-II boundary check.

glossary.definition: A complex whose positive contribution exceeds its negative contribution overall.
A regional axis estimate based on the signs of selected perpendicular limb leads.
A lead whose polarity helps determine which side of a category boundary the axis lies on.

deepDive.title: Each polarity restricts the possible half-plane
deepDive.text: A positive net QRS in a lead places the mean vector within 90° of that lead’s positive direction. A negative net QRS places it more than 90° away. Lead I therefore separates generally rightward from generally leftward projections, while aVF separates superior from inferior projections. Their intersection gives an initial quadrant. Think of this as intersecting allowable regions on the hexaxial circle. The method is stronger when you can explain why an angle is allowed or excluded instead of reciting a table without its geometry.

deepDive.title: Why lead II resolves the leftward boundary
deepDive.text: Lead I positive with aVF negative does not automatically mean left axis deviation. That quadrant includes the region from 0° towards −90°, but the introductory adult reference range extends to −30°. Lead II, whose positive direction is +60°, has a perpendicular boundary at −30°. A positive net QRS in II supports an axis on the reference-range side of that boundary; a negative net QRS supports a more leftward axis. A nearly balanced II suggests a boundary estimate. This is the reason for the extra lead-II check, not an arbitrary exception to the quadrant method.

deepDive.title: Use the whole ventricular complex
deepDive.text: Classify net polarity using the balance of positive and negative components, not the existence of any R wave. A complex with a small R and a deep S is predominantly negative. Conversely, a small initial q does not make the whole complex negative if the following R dominates. Where several components or similar positive and negative contributions make the decision uncertain, record the lead as near-equiphasic and cross-check with other limb leads. Do not force a quadrant from a tiny net difference that could be explained by baseline movement or measurement noise.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical ECG has a positive net QRS in I, a negative net QRS in aVF and a positive net QRS in II. Which region is supported, and why is the answer not automatically left axis deviation?
steps: I positive places the vector in the −90° to +90° half-plane.
aVF negative restricts it to the superior portion of that region.
II positive keeps it on the side nearer the +60° positive pole, above the −30° boundary.
Combine the three findings to obtain an approximate −30° to 0° region.
guidedExercise.answer: A mildly leftward axis within approximately −30° to 0°, which remains inside the source’s adult reference region.
guidedExercise.explanation: Lead II supplies the extra boundary information missing from I and aVF alone. The result is a region rather than a precise numerical angle because only polarity information was supplied.

objectives.title: Estimate axis with an equiphasic lead and its perpendicular
objectives.why: The perpendicular method gives a reproducible estimate when the QRS is balanced in a limb lead, provided the correct one of two possible directions is selected.
know: An approximately equiphasic QRS has positive and negative components that balance. It indicates little net projection of the mean ventricular vector onto that lead. Geometrically, the mean axis is therefore approximately perpendicular to the lead’s axis. There are always two perpendicular possibilities separated by 180°, so identifying an equiphasic lead alone does not finish the calculation.

Choose another lead that is perpendicular to the equiphasic one and inspect its overall QRS polarity. If it is positive, choose the direction pointing towards that lead’s positive pole. If it is negative, choose the opposite direction. For example, aVF is at +90°. An equiphasic aVF suggests an axis near 0° or 180°; a positive lead I selects the 0° possibility. Similarly, an equiphasic lead III at +120° gives −150° or +30°, and a negative aVR selects the +30° direction.

When no lead is exactly equiphasic, choose the most nearly balanced lead and treat the perpendicular direction as an approximation. The source illustrates refining the estimate by considering whether that nearly balanced lead is slightly positive or negative. Such refinements should remain proportional to measurement quality. Do not imply degree-level precision from a noisy trace or a visually estimated balance. If all limb-lead complexes are approximately balanced, the frontal axis may be indeterminate rather than meaningfully calculable by this shortcut.

steps.title: Identify the best balanced lead
steps.text: Compare the positive and negative QRS contributions in all six limb leads.

steps.title: Find the two perpendicular directions
steps.text: Mark directions 90° either side of that lead’s positive axis.

steps.title: Choose the correct polarity
steps.text: Use a clear perpendicular lead to select the direction towards or away from its positive pole.

steps.title: Report an approximation
steps.text: Use “approximately” and state if no lead is clearly equiphasic.

example.question: Supplemental example: aVF is equiphasic and lead I is predominantly positive. Estimate the mean axis.
working: aVF lies at +90°.
Its two perpendicular possibilities are 0° and 180°.
Lead I is positive, so the vector points towards 0° rather than away.
example.answer: Approximately 0°.

pitfalls: Choosing either perpendicular direction without a polarity check.
Calling a tiny QRS “equiphasic” just because it is hard to see.
Manufacturing an exact angle when several leads are nearly balanced.

practice.prompt: An equiphasic aVF suggests which two approximate axis possibilities?
practice.explanation: The mean vector is approximately perpendicular to aVF’s +90° axis.
practice.hint: Rotate the aVF axis by 90°.

practice.prompt: Lead III is equiphasic and aVR is predominantly negative. Which approximate axis is supported?
practice.explanation: The two perpendicular options to lead III are −150° and +30°. A negative aVR points away from its −150° pole, selecting +30°.
practice.hint: Use aVR to choose between the two perpendicular possibilities.

objectives.mastery: Select both perpendicular candidates, use a second lead to choose between them and report appropriate uncertainty.

glossary.definition: A QRS complex with approximately balanced positive and negative components.
An axis estimate using a balanced lead and the polarity of a lead at 90° to it.
An axis that cannot be meaningfully assigned from the available frontal-plane QRS balance.

deepDive.title: Perpendicular gives two possibilities
deepDive.text: When the net QRS is approximately balanced in one limb lead, the mean frontal vector is approximately perpendicular to that lead’s axis. A perpendicular line has two opposite directions, so this observation alone does not determine which direction is correct. Inspect a suitable lead aligned with that perpendicular line, or use another clear polarity observation to choose between them. The course example with equiphasic aVF and positive lead I illustrates the selection of 0° rather than the opposite direction at 180°.

deepDive.title: Nearly equiphasic means an approximate result
deepDive.text: Real tracings often lack a perfectly balanced lead. Start with the most nearly equiphasic lead to obtain a perpendicular estimate, then use its small residual positive or negative projection to decide which way the vector is displaced. The course’s +105° example begins near +90° because I is almost balanced, then moves slightly further right because I is weakly negative while aVF is positive. The 15° adjustment is a convenient visual estimate in that example, not a universal correction that should be applied whenever a lead is almost balanced.

deepDive.title: Cross-check the estimate against the other leads
deepDive.text: Once you propose an angle, predict which limb leads should be positive, negative or near-equiphasic and compare those predictions with the recording. This reverse check exposes a mistaken choice of the opposite perpendicular direction or a misread polarity. If the predictions do not broadly agree, return to waveform balance and recording quality rather than averaging incompatible answers. Very low amplitudes, unusual multi-component complexes or broadly equiphasic limb leads can make the axis indeterminate. A qualified region estimate is preferable to a precise-looking angle unsupported by the available signals.

guidedExercise.prompt: In a hypothetical ECG, lead III is equiphasic and aVR is predominantly negative. Use the perpendicular method to choose an approximate axis.
steps: Lead III is oriented at +120°.
Its perpendicular directions are approximately +30° and −150°.
aVR points towards −150°, so a negative QRS there favours the opposite direction.
Choose approximately +30°, then check whether the remaining limb-lead polarities agree.
guidedExercise.answer: Approximately +30°.
guidedExercise.explanation: The equiphasic lead provides the perpendicular line; aVR determines which end of that line is appropriate. The result remains an estimate because equiphasic appearance and net polarity are visual measurements. Always cross-check.

objectives.title: Combine axis evidence with technical quality and clinical context
objectives.why: The axis estimate becomes useful when its supporting evidence and limitations are explicit, rather than used as a stand-alone disease label.
know: Each limb lead constrains the possible QRS axis. A positive QRS restricts the axis to directions within approximately 90° of that lead’s positive pole; a negative QRS restricts it to the opposite half-plane. Combining several consistent lead observations narrows the permitted region. This is useful when there is no exactly equiphasic lead and helps explain why the final estimate is reasonable.

The estimate should be internally consistent. If an estimated direction would project positively into a lead with a clearly negative QRS, revisit the measurements, the polarity judgement and the choice between opposite perpendicular candidates. Unexpected axis patterns also require an acquisition check. Limb-electrode interchange or other recording errors can change the displayed projections and should not be overlooked in favour of a dramatic diagnosis.

When the axis is genuinely abnormal, consider its relationship to the whole ECG rather than assuming one cause. A fascicular conduction pattern, ventricular loading, altered anatomy or other processes can contribute. The source’s listed disease associations are possibilities, not proof. A sound report can state a rightward or leftward region, identify the leads supporting that conclusion, describe QRS width and morphology separately, and recommend contextual review where interpretation remains uncertain. For indeterminate or nearly balanced cases, acknowledging the limitation is more accurate than inventing a precise number.

steps.title: State the evidence
steps.text: List the main positive, negative and balanced limb leads.

steps.title: Test the estimate
steps.text: Check that the proposed vector is compatible with those projections.

steps.title: Check acquisition
steps.text: Reassess electrode labels and placement when the pattern is unexpected.

steps.title: Integrate cautiously
steps.text: Interpret axis alongside width, morphology, prior ECGs and clinical context.

example.question: Supplemental example: I is negative, II positive and aVR positive. What region is consistent with all three signs?
working: Negative I places the vector away from the leftward half-plane.
Positive II restricts it to −30° through +150°.
Positive aVR restricts it to the half-plane centred on −150°.
The overlapping rightward region is approximately +120° to +150°.
example.answer: A rightward axis region around +120° to +150°; the source demonstrates an approximate +135° example.

pitfalls: Listing an axis category without its supporting leads.
Using an axis association as a definitive disease diagnosis.
Ignoring possible electrode interchange when findings are inconsistent.

practice.prompt: If your proposed axis predicts a positive lead I but the recorded QRS in I is clearly negative, what should you do?
options: Recheck the estimate and recording quality
practice.explanation: The estimate should be compatible with the observed projections; inconsistency warrants review.
practice.hint: Test the geometry against the measured lead polarity.

practice.prompt: Right-axis deviation by itself proves which diagnosis?
practice.explanation: Several physiological, pathological and technical factors can produce a rightward axis.
practice.hint: An association is not a diagnosis.

objectives.mastery: Explain an axis estimate from multiple leads, check for contradictory evidence and describe why clinical and technical context remain necessary.

glossary.definition: A 180° region of possible vector directions constrained by one lead’s polarity.
Incorrect connection of labelled electrodes, potentially altering ECG appearances.
Considering several possible explanations for a described ECG finding.

deepDive.title: Interrogate unexpected combinations
deepDive.text: An axis estimate belongs inside a complete ECG interpretation. If the direction seems unexpected, ask whether the limb leads are internally coherent, whether the P-wave pattern also appears unusual, and whether previous recordings used comparable electrode placement and calibration. The source explicitly includes swapped limb connections among possible explanations of an apparent rightward axis. Technical review is therefore part of the differential process, not an afterthought added only when the final diagnosis feels inconvenient. A correct anatomical interpretation cannot be built on an incorrect assumption about the electrical connections.

deepDive.title: Use associations as questions to investigate
deepDive.text: Axis deviation can accompany altered conduction, ventricular electrical dominance or anatomical variation. These are prompts to inspect other evidence. A leftward axis should lead you to examine QRS morphology and timing; a rightward axis should be considered alongside precordial progression, other chamber-related findings and technical quality. The angle itself does not measure ventricular mass or identify a congenital defect. In an academic defence, explain which additional findings would support or weaken each possible interpretation rather than presenting a list of conditions as if the axis had established them.

deepDive.title: Know when no stable direction is defensible
deepDive.text: The source describes an indeterminate axis when the limb-lead complexes are all approximately balanced. In practice, uncertainty can also arise when signals are too small or complex to assign a consistent net direction. Distinguish this from an extreme axis: an extreme direction is an interpretable vector in a particular region, while an indeterminate result means that a reliable direction has not been established. State the reason for uncertainty, review the source tracing and, where appropriate, compare a technically satisfactory repeat. Precision in the wording is more useful than an unsupported exact angle.

guidedExercise.prompt: You estimate a rightward axis from one tracing, but the repeat has a very different limb-lead pattern and the electrode connections were not documented. What should your next explanatory step be?
steps: Confirm lead labels, physical connections and recording quality.
Compare P-wave orientation and limb-lead relationships as well as QRS polarity.
Re-estimate the axis on a technically satisfactory recording.
Discuss possible biological associations only after deciding that the electrical views are trustworthy.
guidedExercise.answer: Treat the apparent change as unresolved until technical comparability is checked; do not label a new anatomical or conduction abnormality from the angle alone.
guidedExercise.explanation: The source’s technical and clinical associations require integration. This exercise tests the order of reasoning rather than a diagnostic rule based on a single axis value.

title: Supraventricular arrhythmias
sourceFilename: D1-4. supraventricular arrhythmias DipECG amended Mar 2026.pdf
summary: Differentiate atrial and junctional rhythm patterns using rate, regularity, P-wave morphology and atrioventricular relationships.

objectives.title: Classify sinus-rate variation and changing atrial pacemaker patterns
objectives.why: An irregular rhythm is not automatically atrial fibrillation, and a fast rhythm is not automatically paroxysmal SVT.
know: Sinus-origin rhythms retain an atrial activation pattern compatible with the sinus node. The course describes a usual adult sinus rate of 60–100 bpm, sinus bradycardia below 60 bpm and sinus tachycardia above 100 bpm. These are rate descriptions, not complete explanations. Sleep, exercise, autonomic tone and clinical illness can influence the rate, so the significance depends on the setting rather than the label alone.

Respiratory sinus arrhythmia describes cyclical variation in sinus timing, typically speeding with inspiration and slowing with expiration. P-wave morphology remains compatible with sinus activation even though consecutive intervals vary. Compare the pattern over a sufficiently long strip; a short segment can exaggerate the appearance of randomness. Atrial and ventricular timing should still be assessed separately if conduction is not one-to-one.

A wandering atrial pacemaker pattern has changing P-wave shapes and an irregular atrial rhythm, generally at a normal or slow rate in the source examples. The changing morphology reflects changing atrial activation rather than the absence of organised P waves. Establish what atrial activity is actually visible before naming the rhythm. Distinguish gradual sinus variation from isolated premature beats, sustained focal atrial tachycardia and disorganised atrial activity. None of these distinctions requires a treatment recommendation: the first learning task is to describe the electrical evidence accurately.

steps.title: Measure the rate
steps.text: Calculate atrial and ventricular rate where the relationship is not obvious.

steps.title: Inspect P-wave morphology
steps.text: Ask whether it is stable and sinus-compatible or changes from beat to beat.

steps.title: Characterise the irregularity
steps.text: Look for cyclical variation, isolated early beats or less organised timing.

steps.title: Name the pattern proportionately
steps.text: Do not infer a more specific mechanism than the available atrial evidence supports.

example.question: Supplemental example: the rate varies gradually with breathing and the P-wave shape remains consistent.
working: The timing change is cyclical rather than isolated prematurity.
The atrial morphology remains sinus-compatible.
example.answer: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is a plausible description in the appropriate clinical context.

pitfalls: Equating every irregular pulse with AF.
Diagnosing an atrial focus from rate alone.
Calling sinus tachycardia harmless without considering why it is present.

practice.prompt: Which feature supports respiratory sinus arrhythmia rather than AF?
options: Cyclical timing variation with consistent sinus P waves
Complete absence of organised atrial activity
practice.explanation: The atrial activation pattern remains organised and sinus-compatible while its timing varies with respiration.
practice.hint: Look at both timing and P-wave shape.

practice.prompt: A rate of 110 bpm with sinus-compatible P waves should initially be described as:
practice.explanation: The source uses a sinus rate above 100 bpm as sinus tachycardia. Its cause requires context.
practice.hint: Preserve the sinus-origin evidence while naming the rate.

objectives.mastery: Differentiate sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, respiratory sinus arrhythmia and a changing atrial-pacemaker pattern from their supplied features.

glossary.definition: A sinus-origin rhythm with a rate above the usual adult resting range.
Variation in timing between sinus-origin activations.
An atrial rhythm pattern with changing P-wave morphology and irregular atrial timing.

deepDive.title: Rate is only one descriptive dimension
deepDive.text: Sinus bradycardia and sinus tachycardia retain a sinus activation sequence while changing the cycle rate. Sinus arrhythmia retains sinus-origin atrial activity with varying cycle lengths. The source notes common physiological settings such as sleep, exercise and respiratory variation, but the ECG label alone does not establish whether a particular episode is appropriate for its circumstances. Describe origin, rate and regularity separately. This produces a richer account than calling a tracing normal or abnormal solely because its numerical rate is above or below a reference value.

deepDive.title: Atrial morphology helps track the pacemaker
deepDive.text: A wandering atrial pacemaker pattern has changing P-wave configurations together with variable atrial timing and a relatively slow or ordinary overall rate in the source description. Compare like with like in the same lead: different leads normally show different views of the same atrial activation. An apparent change caused only by switching the displayed lead is not evidence of a changing pacemaker. Inspect whether the atrial shape changes within a continuous lead and whether PR timing changes with it. These observations connect the waveform to a changing activation origin rather than to rate alone.

deepDive.title: Distinguish gradual variation from isolated prematurity
deepDive.text: A rhythm that gradually speeds and slows is different from an otherwise regular sequence interrupted by an early atrial event. Plot successive PP intervals mentally or on a time-labelled strip and inspect the P-wave shapes. The first pattern may support sinus-rate variation; the second raises a premature atrial impulse as a different possibility. The source connects respiratory sinus variation with inspiration and expiration, but a static ECG without a respiratory record cannot prove that linkage. Use language that matches what was actually observed rather than adding a cause that was not recorded.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical single-lead strip has similar P-wave shapes while PP intervals change gradually from 0.9 to 0.75 s and back. There is no recorded respiratory signal. What can you describe and what remains unproven?
steps: Confirm that the comparison is within one continuous lead.
Describe similar P-wave morphology and gradual variation in atrial cycle length.
Check that the P–QRS relationship remains consistent.
Avoid claiming a demonstrated respiratory relationship without accompanying respiratory information.
guidedExercise.answer: Sinus-arrhythmia-like timing is supported if the other sinus features are present; respiratory linkage is plausible in an appropriate setting but is not established by these observations.
guidedExercise.explanation: The answer preserves the distinction between rhythm description and an inferred physiological cause. An isolated early P wave would require a different analysis.

objectives.title: Recognise a premature atrial beat and a concealed premature P wave
objectives.why: An early atrial depolarisation can distort the preceding T wave or interrupt an otherwise regular rhythm without being a ventricular ectopic beat.
know: A premature atrial beat originates in atrial tissue outside the sinus node and occurs earlier than the next expected sinus activation. The source lists several synonymous terms, including atrial ectopic, premature atrial contraction and atrial extrasystole. The key observation is premature atrial activity, usually with a P-wave shape different from the surrounding sinus P waves.

The premature P may fall on the preceding T wave and be partly hidden by it. Compare that T wave with neighbouring beats and look for a reproducible extra notch or changed contour at the expected time of the early atrial activation. If ventricular conduction follows its usual route, the subsequent QRS may resemble the surrounding complexes. However, a premature atrial impulse can also conduct aberrantly or fail to conduct, so a narrow QRS is helpful evidence rather than an absolute requirement.

Assess the rhythm in sequence: establish the underlying cycle length, identify the early atrial event, determine whether and how it is followed by QRS, and describe the subsequent pause. Do not classify every pause as sinus arrest or every wide premature complex as ventricular without inspecting the atrial activity. A longer rhythm strip and multiple leads can clarify a partially concealed P wave. The supplied teaching example illustrates a pattern; a clinical recording can remain uncertain when noise or overlapping waves prevent a reliable atrial measurement.

steps.title: Establish the background rhythm
steps.text: Compare several preceding sinus cycles.

steps.title: Search for the early P
steps.text: Look before the early QRS and on the preceding T wave.

steps.title: Assess ventricular response
steps.text: Determine whether conduction is usual, aberrant or absent.

steps.title: Describe the pause
steps.text: State the observed timing rather than assuming a mechanism from the pause alone.

example.question: Supplemental example: an otherwise regular tracing contains an early, differently shaped P wave on a T wave, followed by a narrow QRS.
working: The atrial event is premature.
Its shape differs from the surrounding sinus P waves.
The QRS can be generated through the usual ventricular conduction system.
example.answer: A conducted premature atrial beat is supported by the supplied description.

pitfalls: Missing a premature P wave because it overlaps a T wave.
Assuming every premature atrial beat must have a narrow QRS.
Diagnosing a pause without first inspecting the preceding atrial event.

practice.prompt: Where may a premature atrial P wave be concealed?
practice.explanation: Premature atrial activation can occur early enough to deform the preceding T wave.
practice.hint: Compare the T-wave contour with adjacent beats.

practice.prompt: Which observation most directly supports an atrial premature beat?
options: An early P wave of different morphology
A heart rate of exactly 60 bpm
The presence of six chest electrodes
practice.explanation: The premature atrial activation and its changed morphology are direct atrial evidence.
practice.hint: Identify the event that happens early.

objectives.mastery: Identify the premature atrial activation, its possible concealment and its relationship to ventricular conduction.

glossary.definition: An atrial depolarisation arising earlier than expected outside the sinus node.
A P wave partly or wholly obscured by another waveform.
Altered ventricular activation of a supraventricular impulse through an abnormal conduction pattern.

deepDive.title: Prematurity is a timing judgement
deepDive.text: A premature atrial beat occurs earlier than the next atrial event expected from the preceding rhythm. Establish that expectation before calling a beat premature. Compare PP intervals and inspect whether the early P differs from the preceding sinus P waves in the same lead. The QRS may still look similar because the ventricles can be activated through the usual conduction route after the early atrial impulse. A similar QRS does not therefore exclude atrial ectopy; the crucial evidence is often the atrial timing rather than the ventricular shape.

deepDive.title: Search the preceding T wave
deepDive.text: The source emphasises that an early P wave may overlap the T wave before it. This can produce a notch or altered contour that is easy to overlook if attention begins only at the apparent pause afterwards. Compare that T wave with neighbouring T waves and inspect another lead where atrial activity may be clearer. A non-conducted early atrial impulse can create a pause in the ventricular sequence without proving sinus arrest or AV block. The visible pause is the starting observation, not the final mechanism.

deepDive.title: Describe the ventricular response separately
deepDive.text: After identifying a premature atrial event, determine whether it is followed by a QRS, whether ventricular activation remains narrow or appears altered, and how the subsequent timing changes. Early arrival may meet the conduction system in a different recovery state, so the ventricular response need not look identical every time. The source introduces a normal QRS and a pause as a simple teaching example, but those features should not be treated as mandatory in every real atrial premature beat. An interpretation is stronger when the atrial evidence and ventricular response are both made explicit.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical otherwise regular strip has one T wave with an extra notch, followed by a long RR interval. What observations would help distinguish a concealed premature atrial event from a primary pause mechanism?
steps: Compare the notched T wave with adjacent T waves in the same lead.
Look for an atrial waveform occurring earlier than the expected next sinus P.
Inspect another lead for the timing and polarity of that possible P wave.
Determine whether a QRS response follows the early atrial event and how later P waves resume.
guidedExercise.answer: An early concealed P wave and its subsequent conduction behaviour would support a premature atrial mechanism; the long RR interval alone cannot identify its cause.
guidedExercise.explanation: This is a reasoning exercise rather than a diagnosis from an unseen image. It directs attention to the atrial event that may be hidden before the apparent pause.

objectives.title: Distinguish sinus tachycardia from focal atrial tachycardia
objectives.why: The atrial activation pattern and onset behaviour are more informative than a fast rate by itself.
know: Sinus tachycardia retains sinus-compatible P-wave morphology and often changes gradually with physiological demand or an underlying clinical cause. In focal atrial tachycardia, atrial activation arises from a non-sinus focus, so P-wave morphology commonly differs from the person’s sinus tracing. The source illustrates atrial rates around 120–250 bpm, but rate ranges overlap between mechanisms and should not be treated as decisive classifiers.

Identify whether each visible P precedes QRS and whether the atrial and ventricular rates are the same. Atrial tachycardia can continue with incomplete conduction to the ventricles; the atrial rhythm can therefore be faster than the ventricular rhythm. P waves may merge with preceding T waves, particularly at fast rates. Lead V1 can be useful for atrial assessment in the course examples, but no single lead guarantees that the atrial activity will be visible.

The lecture contrasts gradual sinus onset with sudden atrial-tachycardia onset. That is a useful example, not a universal rule: automatic focal atrial tachycardia can accelerate and decelerate gradually. This qualification is supported by the ESC guideline. Compare the current P-wave pattern with a sinus recording where available, inspect onset and termination if captured, and report uncertainty when waves are obscured. These observations support rhythm interpretation; the learner should not infer a treatment or a benign cause from the rate pattern alone.

steps.title: Identify atrial activity
steps.text: Inspect P waves and compare them with the available sinus baseline.

steps.title: Separate atrial and ventricular rates
steps.text: Count atrial deflections and QRS complexes over the same interval.

steps.title: Examine onset if available
steps.text: Describe sudden or gradual change without treating it as an absolute mechanism test.

steps.title: Conclude with limitations
steps.text: Use a descriptive supraventricular-tachycardia label if the atrial evidence is insufficient.

example.question: Supplemental example: non-sinus P waves occur regularly at 180/min while QRS complexes occur at 90/min.
working: The atrial rate is twice the ventricular rate.
Not every atrial activation is followed by QRS.
The non-sinus P-wave pattern supports an atrial tachycardia mechanism.
example.answer: Atrial tachycardia with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction is supported by the supplied description.

pitfalls: Calling any gradual tachycardia sinus without reviewing P waves.
Assuming the ventricular rate equals the atrial rate.
Treating a teaching rate range as a diagnostic boundary.

practice.prompt: Which finding supports focal atrial tachycardia over sinus tachycardia?
options: P-wave morphology differing from the person’s sinus pattern
Upright R in lead I alone
practice.explanation: A changed atrial activation pattern supports a non-sinus origin, whereas rates overlap.
practice.hint: Compare atrial morphology with a sinus baseline.

practice.prompt: Can every atrial tachycardia be recognised by sudden onset?
options: No; automatic focal atrial tachycardia can show gradual acceleration
Yes, if the ECG is recorded at 25 mm/s
No atrial tachycardia ever starts suddenly
practice.explanation: The sudden-onset teaching contrast has exceptions, including warm-up and cool-down with automatic focal AT.
practice.hint: Different atrial mechanisms can behave differently.

objectives.mastery: Use atrial morphology, atrioventricular relationship and onset behaviour together, including the limitation of the sudden-onset rule.

glossary.definition: An organised atrial tachycardia arising from a localised non-sinus origin.
Gradual acceleration that can occur with an automatic tachycardia mechanism.
The relation between the number of atrial activations and conducted ventricular activations.

references.label: Supplementary qualification: 2019 ESC SVT guideline, section 9.1.1.1 (automatic AT may warm up/cool down)

deepDive.title: Compare atrial identity, not just speed
deepDive.text: Sinus tachycardia and focal atrial tachycardia can both produce a fast ventricular rhythm. The source compares the shape and timing of P waves, the behaviour at onset and termination, and the atrioventricular relationship. A P wave that resembles the person’s baseline sinus P in the same lead supports one interpretation; a reproducibly different atrial activation pattern supports another. Rate ranges overlap, so choosing a mechanism from speed alone is unreliable. Begin with a descriptive account of atrial activity and acknowledge when it is obscured.

deepDive.title: Use onset and termination as evidence, not absolutes
deepDive.text: The source contrasts gradual sinus acceleration or slowing with abrupt paroxysmal tachycardia. This is useful pattern evidence, but it should not be inflated into a universal law that all focal atrial tachycardias start and stop abruptly. Some mechanisms can show a warm-up or cool-down pattern. A short strip captured only after the rhythm is established may contain no onset information at all. State whether the transition was actually recorded before using it to support the proposed mechanism.

deepDive.title: Look for atrial activity through ventricular events
deepDive.text: Atrial tachycardia may continue with different conduction ratios, so the atrial rate and ventricular response can differ. Search for P waves partly superimposed on T waves and compare leads where the atrial signal is clearer, including the source’s suggested attention to V1. When a regular fast tracing has no confidently separable atrial activity, an appropriately broad description is more defensible than a confident focal-mechanism label. Clinical circumstances may suggest reasons for sinus acceleration, but the rhythm strip alone does not establish exercise, anxiety, anaemia or any other cause.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical tachycardia has a ventricular rate of 150/min. P waves appear different from baseline, and two atrial events are visible for some ventricular responses. No onset was recorded. How should the evidence be organised?
steps: State that rate alone does not distinguish the mechanism.
Compare the atrial morphology with baseline in the same lead.
Count atrial events separately from QRS complexes and describe any non-one-to-one relationship.
Avoid calling the onset abrupt or gradual when the transition was not captured.
guidedExercise.answer: Different atrial morphology and an atrial-to-ventricular ratio greater than one support an atrial tachycardia-type interpretation, but mechanism and clinical cause require further evidence.
guidedExercise.explanation: The strength of the answer comes from the observed atrial evidence. An unrecorded onset cannot be used as a supporting fact, and a ventricular rate of 150/min is not a unique diagnostic signature.

objectives.title: Compare AVNRT and AVRT without overclaiming a surface-ECG mechanism
objectives.why: The surface ECG can suggest a re-entry mechanism, but overlapping appearances often justify a broader description.
know: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia describes a clinical pattern of abrupt, rapid, usually regular tachycardia. Typical examples in this lecture are AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia and AV re-entrant tachycardia. A narrow QRS indicates rapid ventricular activation through the usual conduction system in many such rhythms, but QRS width alone does not prove their exact mechanism. A supraventricular rhythm can also be broad because ventricular conduction is altered.

In typical AVNRT, the re-entry circuit involves AV nodal pathways and atrial and ventricular activation can be nearly simultaneous. P waves may be hidden in QRS or appear as small additional deflections just after it, including a pseudo r-prime in V1 or pseudo S in inferior leads. In usual orthodromic AVRT, the circuit uses the AV node in one direction and an accessory pathway in the other. Retrograde atrial activation may be visible after QRS. A concealed accessory pathway may leave no obvious pre-excitation in sinus rhythm.

Compare the tachycardia with a sinus ECG where available, and inspect the timing of atrial deflections rather than relying on a rate range or a single tiny notch. The source itself warns that the P wave may be impossible to identify and a specific PSVT mechanism may remain uncertain. A justified report can therefore describe a regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia without declaring AVNRT or AVRT proven. This lesson teaches pattern recognition and uncertainty, not drug selection or an instruction to terminate a tachycardia.

steps.title: Describe the rhythm first
steps.text: Record rate, regularity and QRS width.

steps.title: Search for retrograde atrial activity
steps.text: Inspect just after QRS and compare V1 and inferior leads with the sinus tracing.

steps.title: Link the possible circuits
steps.text: Contrast AV nodal re-entry with an accessory-pathway-dependent circuit.

steps.title: Keep the label proportionate
steps.text: State when the surface ECG supports only a broader regular-SVT description.

example.question: Supplemental example: a regular 180 bpm narrow-complex rhythm has no reliably identifiable P waves. Can it be called proven AVNRT?
working: The rate, regularity and narrow QRS support a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
Hidden atrial activity is compatible with typical AVNRT but is not uniquely diagnostic.
example.answer: No. AVNRT may be suspected, but the supplied evidence does not prove the mechanism.

pitfalls: Treating the absence of sinus pre-excitation as exclusion of AVRT.
Using a rigid RP cut-off as an infallible mechanism test.
Calling every QRS notch a retrograde P wave.

practice.prompt: What is an essential component of an AVRT circuit?
options: A sinus pause in every cycle
An always-visible delta wave during sinus rhythm
practice.explanation: An accessory pathway forms part of the AVRT circuit; it may conduct only retrogradely and be concealed on a sinus ECG.
practice.hint: Distinguish the circuit anatomy from whether it is visible in sinus rhythm.

practice.prompt: When atrial activity cannot be resolved in a regular narrow-complex tachycardia, the best response is to:
options: Use a supported descriptive label and record uncertainty
Call it atrial fibrillation solely because P is not seen
practice.explanation: A proportionate description is more reliable than a mechanism label unsupported by visible atrial evidence.
practice.hint: Match diagnostic specificity to the evidence available.

objectives.mastery: Explain the two re-entry concepts, recognise supportive atrial-timing clues and acknowledge when the ECG cannot distinguish them.

glossary.definition: Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia, involving re-entry through AV nodal pathways.
Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia using an accessory pathway as part of its circuit.
An accessory pathway without manifest antegrade pre-excitation on the sinus ECG, often conducting retrogradely.

deepDive.title: Re-entry explains repeated activation
deepDive.text: The source diagrams distinguish a re-entry circuit involving AV nodal pathways from a larger circuit involving an accessory atrioventricular pathway. In typical AVNRT, atrial and ventricular activation can occur nearly together, making retrograde atrial activity hard to separate from QRS. In orthodromic AVRT, ventricular activation usually proceeds through the normal AV conduction route while the accessory pathway participates in the return limb. These mechanisms explain why a supraventricular tachycardia can be rapid, regular and often narrow without its atrial activity being obvious on every surface tracing.

deepDive.title: Interpret small deflections by comparison
deepDive.text: A pseudo-r in V1 or pseudo-s in an inferior lead can reflect retrograde atrial activation superimposed near the ventricular complex. The source compares tachycardia with sinus rhythm to show why an extra small deflection is easier to recognise when it was absent before. Do not label every terminal notch as a retrograde P wave. Baseline ventricular morphology, noise and overlap can produce uncertainty. Compare consistent repeated events across leads and ask whether the proposed atrial timing fits the rest of the rhythm.

deepDive.title: A narrow regular tachycardia need not have a named circuit
deepDive.text: The source explicitly recognises that atrial activity may be too obscured to distinguish tachycardia types confidently. A concealed accessory pathway may participate in AVRT without producing an obvious pre-excitation pattern during sinus rhythm. Conversely, timing distinctions such as a short RP interval are supportive clues rather than a universal mechanism test. In an educational report, separate the broad rhythm description from a proposed mechanism and state the evidence for that proposal. This lesson teaches circuit reasoning, not unsupervised pharmacological testing or treatment decisions.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical regular narrow-complex tachycardia has no clearly separable P waves. A tiny terminal deflection is seen in V1, but no baseline sinus ECG is available. Must you name AVNRT?
steps: Describe regularity, ventricular rate and QRS width first.
Identify the small V1 deflection as a possible, not proven, atrial event.
Note the absence of a baseline comparison and the possibility of overlapping atrial activity.
Use a broader supraventricular tachycardia description if the mechanism cannot be established.
guidedExercise.answer: No. AVNRT may be a consideration, but a regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia description with an uncertain mechanism is more defensible on the supplied evidence.
guidedExercise.explanation: The source cautions that surface P-wave identification can be impossible. Avoiding an unsupported circuit label is accurate interpretation, not failure to recognise a rhythm.

objectives.title: Recognise junctional rhythms and distinguish AV dissociation from complete block
objectives.why: Independent atrial and ventricular activity is an observation; its mechanism is not always complete atrioventricular block.
know: Pacemaker activity can arise outside the sinus node. The course discusses junctional escape and accelerated junctional rhythms. An escape rhythm occurs when a subsidiary focus takes over after a higher pacemaker slows or fails to activate the ventricles in time. An accelerated junctional rhythm occurs when junctional automaticity exceeds the competing sinus rate. These descriptions concern the relationship between pacemaker rates and activation, not simply whether P waves are easy to see.

With retrograde atrial conduction, a P wave may occur before, within or after the QRS and can be negative in the inferior leads. If sinus atrial activity continues independently, P waves can march through at their own rate while the junctional rhythm activates the ventricles. Compare PP and RR timing separately, and inspect whether any P occurs at a time when it can conduct. A short strip may obscure the relationship.

AV dissociation means that atria and ventricles are activated independently. Complete AV block is one cause, but the two terms are not interchangeable. A junctional focus can outrun a slow sinus rhythm, producing dissociation without proof of failed atrioventricular conduction. The source explicitly demonstrates this distinction. State the observed atrial and ventricular rates, P-wave direction and timing, QRS morphology, and whether the available recording actually establishes block. Clinical significance depends on the wider context and is not determined by the rhythm label alone.

steps.title: Find atrial activity
steps.text: Look for P waves before, within or after QRS and through longer strips.

steps.title: Compare the clocks
steps.text: Measure PP and RR intervals independently.

steps.title: Describe competition or escape
steps.text: Assess which pacemaker appears to control ventricular activation.

steps.title: Separate observation from mechanism
steps.text: Use AV dissociation without automatically asserting complete AV block.

example.question: Supplemental example: sinus P waves occur at 45/min and narrow QRS complexes at 50/min, with changing P–QRS relationships.
working: The atria and ventricles have different regular rates.
The junctional rhythm may outrun the slower sinus node.
Independent timing alone does not prove that an appropriately timed P wave would fail to conduct.
example.answer: AV dissociation with a possible junctional escape rhythm; complete AV block is not established by the supplied information alone.

pitfalls: Using AV dissociation as a synonym for complete AV block.
Assuming a P wave after QRS cannot be atrial activity.
Ignoring atrial activity because ventricular complexes are regular.

practice.prompt: AV dissociation means:
options: Complete AV block in every case
Absence of all atrial electrical activity
Atrial rate always exactly twice ventricular rate
practice.explanation: Dissociation describes independent activation; several mechanisms can produce it.
practice.hint: Describe the relationship before naming its cause.

practice.prompt: A retrograde P wave in a junctional rhythm may appear:
practice.explanation: Its visible timing depends on the relative timing of atrial and ventricular activation.
practice.hint: The atria and ventricles may activate close together.

objectives.mastery: Identify a possible junctional rhythm and explain why AV dissociation alone does not establish complete AV block.

glossary.definition: A subsidiary junctional rhythm that activates the heart when higher pacemaker activity is too slow or fails to arrive in time.
A junctional rhythm with increased automaticity relative to the competing sinus pacemaker.
Independent activation of atria and ventricles.

deepDive.title: An escape can be protective rather than premature
deepDive.text: An escape rhythm arises when a lower pacemaker takes over after the usual dominant activity is too slow or fails to reach the ventricles effectively. Its timing is late relative to the preceding rhythm, unlike a premature ectopic beat that arrives early. The source contrasts junctional escape with accelerated junctional rhythm, in which junctional activity can compete with or outpace sinus activity. Describing the timing and relative atrial and ventricular rates helps explain why the same general origin can appear in different rhythm situations.

deepDive.title: Atrial activation can appear in several positions
deepDive.text: Junctional-origin activity may reach atria retrogradely, so a P wave can occur before, within or after the QRS, depending on timing and conduction. A negative inferior P wave after QRS can therefore be more informative than simply asking whether a P is visible before it. The absence of a separately visible P does not prove atrial inactivity. Follow the expected atrial sequence in other leads and inspect whether atrial and ventricular timing remain linked or instead drift relative to one another.

deepDive.title: AV dissociation describes independence, not its sole cause
deepDive.text: AV dissociation means that atrial and ventricular activity are not maintaining their usual consistent relationship. The source provides examples in which competing pacemakers and timing prevent atrial impulses from conducting, without demonstrating pathological complete AV block. Compare atrial and ventricular rates, look for changing PR relationships, and examine whether a P wave ever occurs at a time when conduction could be assessed. A short segment showing independence does not by itself establish that every atrial impulse is blocked under all circumstances. State the observation and qualify the mechanism.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical strip has a junctional-like ventricular rhythm at 55/min and sinus P waves at 50/min. The P waves move through different positions relative to QRS. Does the independence prove complete AV block?
steps: Count atrial and ventricular activity separately.
Recognise that the ventricular pacemaker is slightly faster than the atrial one.
Describe the varying atrioventricular relationship as AV dissociation.
Consider competition and timing before claiming failure of all possible antegrade conduction.
guidedExercise.answer: The strip demonstrates AV dissociation, but that observation alone does not prove complete AV block; a competing junctional rhythm is an alternative explanation.
guidedExercise.explanation: The relative rates and changing positions are central to the reasoning. The example mirrors the source’s distinction between electrical independence and an automatically inferred block mechanism.

objectives.title: Identify the ECG pattern of atrial fibrillation and its limitations
objectives.why: Recognising disorganised atrial activity requires more than noticing an irregular ventricular rhythm.
know: Atrial fibrillation involves disorganised atrial electrical activation rather than a consistent repeating sinus P-wave pattern. The course contrasts sinus rhythm with AF, highlighting absent discrete P waves, fibrillatory activity and an irregular ventricular response when atrioventricular conduction varies. Inspect the atrial baseline in several leads and over enough time to avoid mistaking noise or one poorly seen P wave for fibrillation.

Fibrillatory deflections can be coarse or fine. Their amplitude does not by itself establish severity, duration or embolic risk. V1 may display atrial activity more clearly in the source examples, while other leads help distinguish baseline noise from genuine electrical activity. The ventricular rate may be rapid, usual or slow; report it separately using a timed QRS count when the rhythm is irregular.

An irregular ventricular rhythm alone is not sufficient to diagnose AF. Sinus arrhythmia, premature beats, multifocal atrial activity and flutter with variable conduction can also be irregular. Conversely, ventricular pacing or advanced conduction disease can make the ventricular rhythm more regular despite ongoing fibrillation, so the usual irregularity rule has exceptions. Use the visible atrial evidence and the whole recording, and seek appropriate clinical interpretation when the pattern remains uncertain. Temporal labels such as paroxysmal or permanent require history and clinical decisions, not a single short ECG strip.

steps.title: Inspect the atrial baseline
steps.text: Look for a reproducible P-wave pattern versus disorganised atrial activity.

steps.title: Assess RR variation
steps.text: Compare multiple intervals and note whether the response is irregularly irregular.

steps.title: Calculate the average ventricular rate
steps.text: Use a known-duration strip rather than one RR interval.

steps.title: State uncertainty and context
steps.text: Distinguish AF-pattern recognition from decisions about duration, risk or treatment.

example.question: Supplemental example: a ten-second strip has no consistent P waves, disorganised atrial activity and 15 irregularly spaced QRS complexes.
working: The atrial pattern supports AF.
The ventricular response is irregular.
The average ventricular rate is 15 × 6.
example.answer: The supplied description supports AF with an average ventricular rate of approximately 90 bpm.

pitfalls: Diagnosing AF from irregularity alone.
Using coarse versus fine baseline activity as a direct measure of clinical severity.
Assigning a temporal AF category from one short tracing without history.

practice.prompt: Which combined pattern most supports AF in an otherwise interpretable recording?
options: Consistent sinus P waves with cyclical RR changes
No repeating discrete P-wave pattern, disorganised atrial activity and irregular RR intervals
Sawtooth atrial waves exactly every 200 ms with fixed 2:1 conduction
One early P wave followed by a pause
practice.explanation: The combined atrial and ventricular evidence supports AF more strongly than irregularity alone.
practice.hint: Look for both disorganised atrial activation and its ventricular response.

practice.prompt: An irregular ten-second strip contains 18 QRS complexes. Estimate the mean ventricular rate.
practice.hint: Count ventricular activations across the full known interval.

objectives.mastery: Describe the atrial evidence, irregularity and average ventricular rate supporting an AF pattern, with at least one important exception.

glossary.definition: Disorganised atrial electrical activation without a consistent repeating discrete P-wave pattern.
The irregular atrial electrical activity associated with AF.
A rhythm description in which successive cycle lengths vary without a repeating pattern.

deepDive.title: Combine atrial and ventricular evidence
deepDive.text: The introductory AF pattern combines disorganised atrial activity, absence of consistent discrete P waves and an irregular ventricular response. These observations work together. Irregular RR intervals alone can arise from other rhythms, while failure to see P in a single noisy lead is not sufficient evidence that organised atrial activity is absent. Examine a continuous rhythm strip and more than one lead where available. State the duration and quality of what was observed rather than implying that a brief sample characterises every moment of a longer recording.

deepDive.title: Coarse and fine describe visibility
deepDive.text: The source uses coarse and fine AF to distinguish more obvious from lower-amplitude atrial deflections. These are descriptions of the visible signal, not independent diagnoses or a measure of clinical severity. A nearly flat baseline between ventricular complexes does not automatically mean there is no atrial electrical activity. Lead orientation, amplitude and recording quality affect how well it is seen. The source highlights V1 as a potentially useful view, but the best evidence should be assessed across the actual available recording rather than assuming one lead will always settle the question.

deepDive.title: Describe the ventricular response without adding clinical conclusions
deepDive.text: A ventricular response may be described as rapid, slow or otherwise characterised by its measured rate, but those labels require the actual rate calculation and observation window. A short-strip estimate does not establish symptoms, haemodynamic effects or the cause of the rhythm. Do not use the source’s introductory historical frequency figures or simplified temporal categories as current patient-management rules. This objective is about recognising and explaining an ECG pattern. Clinical classification and management require history, duration information and appropriate clinical assessment beyond the waveform description.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical ten-second tracing contains 18 QRS complexes with markedly variable RR intervals. No consistent P-wave sequence is identifiable in several suitable leads, and irregular atrial deflections are visible. Write a cautious pattern description.
steps: Calculate the average ventricular response as 18 × 6 = 108/min.
Describe the RR variability instead of assigning the same cycle rate to every beat.
Combine the ventricular findings with the absence of a reproducible P-wave sequence and irregular atrial activity.
Do not infer symptom severity or long-term AF classification from the short recording.
guidedExercise.answer: An AF-compatible ECG pattern with an irregular ventricular response averaging approximately 108/min over the observed ten seconds.
guidedExercise.explanation: The pattern conclusion rests on both atrial and ventricular evidence. The average rate is explicitly tied to the sample duration, and the description does not claim a clinical history that was not supplied.

objectives.title: Recognise atrial flutter and calculate the ventricular response
objectives.why: Flutter can be concealed within an apparently regular tachycardia, especially when every second atrial activation conducts.
know: Atrial flutter is an organised rapid atrial rhythm. Typical flutter commonly involves a large re-entry circuit in the right atrium, but not all flutter mechanisms or surface patterns are identical. The course demonstrates atrial activity near 300/min and repetitive flutter deflections that may have a sawtooth appearance in inferior leads. Inspect the whole baseline rather than assuming that every visible small deflection is an ordinary P wave.

The ventricular rate depends on atrioventricular conduction. With an atrial rate of 300/min, 2:1 conduction gives a ventricular rate of 150/min and 4:1 conduction gives 75/min. If the conduction ratio changes, the ventricular response becomes irregular despite an organised atrial rhythm. In 2:1 flutter, one atrial deflection can be hidden in QRS or T, making a regular resting ventricular rate near 150/min an important clue rather than proof.

Compare leads II, III, aVF and V1 as useful examples of places to inspect atrial activity. Search for repeating deflections at a faster rate than QRS, including features concealed within the ventricular complexes. Atypical flutter, prior atrial interventions and other factors can modify the classic appearance. A rate of 150/min can also occur in sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT or other rhythms. If atrial activity cannot be established, retain an appropriately broad description. This objective teaches recognition and rate relationships, not an intervention to reveal or terminate a rhythm.

steps.title: Find organised atrial activity
steps.text: Look for repeated flutter deflections independent of the QRS count.

steps.title: Measure atrial cycle length
steps.text: At 25 mm/s, one large square between deflections corresponds to 300/min.

steps.title: Determine conduction ratio
steps.text: Compare the number of atrial activations with QRS complexes.

steps.title: Check for concealed waves
steps.text: Inspect QRS and T for the missing atrial component in a possible 2:1 pattern.

example.question: Supplemental example: atrial flutter is established at 300/min, with four atrial cycles for each QRS. What ventricular rate is expected?
working: The atrial rate is 300/min.
Four atrial activations correspond to one ventricular activation.
example.answer: Approximately 75 bpm with 4:1 atrioventricular conduction.

pitfalls: Treating a regular ventricular rate near 150/min as proof of flutter.
Assuming that flutter always gives a regular ventricular rhythm.
Missing flutter waves hidden within QRS or T.

practice.prompt: An established flutter rhythm has an atrial rate of 300/min and 2:1 conduction. Calculate the expected ventricular rate.
practice.hint: Divide atrial rate by the number of atrial activations per ventricular activation.

practice.prompt: Can flutter produce an irregular ventricular rhythm?
options: Yes, when the AV conduction ratio varies
Only if there are no atrial waves
Only at a paper speed of 50 mm/s
practice.explanation: Organised atrial activity can coexist with variable conduction to the ventricles and irregular RR intervals.
practice.hint: Separate atrial organisation from ventricular response.

objectives.mastery: Identify a flutter pattern when atrial evidence is supplied, calculate fixed-ratio responses and recognise concealed or variable conduction.

glossary.definition: An organised rapid atrial tachyarrhythmia, commonly sustained by macro-re-entry.
A repetitive atrial deflection generated during atrial flutter.
Two atrial activations for each conducted ventricular activation.

deepDive.title: Measure atrial activity separately
deepDive.text: Flutter involves rapid organised atrial activity rather than the disorganised atrial signal introduced in the AF lesson. The source’s typical examples show repeating flutter waves, often conspicuous in inferior leads, with an atrial rate around 300/min. Count the atrial cycle length independently of ventricular complexes. At 25 mm/s, a 200 ms atrial cycle spans one large square and corresponds to 300 atrial events/min. A ventricular rate near 150/min is a clue to consider a 2:1 relationship, not proof of flutter without the atrial evidence.

deepDive.title: A conduction ratio explains the ventricular response
deepDive.text: If every fourth atrial cycle has a ventricular response, an atrial rate of 300/min gives a ventricular rate of about 75/min. The source page 61 enlargement makes the four atrial cycles per ventricular response visible; inspect the repeating atrial sequence through the QRS and T wave rather than counting only the obvious baseline teeth. Ratios can vary, producing an irregular ventricular rhythm even though atrial timing remains organised. This is why ventricular irregularity does not exclude flutter and why a short RR measurement should not replace a full atrial–ventricular analysis.

deepDive.title: Typical clues have limits
deepDive.text: The source concentrates on a familiar right-atrial macro-re-entry pattern and its common surface appearance. Do not extend that description to every possible flutter circuit or insist that every tracing must display an obvious textbook sawtooth in one lead. Atrial activity can overlap ventricular waveforms, especially with 2:1 conduction. Inspect II, III, aVF and V1 where available and compare a longer segment. When the atrial evidence is uncertain, describe the possible mechanism and the missing evidence instead of turning a ventricular rate or a small apparent pseudo-r into a definitive circuit diagnosis.

guidedExercise.prompt: A hypothetical recording shows atrial cycles every 200 ms. Ventricular responses alternate between every third and every fourth atrial cycle. Calculate the two corresponding ventricular cycle rates and explain why a single ventricular rate would be incomplete.
steps: Atrial rate = 60 ÷ 0.20 = 300/min.
With 3:1 conduction, the ventricular cycle is 0.60 s and its cycle rate is 100/min.
With 4:1 conduction, the ventricular cycle is 0.80 s and its cycle rate is 75/min.
Describe variable conduction and calculate a timed average separately if a representative recording duration is available.
guidedExercise.answer: The atrial rate is 300/min, with ventricular cycle rates of 100/min during 3:1 conduction and 75/min during 4:1 conduction; the overall ventricular response is variably timed.
guidedExercise.explanation: Atrial regularity and ventricular regularity are different questions. The example illustrates variable conduction without supplying enough recording duration to calculate an exact overall average ventricular rate.
