title: Bradyarrhythmias and conduction disorders
sourceFilename: D2-1 Bradycardias & conduction disorders DipECG Amended Mar 2026.pdf
summary: Separate failure of impulse formation from failure of conduction; describe atrial and ventricular activity before naming a block.

objectives.title: Distinguish sinus slowing, pauses and escape activity
objectives.why: An apparently slow rate may arise from the sinus node, hidden atrial beats, failed conduction or a protective escape rhythm. The mechanism matters more than a rate label alone.
know: Sinus bradycardia describes sinus-origin atrial activity at a slow rate. It does not, by itself, establish sinus node dysfunction. Rest, athletic conditioning, autonomic influences, medicines and clinical disease can produce similar surface appearances. A normal short recording also cannot exclude intermittent sinus node dysfunction.

The first task during a pause is to ask whether expected P waves are absent or continue without their usual QRS responses. Missing P waves suggest an atrial impulse-formation or exit problem; continuing P waves direct attention towards AV conduction. A premature P wave hidden in a preceding T wave can create an apparent pause and must be sought before choosing either explanation.

Sinoatrial exit block can produce a pause close to a multiple of the preceding sinus cycle. Sinus arrest need not preserve that relation. This is a useful timing distinction, but sinus variability and an incomplete tracing reduce certainty. The sinus node discharge itself is not directly visible on a surface ECG, so a precise mechanism may remain uncertain.

An escape beat is a later protective impulse arising below a temporarily slow or silent pacemaker. Junctional or ventricular escape activity may coexist with sinus bradycardia and produce AV dissociation. Correlate pauses with symptoms and recording context; do not turn a single pause duration into an automatic diagnosis or a treatment decision.

steps.title: Track atrial timing
steps.text: Measure successive PP intervals before, through and after the pause.

steps.title: Find all atrial events
steps.text: Inspect T waves and other leads for an early hidden P wave.

steps.title: Describe the escape
steps.text: Record whether a later QRS occurs and whether P waves relate to it.

example.question: Hypothetical teaching example: sinus PP intervals are near 1.0 s, then the next visible sinus P occurs after 2.0 s. What can be reported?
working: The pause is close to twice the baseline sinus cycle.
No premature P wave is specified, but a longer multi-lead recording is needed to exclude one.
The timing supports a possible sinoatrial exit-block pattern; it does not prove sinus-node disease.
example.answer: A sinus pause with timing compatible with sinoatrial exit block; qualify the mechanism and seek context.

pitfalls: Calling every slow sinus rhythm sinus node disease.
Calling AV dissociation complete AV block without considering competing pacemakers.

practice.prompt: What is the first useful question when a pause appears?
options: Are expected P waves missing or still marching through?
practice.explanation: Atrial timing separates absent atrial activation from failed AV conduction and exposes hidden premature atrial beats.
practice.hint: Follow the P waves.

practice.prompt: A junctional escape rhythm is slightly faster than a slow sinus rhythm. Independent P waves are visible. What is justified?
options: AV dissociation, without proving complete AV block
Complete AV block in every case
practice.explanation: Competing sinus and junctional pacemakers can dissociate without establishing that all atrial impulses are blocked.
practice.hint: Dissociation describes a relationship, not its cause.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: A later impulse from a subsidiary pacemaker when the expected dominant impulse is absent or delayed.
Failure of a sinus impulse to reach and activate the atria; the sinus discharge is not directly visible on a surface ECG.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Separate the two electrical clocks
deepDive.text: A slow ventricular rate is an observation, not yet an explanation. First identify the atrial events and measure successive PP intervals; then identify QRS complexes and measure RR intervals separately. If P waves slow or disappear, impulse formation or exit may be involved. If regular P waves continue through a ventricular pause, failed AV conduction becomes more relevant. The course also shows a junctional rhythm slightly faster than the sinus rate. In that situation the ventricles can follow an escape focus while the slower atrial rhythm continues independently, without demonstrating complete AV block.

deepDive.title: Analyse a pause as a sequence
deepDive.text: Start several cycles before a pause and continue beyond its termination. Compare the prolonged PP interval with the preceding sinus cycle, but use the actual neighbouring measurements rather than one conveniently selected interval. A near-multiple can support sinoatrial exit block; a non-multiple may fit arrest or another disturbance. Neither relation records the sinus-node discharge directly. The source itself notes that definitions of sinus pauses vary and that some pauses are not pathological. Search the preceding T wave for an early atrial deflection before deciding that the sinus impulse was absent.

deepDive.title: Explain what terminates the pause
deepDive.text: The first beat after the pause contains useful information. A visible P followed by a familiar QRS may represent resumed sinus conduction. A later QRS without an appropriately timed preceding P may be an escape event; its width and relation to atrial activity help describe its origin. An escape beat is late relative to the expected rhythm, whereas a premature beat arrives early. The source’s post-tachycardia example links a prolonged recovery interval, escape activity and later sinus recovery. It illustrates why a longer continuous record can be more informative than one isolated segment.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original timing exercise: PP intervals before a pause are 980, 1,020 and 1,000 ms. The next P wave occurs 2,000 ms after the preceding P. A later narrow QRS has no clearly related preceding P. Write an observation and a qualified mechanism.
steps: Establish that the baseline sinus cycle is approximately 1,000 ms.
Describe the prolonged PP interval as approximately twice that cycle.
Identify the later narrow QRS separately; look for a hidden premature P and inspect other leads.
Keep timing compatibility separate from a diagnosis of sinus-node disease.
guidedExercise.answer: A sinus pause near two baseline cycles, compatible with sinoatrial exit block, with a possible junctional escape event; the precise mechanism remains provisional.
guidedExercise.explanation: The arithmetic supports a pattern, not direct observation of the sinus node. Irregular baseline timing, hidden atrial ectopy and the limited strip can change the interpretation. Neither the duration alone nor a single escape event establishes a complete clinical diagnosis.

objectives.coverageNote: All lecture text reviewed. Source examples require the original multi-lead/continuous strips; the exercise is newly constructed and is not a reinterpretation of a supplied patient tracing.

objectives.title: Describe fascicular and bundle branch conduction patterns
objectives.why: QRS width, frontal axis and morphology together help describe delayed ventricular activation without treating any single feature as diagnostic.
know: Ventricular conduction normally distributes activation rapidly through the His–Purkinje network. Delay in one bundle or fascicle changes the sequence of depolarisation. The resulting ECG should be described using measured QRS duration, appropriate lead morphology and the frontal QRS axis rather than an isolated label.

Complete right bundle branch block in adults typically combines QRS duration of at least 120 ms with a terminal rightward force in V1 and a broad terminal S in lateral leads such as I and V6. Left bundle branch block produces a broad QRS with predominantly negative right-precordial activation and broad lateral R waves; normal small lateral septal q waves are usually absent. A wide QRS without a consistent recognised pattern can be reported as a non-specific intraventricular conduction delay.

Fascicular block primarily changes frontal activation direction. Left anterior fascicular block is considered when substantial left-axis deviation has a supporting limb-lead pattern. Left posterior fascicular block is uncommon and requires exclusion of other causes of right-axis deviation. Axis deviation alone is insufficient: infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, lead errors and other activation changes can mimic parts of the pattern.

ST and T waves may be secondarily altered because depolarisation is abnormal. Such repolarisation changes should not be assessed as though the QRS were normally conducted. Describe combined defects explicitly, for example right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block and a prolonged PR interval, rather than assuming that a PR delay proves failure in a third fascicle.

steps.title: Measure first
steps.text: Use the widest convincing QRS duration across the available leads.

steps.title: Compare V1 and lateral leads
steps.text: Check that the terminal forces and lateral morphology support the proposed bundle pattern.

steps.title: Add axis and context
steps.text: Describe additional fascicular features while considering alternative causes.

example.question: A hypothetical ECG has QRS duration 150 ms, terminal R′ in V1 and broad terminal S waves in I and V6. What description is supported?
working: 150 ms exceeds the adult complete-bundle-block duration threshold.
The terminal right-precordial and lateral forces fit delayed right ventricular activation.
State the pattern and assess the underlying rhythm and axis separately.
example.answer: A right bundle branch block pattern is supported; duration alone would not have established it.

pitfalls: Diagnosing fascicular block from axis alone.
Equating a prolonged PR plus two ventricular conduction defects with proven three-fascicle disease.

practice.prompt: Which combination best supports a complete RBBB pattern?
options: QRS 150 ms, terminal R′ in V1 and broad S in I/V6
QRS 80 ms and a tall T wave
practice.explanation: The duration and distribution of terminal forces are complementary observations.
practice.hint: Combine duration with morphology.

practice.prompt: Why describe RBBB, left anterior fascicular block and PR prolongation separately?
options: PR delay always proves posterior fascicular block
The delay causing a long PR cannot be localised to a remaining fascicle from the surface ECG alone
practice.explanation: PR prolongation can reflect AV nodal or His–Purkinje delay; a surface tracing does not justify the assumed localisation.
practice.hint: A measured interval is not an anatomical map.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Delayed conduction within a subdivision of the left bundle system, inferred from a characteristic activation pattern.
An ST–T alteration resulting from an abnormal ventricular depolarisation sequence.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Relate morphology to the activation sequence
deepDive.text: Bundle-branch patterns become easier to understand when the early and late parts of QRS are considered separately. The course diagrams show normal septal activation from left to right. In RBBB, early septal and left ventricular activation can remain relatively familiar while delayed right ventricular activation changes the terminal forces. This explains why the terminal R in V1 and terminal S in lateral leads are interpreted together. In LBBB, the septal activation sequence and the subsequent spread through the left ventricle change, affecting both the beginning and the later portion of QRS.

deepDive.title: Use width, lead distribution and axis together
deepDive.text: Measure QRS duration across the available leads and then inspect the distribution of positive and negative forces. The lecture pairs a broad terminal positive deflection in V1 with a broad lateral S for RBBB, and a predominantly negative V1 with broad lateral R waves for LBBB. A single notched complex is insufficient. Fascicular patterns direct attention to the frontal axis, but axis deviation also has alternative causes. The source explicitly cautions that marked left axis deviation associated with LBBB or large inferior Q waves should not automatically be relabelled as left anterior fascicular block.

deepDive.title: Describe combinations without inventing their anatomical level
deepDive.text: When multiple findings coexist, a component-by-component report is usually clearer than a compressed label. State the bundle-branch pattern, axis/fascicular evidence and PR interval separately. A long PR interval does not itself show which of the AV node or ventricular fascicles is responsible for the delay. The course also includes broad complexes that do not fit a typical right or left bundle-branch pattern. Calling these a non-specific intraventricular conduction abnormality preserves useful information without forcing an unsupported category. ST–T changes may be secondary to altered activation and should be interpreted in that framework.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original reporting exercise: a QRS lasts 150 ms, has a broad terminal positive deflection in V1, a broad terminal S in I and V6, and a frontal axis of −55°. PR is 240 ms. How should the findings be organised?
steps: Identify the RBBB-like morphology using both right-precordial and lateral leads.
Describe the leftward axis and assess the full pattern for a left anterior fascicular component.
Record the prolonged PR interval separately.
Avoid claiming that the PR delay proves disease in a third ventricular fascicle.
guidedExercise.answer: Describe RBBB morphology, marked left axis deviation with a possible associated left anterior fascicular pattern, and PR prolongation, rather than asserting an anatomically proven “trifascicular” block.
guidedExercise.explanation: The report preserves measurable findings while separating them from the inferred conduction anatomy. A comparison ECG and complete lead review can strengthen or weaken the fascicular interpretation.

objectives.coverageNote: Diagram sequences and example text reviewed; comprehensive visual remeasurement of every supplied bundle-branch tracing has not been performed.

objectives.title: Differentiate first-degree and Mobitz-pattern AV conduction delay
objectives.why: An AV-block description requires P-wave timing and PR behaviour, not simply a missing QRS complex.
know: First-degree AV block describes a prolonged PR interval with every atrial impulse still followed by a ventricular response. In adults, a PR interval longer than 200 ms is conventionally prolonged. The measurement runs from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS, so a hidden P-wave onset or an inappropriate lead can distort it.

Second-degree AV block means that some atrial impulses fail to conduct to the ventricles. In a typical Mobitz I, or Wenckebach, sequence, conducted PR intervals lengthen before a non-conducted P wave; conduction then resumes with a shorter PR interval. Grouped beating supports this pattern, but long cycles, subtle changes and P waves overlapping T waves can make it less obvious.

Mobitz II describes intermittent failure of conduction despite unchanged PR intervals in the relevant conducted beats, with stable atrial timing and no preceding pattern of progressive PR prolongation. A wide QRS may accompany His–Purkinje disease, but QRS width is not the defining criterion and a narrow complex does not automatically exclude an infranodal problem.

Always establish that a supposedly blocked P wave is a normally timed atrial impulse. A premature atrial beat reaching refractory tissue can fail to conduct and mimic AV block. The distinction is made by timing, morphology and the sequence surrounding the event. Anatomical site and clinical significance cannot be reduced to a single textbook pattern or inferred from a short isolated strip without qualifications.

steps.title: Mark every P wave
steps.text: Record whether PP timing is stable and whether the non-conducted event is premature.

steps.title: Measure the sequence
steps.text: Write successive PR intervals rather than judging a single pair by eye.

steps.title: Name the demonstrated pattern
steps.text: Use first-degree, Mobitz I or Mobitz II only when the required sequence is visible.

example.question: Hypothetical PR intervals are 180, 220 and 250 ms, followed by a normally timed P without a QRS; the next conducted PR is 180 ms.
working: Atrial impulses remain on time.
The PR progressively lengthens before non-conduction.
PR shortening after the pause starts a new cycle.
example.answer: This is a typical Mobitz I (Wenckebach) sequence.

pitfalls: Calling a premature blocked atrial beat Mobitz II.
Assuming that all Wenckebach block is harmless or always AV-nodal.

practice.prompt: Which observation defines first-degree AV block?
options: Every P conducts with a prolonged PR interval
No relationship between P and QRS
A wide QRS regardless of PR
practice.explanation: First-degree AV block is delay with maintained 1:1 AV conduction.
practice.hint: First-degree involves delay rather than intermittent dropped conduction.

practice.prompt: PR intervals progressively lengthen, then a normally timed P is not followed by a QRS. The next PR is shorter. Which pattern fits?
options: Mobitz II solely because a QRS is missing
practice.explanation: The changing PR sequence is the key evidence for Wenckebach.
practice.hint: Use the entire sequence.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Time from onset of atrial depolarisation to onset of ventricular depolarisation.
A typical Mobitz I sequence of progressive AV conduction delay before a non-conducted atrial impulse.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Measure a relationship, not a single interval
deepDive.text: AV conduction analysis requires a series of atrial events and ventricular responses. Mark each P onset and QRS onset, then measure the PR interval for every conducted beat in a group. A first-degree pattern retains conduction of each atrial impulse but with a prolonged PR interval. When atrial impulses sometimes fail to produce a QRS, the task changes to analysing the sequence of conducted and non-conducted events. A P wave can lie partly within a preceding T wave, especially when conduction is very delayed, so apparent absence should be checked in other leads.

deepDive.title: Reconstruct the Wenckebach sequence
deepDive.text: Progressive PR prolongation makes the ventricular timing differ from the atrial timing. The increments need not be equal: the source illustrates a relatively large early increment followed by smaller later increments. After a non-conducted atrial impulse, the next conducted PR is shorter and a new group begins. A short strip can therefore show grouped beating without making the entire progression obvious. Long Wenckebach sequences and concealed atrial deflections are specifically highlighted in the course. The mechanism should be supported by measured PR changes rather than by the visual impression of a pause alone.

deepDive.title: Do not turn usual associations into definitions
deepDive.text: The source contrasts typically narrow-QRS Wenckebach examples with often broad-QRS Mobitz II examples. These are useful associations, but the classification is based on the behaviour of AV conduction, not on QRS width alone. A fixed PR before and after an unexpectedly non-conducted sinus P supports a Mobitz II pattern only after competing explanations have been considered. Premature atrial impulses, concealed events and incomplete rhythm strips can mimic apparent dropped beats. Describe the demonstrated sequence first, then state how confidently it fits a named pattern and which additional recording would clarify it.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original sequence exercise: five regular sinus P waves occur. The first four PR intervals are 200, 260, 290 and 300 ms; the fifth P has no QRS response. The next conducted PR is 210 ms. Explain the pattern.
steps: Confirm regular atrial timing rather than a premature fifth atrial event.
Compare all four conducted PR intervals.
Identify the non-conducted P and the shorter PR at the start of the next group.
Report the whole sequence rather than naming the pause in isolation.
guidedExercise.answer: The described sequence supports a Wenckebach/Mobitz I AV-conduction pattern.
guidedExercise.explanation: The decisive evidence is progressive PR lengthening, a non-conducted atrial impulse and resetting to a shorter PR. The numerical increments become smaller, demonstrating why equal step sizes are not required.

objectives.coverageNote: The additional exercise is synthetic. Source treatment/prognostic simplifications are not used as patient-specific recommendations.

objectives.title: Report 2:1 and high-grade AV block without overclassification
objectives.why: Alternate blocked P waves are easy to hide in T waves, and a 2:1 ratio alone cannot establish a Mobitz subtype.
know: In 2:1 AV block, two atrial depolarisations occur for each ventricular response. Because only one conducted PR is seen between blocked impulses, the strip does not show the sequence needed to distinguish Mobitz I from Mobitz II. Report the demonstrated ratio rather than forcing a subtype that the recording cannot support.

An apparently regular slow ventricular rhythm can therefore conceal a much faster atrial rhythm. Look at leads in which atrial activity is conspicuous and inspect the terminal T wave for a repeating additional deflection. Demonstrating regular P waves at twice the ventricular rate is more persuasive than assuming that every visible P belongs to the following QRS.

The QRS may be narrow or broad. Width and associated conduction abnormalities may influence concern about the site of disease, but they do not definitively localise 2:1 block. A prolonged PR in the conducted beats can be reported without adding a separate first-degree block label that obscures the higher-degree disturbance.

High-grade or advanced AV block describes multiple consecutive atrial impulses failing to conduct; reports should include the observed P:QRS ratio and any intermittent conduction. Occasional conducted beats make the ventricular rhythm irregular and distinguish advanced block from a sustained interval of complete block. PP intervals may also vary, including ventriculophasic sinus variation, so use a sufficiently long multi-lead recording and avoid relying only on exact numerical ratios.

steps.title: Search for hidden P waves
steps.text: Compare P-wave shape and timing in more than one lead.

steps.title: State the ratio
steps.text: Count atrial events and ventricular responses over a clear segment.

steps.title: Respect the limitation
steps.text: Do not assign a Mobitz subtype to a persistent 2:1 sequence from the ratio alone.

example.question: Hypothetical atrial rate is 100/min and ventricular rate is 50/min, with a fixed PR for each conducted beat and alternate normally timed P waves without QRS responses.
working: There are two atrial impulses for every ventricular response.
The fixed conducted PR does not reveal whether progressive delay would occur in a longer conduction sequence.
A narrow QRS is useful description but does not settle the level of block.
example.answer: Report 2:1 AV block, with QRS width and conducted PR; do not automatically call it Mobitz II.

pitfalls: Calling apparent sinus bradycardia without searching for P waves on T waves.
Using a fixed PR in 2:1 conduction as proof of Mobitz II.

practice.prompt: A persistent 2:1 AV block should be classified as:
options: 2:1 AV block unless additional evidence establishes the mechanism
Complete AV block in every case
practice.explanation: A 2:1 sequence lacks the series of conducted beats needed for Mobitz pattern classification.
practice.hint: What sequence is missing?

practice.prompt: Two consecutive normally timed P waves fail to conduct, then a later atrial impulse does conduct. What should the report preserve?
options: The evidence of intermittent conduction and an advanced AV-block pattern
A claim that no atrial impulses ever conduct
A ventricular rate without atrial description
An automatic diagnosis of sinus arrest
practice.explanation: Intermittent conduction is important evidence and should not be discarded by a complete-block label.
practice.hint: Some conducted beats matter.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: An AV conduction pattern with two atrial depolarisations for every ventricular response.
Advanced AV block with multiple consecutive non-conducted atrial impulses; state the actual observed pattern.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Understand the information missing in 2:1 conduction
deepDive.text: In a 2:1 pattern, one atrial impulse conducts and the next does not. There are therefore no adjacent conducted PR intervals within the alternating sequence from which to demonstrate progressive prolongation or unchanged conduction across multiple successive conducted beats. That missing information is why the ratio alone cannot establish a Mobitz subtype. QRS width can inform the wider assessment but does not restore the missing sequence. A careful report states the atrial rhythm, the 2:1 AV relationship, the ventricular rate and the QRS features without pretending that the block level has been proven.

deepDive.title: Search systematically for the other atrial event
deepDive.text: A ventricular rhythm at half the atrial rate can look like uncomplicated sinus bradycardia when the second P wave is hidden. Examine the T wave and ST segment for repeated notches or contour changes at the predicted atrial time. A genuine atrial sequence should be traceable through several cycles and, where possible, across more than one lead. The course shows that changing atrial rate can move previously visible blocked P waves into the T waves. Do not rely on one lead or one visible pairing when assessing whether atrial events are being missed.

deepDive.title: Distinguish advanced conduction loss from complete independence
deepDive.text: When more than one consecutive atrial impulse is non-conducted, describe the observed ratio and the runs of failed conduction. The course notes that definitions of high-grade block are not entirely uniform. Importantly, occasional genuine conducted beats mean that complete absence of AV conduction has not been demonstrated. A changing ventricular sequence may contain both escape events and conducted events. Assess each event’s timing and morphology before assuming a single fixed mechanism. Ventriculophasic variation can also make the PP intervals slightly unequal, so perfect atrial regularity is not an absolute prerequisite for interpreting these examples.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: P waves occur about every 400 ms. QRS complexes occur every 800 ms with a consistent relation to alternate P waves. The other P waves distort the T waves. QRS duration is 140 ms. What can and cannot be concluded?
steps: Calculate atrial and ventricular rates independently.
Confirm that the hidden deflections occur at the predicted atrial times.
Name the demonstrated 2:1 AV-conduction pattern.
Describe the broad QRS without assigning a Mobitz subtype from width alone.
guidedExercise.answer: Atrial activity approximately 150/min with a ventricular response approximately 75/min and 2:1 AV block, with broad QRS complexes; the Mobitz subtype is not established by this strip.
guidedExercise.explanation: The regular alternate relationship supports 2:1 conduction, but it supplies no consecutive conducted PR sequence. A longer record showing a change in conduction may provide additional classification evidence.

objectives.coverageNote: All high-grade/2:1 source text reviewed; figure-dependent distinctions still require direct inspection of the private originals.

objectives.title: Distinguish complete AV block from AV dissociation
objectives.why: AV dissociation is a descriptive observation shared by several mechanisms; complete AV block is a claim about absent conduction.
know: Complete, or third-degree, AV block means that atrial impulses do not conduct to the ventricles during the observed interval. A subsidiary pacemaker usually maintains ventricular activation. In the typical sinus-rhythm example, sinus P waves continue at a faster rate than the slow regular escape rhythm, and the PR relation continually changes.

AV dissociation means that the atria and ventricles are being activated independently. That observation is necessary in the usual complete-block pattern but is not sufficient to prove complete AV block. A junctional rhythm that competes with a slow sinus rate, or a ventricular tachycardia that outruns the atria, can also produce independent atrial and ventricular activity.

Count atrial and ventricular rates separately and search carefully for conducted capture. A ventricular rhythm made irregular by occasional genuinely conducted impulses is better described as advanced intermittent block than as uninterrupted complete block. Conversely, atrial and ventricular rates may coincidentally have a near-integer ratio without a fixed conduction relationship; this is why an apparently exact 2:1 rate relation can mislead.

Escape QRS width gives useful information about ventricular activation but does not establish a precise anatomical level by itself. A narrow junctional escape is often faster than a distal broad-complex escape, although structural or pre-existing conduction disease can modify the appearance. Symptoms, reversible influences and prolonged recordings matter. This learning objective is about documenting ECG evidence, not deciding a pacing indication or treatment.

steps.title: Calculate two rates
steps.text: Use PP intervals for the atria and RR intervals for the ventricles.

steps.title: Test the relationship
steps.text: Look for a fixed PR or for independent P waves marching through QRS and T waves.

steps.title: Seek exceptions
steps.text: Identify any conducted beats and report the duration and limitations of the sampled interval.

example.question: Teaching example: P waves march at 80/min, broad QRS complexes at 35/min, and PR intervals vary throughout a long clear strip with no conducted beats.
working: The atrial rhythm is faster than the ventricular escape rhythm.
Atrial and ventricular activations are independent.
No conducted beats are demonstrated in the reviewed segment.
example.answer: The pattern supports complete AV block with a broad-complex escape rhythm during that segment.

pitfalls: Equating every instance of AV dissociation with complete block.
Calling a near-exact atrial:ventricular rate ratio 2:1 conduction without testing the PR relationship.

practice.prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: AV dissociation always means complete AV block
AV dissociation describes independent atrial and ventricular activation and requires a mechanism assessment
A broad QRS proves complete AV block
Complete AV block requires an atrial rate of exactly 80/min
practice.explanation: Dissociation is a relationship; competing pacemakers and ventricular rhythms can also cause it.
practice.hint: Separate description from mechanism.

practice.prompt: Atrial rate 38/min, junctional rate 42/min and independent P waves are observed. What is not yet justified?
options: Declaring complete AV block solely from the dissociation
practice.explanation: A slightly faster junctional pacemaker may dissociate from sinus activity without proving complete conduction failure.
practice.hint: Which pacemaker is faster?

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Independent atrial and ventricular activation without a fixed P–QRS relationship.
A conduction disturbance in which atrial impulses fail to reach the ventricles during the observed interval.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Define independence before naming complete block
deepDive.text: AV dissociation means that atrial and ventricular electrical activity are not maintaining a fixed relationship. It describes what the two clocks are doing, rather than the reason they are independent. The source contrasts complete AV block with sinus bradycardia accompanied by a slightly faster junctional rhythm. Both can show dissociation, but their rate relationships and mechanisms differ. Complete AV block requires failure of atrial impulses to conduct to the ventricles; a short interval of apparent independence does not directly demonstrate that every possible atrial impulse is incapable of conduction.

deepDive.title: Look for changing opportunities to conduct
deepDive.text: Mark a run of P waves and ask how their positions move through successive ventricular cycles. In sustained independence the apparent PR relationships change, even if one P happens to precede a QRS at a superficially plausible interval. An almost exact 2:1 atrial-to-ventricular rate ratio can create a misleading impression of fixed conduction. The source’s late quiz example specifically illustrates this problem. Conversely, an occasional ventricular response convincingly linked to a P can indicate residual conduction and challenge a conclusion of complete block. The longer sequence, not the most convenient pairing, should determine the report.

deepDive.title: Describe the escape rhythm as a separate observation
deepDive.text: When ventricular activation is maintained by an escape focus, report its rate, regularity and QRS morphology. Narrow complexes can be compatible with activation through much of the normal ventricular conduction network, whereas broad complexes may suggest a more distal origin or coexisting conduction abnormality. These clues do not measure the anatomical block site directly. The lecture’s examples also include intermittent ventricular standstill, showing why a single stable escape segment may not represent the whole recording. State the recording duration and whether the interpretation rests on a continuous strip or isolated snapshots.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original comparison: tracing A has atrial activity at 36/min and an independent narrow-QRS rhythm at 40/min. Tracing B has atrial activity at 84/min, independent regular broad complexes at 32/min and changing apparent PR intervals. Compare the justified descriptions.
steps: State atrial and ventricular rates for both records.
Recognise independence in each record.
For A, notice that the ventricular rhythm is slightly faster than the atrial rhythm.
For B, consider complete AV block with escape, while checking the longer record for any conducted responses.
guidedExercise.answer: A supports sinus bradycardia with a competing junctional rhythm and AV dissociation. B is compatible with complete AV block and a slow broad-complex escape rhythm, subject to confirmation of absent conduction.
guidedExercise.explanation: Independence is shared by the two descriptions; the mechanism cannot be obtained from that word alone. Rate relationships and demonstrated conduction opportunities change the strength of the conclusion.

objectives.coverageNote: The source explicitly warns that AV dissociation is necessary but insufficient for its complete-block examples. This depth layer preserves that qualification.

objectives.title: Construct a defensible bradyarrhythmia interpretation
objectives.why: A structured report exposes uncertainty and distinguishes a demonstrated rhythm from an unproven cause.
know: Begin a bradyarrhythmia report with recording quality, calibration and the observed ventricular rate. A short strip can sample an intermittent process poorly, and artefact can hide small P waves. The analysis should therefore state what was actually recorded before suggesting an underlying disease mechanism.

Name or describe the atrial activity separately from the ventricular response. Sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter can coexist with a conduction disturbance. Count the atrial events, state whether they are regular, and determine whether they precede the QRS with a consistent interval. This prevents a conduction diagnosis from replacing the atrial rhythm description.

Next state the QRS duration and morphology, the PR sequence where measurable, and the conduction ratio or evidence of dissociation. If pauses are present, describe their timing and whether atrial depolarisation continues. Search actively for concealed premature atrial beats and for P waves within T waves. Document an escape rhythm or periods of ventricular standstill if genuinely shown.

Finish with the supported interpretation and its limits. A phrase such as “sinus rhythm with 2:1 AV block and a broad QRS; Mobitz subtype cannot be established from this segment” is more precise than an unsupported mechanism. The course includes clinical consequences, but urgency and management require the patient’s condition and qualified clinical assessment. A teaching exercise must not provide a self-contained treatment instruction from an isolated schematic.

steps.title: Describe
steps.text: Write atrial rhythm, atrial rate, ventricular rate and QRS features.

steps.title: Relate
steps.text: State the PR sequence, conduction ratio and pause mechanism when demonstrable.

steps.title: Qualify
steps.text: Say what the segment cannot settle and what additional recording or context is needed.

example.question: Write a one-sentence interpretation for a hypothetical regular 45/min broad-QRS rhythm with sinus P waves at 90/min and alternate non-conduction.
working: The atrial activity is sinus and faster than the ventricular response.
Alternate P waves fail to conduct, establishing 2:1 AV block.
The wide QRS is an additional descriptor, not proof of Mobitz II.
example.answer: Sinus rhythm at 90/min with 2:1 AV block, ventricular rate 45/min and broad QRS complexes; Mobitz subtype remains undetermined.

pitfalls: Reporting only “bradycardia” when a conduction ratio is evident.
Reporting a treatment conclusion without clinical information.

practice.prompt: Which is the most defensible report?
options: Mobitz II because the rate is 45/min
Sinus rhythm with 2:1 AV block; subtype uncertain from the available segment
Normal ECG because the QRS is regular
Complete block because the atrial rate is twice the ventricular rate
practice.explanation: It states the directly demonstrated relation without overclassifying the mechanism.
practice.hint: Report the evidence.

practice.prompt: What should be added when an apparent pause contains a suspicious T-wave deflection?
options: A reminder to inspect other leads for a hidden premature P wave
An automatic diagnosis of sinus arrest
An automatic diagnosis of ventricular standstill
practice.explanation: A concealed non-conducted premature atrial beat is an important mimic of sinus pauses and AV block.
practice.hint: Could an atrial event be hidden?

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: The counted relation of atrial depolarisations to ventricular responses in a defined ECG segment.
An interval without ventricular depolarisation; distinguish it from absent atrial activity and artefact.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Build the report from an event inventory
deepDive.text: A defensible bradyarrhythmia report can be assembled in a fixed order: recording quality and calibration, atrial activity and rate, ventricular activity and rate, AV relationships, pauses and escape events, and QRS morphology. This sequence prevents the ventricular rate from becoming the entire diagnosis. It also makes the interpretation auditable: another reader can see which observed features support the proposed mechanism. If part of the record is unclear, identify the particular uncertainty, such as concealed atrial activity or a transition outside the recorded interval, rather than using an unqualified rhythm label.

deepDive.title: Use a ladder-style account of difficult sequences
deepDive.text: For a complex strip, imagine separate atrial, AV-conduction and ventricular rows. Put a mark on the atrial row for each identified P, then align each QRS on the ventricular row. Draw a possible connection only when the timing supports conduction. A P hidden in a T wave can change a supposed sinus pause into failed AV conduction or blocked atrial ectopy. An escape beat may appear after more than one mechanism of pause. This reconstruction is a reasoning aid, not a direct recording of the conduction system, and alternative connections may remain possible.

deepDive.title: Choose the narrowest claim that preserves the evidence
deepDive.text: When the evidence establishes a ratio or relationship but not an anatomical site, report the relationship. When a named mechanism fits but another explanation remains credible, state compatibility and the specific information needed to discriminate them. The course quiz includes sinus-node exit problems, Wenckebach, 2:1 block, complete block and Mobitz II, so the exercise is broader than memorising one slow rhythm. Clinical history, medicines and symptoms can alter the significance of a finding, but this educational report should not invent those facts or turn an ECG pattern into a treatment instruction.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original reporting exercise: a short strip has a ventricular rate near 40/min. Some T waves contain repeated small notches, and only alternate suspected atrial deflections are followed by QRS complexes. The recording is noisy. Draft a report and a next-evidence statement.
steps: Describe the slow ventricular response and the quality limitation.
Identify possible regular atrial activity at approximately twice the ventricular rate.
State that 2:1 AV conduction is a possibility rather than a demonstrated Mobitz subtype.
Specify that clearer simultaneous leads and a longer strip are needed to confirm the hidden atrial events.
guidedExercise.answer: Slow ventricular rhythm with possible concealed alternate atrial events, raising 2:1 AV block; atrial timing and the conduction pattern remain uncertain because of noise and the short record.
guidedExercise.explanation: A qualified report retains the useful suspicion without converting a poorly seen notch into proven atrial activity. The next requested evidence targets the actual ambiguity.

title: Ventricular ectopy and ventricular rhythms
sourceFilename: D2-2 ventricular arrhythmias DipECG amended mar2026.pdf
summary: Recognise ventricular premature activity, slower ventricular rhythms, tachycardia and fibrillation using timing and morphology.

objectives.title: Recognise ventricular premature beats and their patterns
objectives.why: Identifying premature timing and the pattern of ectopy is more useful than labelling every broad QRS as a ventricular beat.
know: A ventricular premature beat is an early ventricular activation arising outside the normal supraventricular conduction sequence. The QRS is commonly broad and morphologically different from surrounding sinus complexes because activation spreads through ventricular myocardium rather than beginning normally in both bundle branches.

Look for the timing of the beat, its QRS appearance, and any preceding atrial depolarisation. A clear premature abnormal P wave followed by a broad QRS may indicate an aberrantly conducted atrial premature beat rather than ventricular ectopy. Atrial activity can be concealed, so “no visible P wave” should not be treated as infallible proof of ventricular origin.

Ventricular bigeminy means that sinus or other baseline beats alternate with ventricular premature beats. In trigeminy, a premature ventricular beat occurs every third beat. A couplet consists of two consecutive ventricular premature beats. Three consecutive ventricular beats may be described as a triplet; classification as a short run of ventricular tachycardia also depends on the rate and the adopted definition.

A pause often follows ventricular premature activity, but some premature beats are interpolated between otherwise expected sinus beats without the usual post-ectopic pause. Different QRS shapes are described as multiform; morphology alone does not prove a count of separate anatomical foci. Record patterns over the available segment without inventing a whole-day burden or prognostic conclusion from a brief teaching strip.

steps.title: Establish baseline
steps.text: Identify the expected beat morphology and underlying cycle.

steps.title: Check prematurity
steps.text: Confirm that the unusual QRS occurs earlier than the next expected baseline beat.

steps.title: Describe the pattern
steps.text: Count isolated beats, bigeminy, trigeminy, couplets or short runs.

example.question: Hypothetical sequence: sinus beat, ventricular premature beat, sinus beat, ventricular premature beat, repeated.
working: Every second beat is premature and has the same ventricular morphology.
The repeating relation is alternating baseline and ectopic activity.
The strip does not establish the percentage burden over 24 hours.
example.answer: Ventricular bigeminy in the recorded segment.

pitfalls: Assuming absence of a pause excludes ventricular ectopy.
Inferring multifocal origin or daily burden solely from a short strip.

practice.prompt: What does ventricular trigeminy describe?
options: Every third beat is a ventricular premature beat
Only three QRS complexes in a recording
practice.explanation: Trigeminy is a repeating timing pattern, not a diagnosis of sustained tachycardia.
practice.hint: Count the repeating cycle.

practice.prompt: Which observation challenges a ventricular origin for a broad premature beat?
options: A clear premature abnormal P wave preceding it
practice.explanation: A premature atrial depolarisation with aberrant ventricular conduction can generate a broad early QRS.
practice.hint: Look upstream for atrial activity.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: A premature beat inserted between baseline beats without the usual ensuing compensatory pause.
Two consecutive ventricular premature beats.

references.label: 2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death

deepDive.title: Use prematurity as the first discriminating feature
deepDive.text: An unusual QRS should first be located in the timing sequence. A premature event occurs earlier than expected from the preceding rhythm; an escape event arrives late after a delayed or absent expected activation. The course’s ventricular premature-beat examples combine early timing, broad morphology and lack of an appropriately related preceding P. Those features should be sought together. A broad QRS alone does not establish ventricular origin because a supraventricular impulse can conduct aberrantly, and a P wave can be obscured. Compare the unusual event with both the preceding atrial activity and the subsequent rhythm.

deepDive.title: Describe distribution and post-event timing
deepDive.text: Bigeminy means an alternating pattern in which sinus-like events and premature events repeat. Trigeminy describes a repeating sequence in which every third event is premature. Couplets and triplets describe two or three consecutive premature ventricular events. These labels record distribution; they do not by themselves quantify the total burden over a day. The source also shows interpolated ventricular beats occurring between sinus beats without the usual conspicuous pause. Therefore a pause after every event is not required. Track the underlying sinus sequence through the unusual beat instead of treating the visible RR interval as the only clock.

deepDive.title: Separate morphology from an assumed number of foci
deepDive.text: Different QRS shapes can reflect different origins, different activation routes or changing fusion with the underlying rhythm. The course uses multiform and polymorphic terminology while acknowledging that differing conduction routes can change appearance. A single lead may underrepresent those differences or exaggerate small positional changes. Report which leads and beats are being compared, whether the morphology is reproducible, and whether there is evidence of an atrial trigger. Avoid assigning a precise anatomical focus or a prognostic category from a short educational strip. Those conclusions require more than pattern naming.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: a regular sinus rhythm has expected QRS complexes at 0, 1 and 2 seconds. A broad additional complex appears at 1.45 seconds without a clear preceding P; the sinus complex at 2 seconds still occurs. Explain the timing.
steps: Establish the one-second underlying cycle.
Locate the additional broad event before the next expected sinus complex.
Note that the subsequent sinus schedule is approximately preserved.
Check atrial timing before favouring a ventricular premature event over aberrant atrial ectopy.
guidedExercise.answer: An early broad event between scheduled sinus beats is compatible with an interpolated ventricular premature beat; the absence of a conspicuous post-event pause does not exclude it.
guidedExercise.explanation: Prematurity separates the additional beat from an escape event. Atrial evidence and multi-lead morphology are still needed to make the ventricular-origin conclusion more secure.

objectives.coverageNote: All ectopy-pattern source text reviewed. No numerical ectopic burden or prognostic claim is inferred from the newly constructed short sequence.

objectives.title: Explain accelerated idioventricular rhythm and fusion
objectives.why: A ventricular rhythm can be relatively slow, and its competition with sinus activation explains fusion and capture beats.
know: An idioventricular rhythm arises from a ventricular pacemaker. The term accelerated idioventricular rhythm is used when its discharge becomes faster than a usual ventricular escape rhythm and may compete with sinus activation. The course uses an illustrative range around 60–100 beats/min; published conventions vary, so the precise boundary should not be treated as a biological switch.

The QRS is usually broad, and independent atrial activity may continue through the ventricular rhythm. Alternatively, ventricular activation may conduct backwards to the atria, creating retrograde P waves after QRS complexes. Either arrangement needs to be described rather than assuming a single atrial relationship for all ventricular rhythms.

A capture beat occurs when a supraventricular impulse conducts to and activates the ventricles during a ventricular rhythm, often producing a more normally conducted QRS. A fusion beat combines activation from the supraventricular and ventricular wavefronts and may look intermediate between baseline and ventricular complexes. These observations help explain competing activation; identifying them requires convincing timing and morphology.

Accelerated idioventricular rhythm is often discussed in reperfusion settings, but the ECG alone cannot prove reperfusion or establish the underlying clinical cause. It also should not be conflated with every regular broad-QRS rhythm near 100 beats/min. Compare onset, rate, atrial relation and prior tracings, and integrate clinical findings. The educational focus is pattern explanation, not an automatic statement that intervention is or is not required.

steps.title: Measure rate
steps.text: Use several representative RR intervals rather than a single beat.

steps.title: Track atrial events
steps.text: Look for independence or retrograde activation.

steps.title: Compare QRS shapes
steps.text: Test whether a candidate capture or fusion beat has the expected timing and intermediate or conducted morphology.

example.question: A hypothetical broad-QRS rhythm is 78/min while P waves independently occur at 70/min. One QRS has morphology intermediate between sinus and ventricular beats.
working: The ventricular rhythm is only moderately faster than the sinus rhythm.
Independent P waves establish competition rather than a fixed PR relation.
An intermediate complex can represent combined wavefront activation.
example.answer: The findings are compatible with accelerated idioventricular rhythm with AV dissociation and a possible fusion beat.

pitfalls: Using a rate boundary alone to decide the mechanism.
Calling an intermediate-looking complex fusion without supporting timing.

practice.prompt: A fusion beat represents:
options: Combined ventricular activation by two wavefronts
Two P waves superimposed in every lead
practice.explanation: A supraventricular and ventricular impulse contribute to the resulting QRS.
practice.hint: Think of wavefronts meeting.

practice.prompt: Can accelerated idioventricular rhythm alone prove successful reperfusion?
options: No; it is an association that needs clinical corroboration
Only if the rate is exactly 80/min
Only if there are no P waves
practice.explanation: The rhythm can be associated with reperfusion but does not independently establish the clinical event.
practice.hint: An ECG association is not a stand-alone causal test.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: A supraventricular impulse that successfully activates the ventricles during an otherwise ventricular rhythm.
A QRS produced by combined ventricular activation from competing wavefronts.

references.label: 2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death

deepDive.title: Understand competition between impulse sources
deepDive.text: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm is presented in the course as a ventricular focus controlling a regular broad-QRS rhythm at a rate overlapping ordinary resting rates. The useful concept is competition: the ventricular focus can temporarily become faster than the sinus-driven ventricular schedule. A surface tracing may then show independent atrial activity or retrograde atrial activation. This differs from assuming that any broad rhythm at a modest rate is ordinary sinus rhythm with bundle-branch block. Examine onset, termination, atrial timing and the relation of the unusual complexes to the baseline rhythm.

deepDive.title: Recognise fusion as a mixed activation event
deepDive.text: When a conducted supraventricular impulse and a ventricular-origin impulse contribute to the same ventricular activation, the resulting QRS can have an intermediate morphology. Compare it with neighbouring conducted and ventricular-origin complexes in the same lead. A true fusion interpretation requires more than one odd-looking beat: the timing should plausibly allow both wavefronts to contribute. Changes in electrode contact, aberrancy or baseline noise can also alter a complex. The course’s transition examples make the relationship easier to understand because the candidate fused beat can be compared with both reference morphologies.

deepDive.title: Use capture and retrograde activity carefully
deepDive.text: An occasional normally conducted ventricular activation amid a ventricular rhythm can provide a capture-like event, while atrial deflections after QRS may represent retrograde conduction. In both cases the timing relationship matters. A P wave happening to overlap a QRS is not evidence that the atrium caused it. The source links accelerated idioventricular rhythm with reperfusion, but an ECG pattern is not proof that a coronary artery has reopened. Describe the electrical pattern separately from a possible clinical setting. Rate ranges in teaching slides are useful context, not substitutes for analysing the mechanism and its transitions.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: broad complexes at approximately 85/min replace a slower sinus-driven rhythm. P waves continue independently. One complex has a shape intermediate between the previous sinus QRS and the broad rhythm. Explain why fusion is considered.
steps: Compare the two established reference morphologies.
Check whether an atrial impulse could reach the ventricle near the timing of the intermediate complex.
Recognise that independent P waves support competing atrial and ventricular activity.
Retain alternatives if the timing or waveform quality is inadequate.
guidedExercise.answer: The sequence is compatible with an accelerated ventricular rhythm with AV dissociation and a possible fusion beat.
guidedExercise.explanation: An intermediate morphology is most informative when it appears in a sequence whose timing supports contributions from both activation pathways. It does not establish reperfusion or a clinical cause.

objectives.coverageNote: The detailed exercise is synthetic; source transitions and fusion/capture examples remain essential for learning their actual visual appearances.

objectives.title: Describe monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with appropriate limits
objectives.why: Ventricular tachycardia can resemble supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy; supportive signs must be combined.
know: Ventricular tachycardia is a fast rhythm arising within the ventricles. In a monomorphic episode, the QRS complexes have a broadly stable shape within each lead. The morphology can differ between leads; “monomorphic” does not mean that all twelve leads look identical.

A broad QRS, very abnormal frontal axis, precordial concordance and slow initial activation can support ventricular origin. The lecture’s very broad QRS examples illustrate clues rather than a universal diagnostic threshold. Some ventricular tachycardias are comparatively narrow, and a supraventricular rhythm with pre-existing bundle branch block can be very broad.

AV dissociation with convincing capture or fusion beats is particularly persuasive in a broad-complex tachycardia, but it may be difficult to demonstrate. Failure to see independent P waves does not exclude ventricular tachycardia. Likewise, an apparently consistent 1:1 atrioventricular relation can reflect retrograde conduction during ventricular tachycardia.

Idiopathic ventricular tachycardias may occur without an obvious structural abnormality. For example, a right ventricular outflow-tract pattern can have a left-bundle-type QRS morphology with an inferior axis. This pattern is a clue to an activation origin, not a complete aetiological or risk assessment. A coherent report records rate, regularity, QRS morphology and atrial evidence while explicitly preserving uncertainty when the mechanism is unresolved.

steps.title: Characterise the tachycardia
steps.text: Measure rate, regularity and QRS duration.

steps.title: Seek high-value evidence
steps.text: Search all leads for independent atrial activity, capture and fusion.

steps.title: Integrate morphology
steps.text: Compare axis and precordial activation and, if available, a prior sinus ECG.

example.question: A hypothetical regular broad-complex tachycardia at 170/min has stable QRS morphology and independent P waves, with one convincingly conducted capture beat.
working: Stable morphology makes the episode monomorphic.
Independent atrial activation and a capture beat strongly support ventricular origin.
The patient’s structural diagnosis cannot be read from this description alone.
example.answer: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is strongly supported; report the specific evidence.

pitfalls: Excluding VT because the patient is young or the rhythm is tolerated.
Using one QRS-width threshold as an absolute rule.

practice.prompt: In monomorphic VT, “monomorphic” means:
options: QRS shape remains broadly stable within a given lead
Every episode has exactly the same rate
practice.explanation: It refers to morphology across beats in the same lead.
practice.hint: Compare consecutive beats in one lead.

practice.prompt: What does absence of visible AV dissociation establish?
practice.explanation: Independent atrial activity is commonly difficult to identify during a fast rhythm.
practice.hint: A useful sign need not be sensitive.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: QRS complexes with the same dominant polarity across the chest leads.
Ventricular tachycardia with a broadly uniform QRS appearance from beat to beat in a given lead.

references.label: 2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death
2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia

deepDive.title: Separate a ventricular mechanism from the descriptive pattern
deepDive.text: Monomorphic describes a repeated QRS appearance within the same lead during a tachycardia. It does not mean that every lead looks alike, nor does it independently establish where the rhythm originates. A regular broad-complex tachycardia can arise from the ventricles or from a supraventricular mechanism with abnormal ventricular conduction. The course’s VT lecture and differential lecture should therefore be read together. Start with the rate, regularity, QRS duration and morphology, then examine evidence of atrial independence, capture, fusion, axis and precordial concordance.

deepDive.title: Look for positive evidence rather than a missing checklist
deepDive.text: Visible dissociated atrial activity or convincing capture/fusion events can substantially strengthen a ventricular-origin interpretation. Their absence on a short strip does not exclude VT because the relevant atrial events may be hidden or the opportunity may not occur. Similarly, an unusual axis or chest-lead concordance can add support, while their absence leaves the differential open. The source lists a broad duration greater than 140 ms among its teaching clues, but that should not be turned into a universal boundary below which VT is impossible. Measurement and mechanism remain separate questions.

deepDive.title: Recognise the limits of a familiar appearance
deepDive.text: Some ventricular tachycardias arise in people without an obvious structural abnormality on the available history, and the lecture includes an outflow-tract example with a bundle-branch-like appearance. This shows why youth, a familiar QRS pattern or a previously unremarkable sinus ECG does not settle the mechanism. A previous ECG can be useful for comparison, but similar morphology is supporting context rather than a substitute for the current rhythm analysis. In a report, distinguish the observed broad regular tachycardia from the degree of confidence in a ventricular origin and from any unproven anatomical localisation.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: a regular tachycardia at 180/min has QRS duration 170 ms. All precordial QRS complexes are predominantly positive. No P waves can be identified confidently. What evidence supports the interpretation, and what does the absence of visible P waves mean?
steps: Describe the measured rate and broad regular complexes.
Identify positive precordial concordance as a supportive clue.
Avoid calling the lack of visible P waves proven AV dissociation.
Keep the current differential and any baseline comparison explicit.
guidedExercise.answer: Regular broad-complex tachycardia with positive precordial concordance, supporting a ventricular-origin interpretation; atrial relationships remain unresolved.
guidedExercise.explanation: A P wave that cannot be seen is different from a P wave demonstrated to be independent. Strong morphology clues should be reported without inventing atrial evidence.

objectives.coverageNote: Clinical management and outcome generalisations from the source are not converted into individual advice. The schematic exercise is not a validated diagnostic test.

objectives.title: Differentiate polymorphic VT, torsades and fibrillation
objectives.why: Describing rhythm organisation and the preceding QT interval prevents misuse of the term torsades de pointes.
know: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia has beat-to-beat variation in ventricular complex morphology. The varying amplitude and direction may make the QRS and T waves difficult to separate, but a sequence of ventricular complexes can still be recognised during an organised tachycardia. It is different from a single fixed broad-complex morphology.

Torsades de pointes is a form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with prolonged repolarisation, typically recognised by a prolonged QT interval in the preceding rhythm and a characteristic waxing-and-waning rotation of the complexes around the baseline. Not every polymorphic VT is torsades; a normal preceding QT directs attention to a different mechanism.

Ventricular flutter describes extremely rapid, relatively organised ventricular oscillation with poor separation between depolarisation and repolarisation. Ventricular fibrillation is disorganised activity in which reproducible P waves and discrete QRS complexes cannot be identified. The course illustrates transitions between ventricular tachycardia, flutter and fibrillation rather than fixed boundaries that every recording must display.

Before interpreting a chaotic trace, consider recording artefact and the full clinical situation. A surface waveform cannot establish whether a person has a pulse or is conscious. These are potentially life-threatening patterns in clinical practice and require immediate qualified assessment when encountered in a real patient. The exercises here teach recognition and limitations, not a resuscitation protocol or treatment selection.

steps.title: Assess organisation
steps.text: Ask whether individual ventricular complexes remain recognisable.

steps.title: Review the preceding rhythm
steps.text: Measure QT in a suitable non-tachycardic segment when available.

steps.title: Name with qualification
steps.text: Reserve torsades for a compatible polymorphic pattern with long-QT context.

example.question: A teaching description gives a twisting polymorphic tachycardia, preceded by a clearly prolonged QT interval.
working: The ventricular morphology varies from beat to beat.
The preceding prolonged QT supplies the repolarisation context.
This combination supports the specific torsades label, unlike morphology alone.
example.answer: Polymorphic VT compatible with torsades de pointes, in a long-QT context.

pitfalls: Calling every polymorphic VT torsades.
Diagnosing a clinical cardiac arrest from an isolated trace without assessing the patient.

practice.prompt: Which additional feature is central to a torsades interpretation?
options: A fixed normal sinus P before every QRS
A narrow QRS in all leads
practice.explanation: Torsades is a long-QT-associated polymorphic VT rather than a synonym for all polymorphic VT.
practice.hint: Look before the episode.

practice.prompt: Which description best fits ventricular fibrillation?
options: Disorganised ventricular activity without reproducible discrete QRS complexes
A normal PR interval and sinus rhythm
Alternating normal and premature ventricular beats
practice.explanation: VF lacks an organised recurring ventricular complex; patient assessment and artefact checks remain essential.
practice.hint: Look for loss of organised ventricular activation.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Ventricular tachycardia with varying QRS morphology from beat to beat.
A polymorphic VT associated with a long-QT repolarisation context and characteristic changing QRS axis/amplitude.

references.label: 2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death

deepDive.title: Distinguish changing morphology from loss of organisation
deepDive.text: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia has recognisable ventricular complexes whose morphology changes from beat to beat. Ventricular fibrillation instead lacks a stable organised QRS sequence. At very high rates, separating QRS from T becomes difficult, and the course places ventricular flutter near that boundary of organisation. Describe the actual features seen rather than forcing precise rate measurements onto an unstructured signal. Recording artefact can also look chaotic, so electrode quality and simultaneous clinical observation matter when interpreting a real record.

deepDive.title: Use the preceding QT context for torsades terminology
deepDive.text: The course describes torsades de pointes as a particular polymorphic VT associated with QT prolongation, often with phasic variation in polarity or amplitude. The important extra information is the repolarisation context before the episode. A twisting visual pattern alone should not be used as a synonym for every polymorphic tachycardia. Seek an interpretable preceding sinus or paced sequence, identify the end of T carefully and consider the correction method and rate. If no baseline repolarisation can be assessed, name the demonstrated polymorphic broad-complex pattern and state that the torsades context is uncertain.

deepDive.title: Report what can be assessed reliably
deepDive.text: In a rapidly changing rhythm, some conventional measurements become unreliable. A computer-generated rate, axis or interval can appear precise even when the underlying waveform does not support that precision. The course’s examples of progression between organised VT, flutter-like activity and fibrillation make continuity particularly useful: onset and preceding rhythm can clarify what an isolated middle segment cannot. Do not infer an electrolyte concentration, drug exposure or inherited channelopathy from the episode alone. These may be relevant contextual explanations, but they are additional evidence rather than properties measured directly by the ECG.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original comparison: record A has identifiable broad complexes with changing shape. Record B is chaotic without a reproducible QRS sequence. A separate interpretable strip before A has a markedly prolonged QT interval. Explain the descriptive distinction.
steps: Decide whether organised ventricular complexes remain identifiable.
Describe A as polymorphic tachycardia and B as fibrillation-like disorganised activity, subject to excluding artefact.
Use the preceding prolonged-QT context to consider torsades for A.
Do not assign a cause from morphology alone.
guidedExercise.answer: A supports a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia pattern; its preceding QT prolongation provides the context for considering torsades. B requires a different description because no organised QRS sequence is established.
guidedExercise.explanation: Organisation and repolarisation context answer different questions. Neither a twisting appearance nor a chaotic signal alone supplies a complete clinical explanation.
