title: Supraventricular rhythms with conduction disturbances
sourceFilename: D2-3 SV arrhythmias with conduction disturbances DipECG amended Mar2026.pdf
summary: Separate atrial rhythm from AV conduction and distinguish aberrant or blocked atrial ectopy from ventricular disease.

objectives.title: Recognise an atrial arrhythmia with an independent escape rhythm
objectives.why: Atrial fibrillation or flutter and complete AV block can coexist; one label does not replace the other.
know: Rhythm origin and AV conduction are separate parts of ECG interpretation. Atrial fibrillation describes disorganised atrial activity, whereas complete AV block describes failure of atrial impulses to activate the ventricles. The same recording can therefore contain both an atrial arrhythmia and an independent ventricular escape rhythm.

Ordinary atrial fibrillation with variable AV conduction produces an irregular ventricular response. A slow and unexpectedly regular ventricular rhythm in the presence of fibrillatory atrial activity should raise suspicion of advanced or complete AV block with an escape rhythm. This is a reason to investigate the relation, not a stand-alone proof: pacing, medicines and other junctional rhythms can also affect regularity.

In atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia, regular atrial activity may be visible independently of a slow ventricular rhythm. Examine whether flutter waves or P waves have a stable relationship to the QRS. A fixed integer ratio can represent conducted atrial activity; drifting relations over a sufficient segment suggest dissociation. The duration of recording and the clarity of atrial activity determine how confidently that distinction can be made.

QRS width helps describe the escape activation but does not precisely locate the block. A narrow junctional escape and a broad ventricular escape are useful patterns, yet pre-existing conduction disease can modify either appearance. Reports should preserve the atrial rhythm, the ventricular rate and regularity, QRS duration, and the evidence for failed conduction. Clinical significance and management require the patient’s condition and context.

steps.title: Identify atrial activity
steps.text: Distinguish fibrillatory waves, flutter activity or discrete atrial P waves.

steps.title: Check ventricular regularity
steps.text: A slow regular response in AF needs an explanation.

steps.title: Report both components
steps.text: Name the atrial rhythm and describe the independent escape or conduction pattern.

example.question: Hypothetical tracing: fibrillatory baseline, no consistent P waves and a narrow-QRS rhythm at a regular 38/min.
working: The atrial appearance supports AF.
The slow regular ventricular response is atypical for ordinary variable conduction in AF.
Consider an independent escape rhythm and assess for AV block, pacing and other explanations.
example.answer: AF with a slow regular ventricular response, suspicious for advanced/complete AV block with an escape rhythm; further assessment is needed.

pitfalls: Assuming all AF must have an irregular ventricular response under every circumstance.
Calling a conduction disturbance the entire rhythm diagnosis.

practice.prompt: What should AF with a slow regular ventricular rhythm prompt?
options: Assessment for AV block or an independent/paced ventricular rhythm
A conclusion that all AV conduction is normal
practice.explanation: Regularisation of the ventricular response needs a mechanism explanation.
practice.hint: AF describes the atria.

practice.prompt: Which report preserves the important distinction?
options: Complete block only; atrial rhythm is irrelevant
Atrial flutter with evidence of an independent slow escape rhythm
Sinus rhythm whenever QRS is regular
practice.explanation: Atrial rhythm and ventricular conduction should both be described.
practice.hint: Two layers of interpretation can coexist.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: A rhythm maintained by a subsidiary pacemaker when dominant impulses are too slow or fail to arrive.
A ventricular response in AF that becomes unusually regular, requiring assessment for pacing, block or another pacemaker.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Describe the atria and ventricles separately
deepDive.text: An atrial rhythm and an AV-conduction disturbance can coexist. The lecture explicitly treats complete AV block as a conduction problem rather than an atrial rhythm. Therefore a report may need two linked descriptions: the atrial process, such as fibrillatory or flutter-like activity, and the mechanism controlling ventricular activation. A slow regular ventricular rhythm during atrial fibrillation is a clue that the ventricles may be following an independent escape focus rather than the usual variably conducted atrial impulses. It is a reason to investigate the relationship, not a reason to stop analysing the recording.

deepDive.title: Use regularisation as evidence to examine
deepDive.text: In AF, ventricular timing is commonly irregular when atrial impulses reach the ventricular conduction system variably. If that response becomes strikingly regular and slow, compare the QRS morphology and the longer sequence. Narrow and broad escape examples are both included in the course. In flutter or atrial tachycardia, atrial events may be individually trackable; determine whether their positions drift relative to QRS rather than maintaining a consistent conduction ratio. A ratio that looks nearly fixed over only a few cycles may reflect coincident rates, so enough continuous recording is needed.

deepDive.title: Avoid reconstructing a PR interval where no P exists
deepDive.text: In fibrillatory atrial activity there may be no consistent discrete P onset from which to measure PR. Do not manufacture an interval from an arbitrary baseline oscillation. Instead describe the atrial appearance, ventricular rate and regularity, and whether the QRS sequence appears independent. Flutter-like activity can provide a different atrial clock, but wave visibility may change across leads. The label should match what is actually demonstrable. Clinical causes of slow conduction or escape activity require additional history and assessment; they are not established solely by recognising that the atrial and ventricular descriptions differ.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: the baseline has fibrillatory activity without consistent P waves. QRS complexes are narrow and occur every 1.5 seconds over a prolonged segment. Explain what should be investigated.
steps: Recognise the approximately 40/min ventricular rhythm.
Describe its unusual regularity in the setting of fibrillatory atrial activity.
Consider an independent junctional escape rhythm with impaired AV conduction.
Seek longer continuous evidence and relevant context rather than measuring an artificial PR interval.
guidedExercise.answer: Fibrillatory atrial activity with a slow regular narrow-QRS ventricular rhythm raises concern for an independent escape mechanism and advanced or complete AV-conduction disturbance.
guidedExercise.explanation: The atrial rhythm and ventricular mechanism must both be described. Regularisation is a useful clue, but a complete clinical conclusion needs confirmation beyond an isolated description.

objectives.coverageNote: Atrial arrhythmia/escape source examples are mapped; the original strips are required to inspect their atrial baseline appearances.

objectives.title: Identify aberrant supraventricular conduction and Ashman patterns
objectives.why: A supraventricular impulse can produce a broad QRS when a bundle branch is temporarily refractory.
know: Aberrant conduction is altered ventricular activation of an impulse that originates above the ventricles. A premature atrial impulse may reach a bundle branch before that branch has recovered, creating a broad QRS despite supraventricular origin. The altered shape is therefore a property of conduction, not proof that the beat originated in a ventricle.

Look for a premature atrial P wave before the broad QRS, compare the initial QRS forces with ordinarily conducted beats, and examine the cycle lengths leading into the event. Some atrial tachycardias begin with narrow QRS complexes before developing a bundle-branch pattern as rate or refractoriness changes. This can support aberrancy, while still requiring consideration of competing explanations.

The Ashman phenomenon is classically seen in atrial fibrillation when a relatively long RR interval is followed by a shorter interval and an aberrantly conducted beat. Recovery properties after the longer cycle influence conduction of the next early impulse. The lecture also shows consecutive aberrant beats, so a run of broad QRS complexes is not automatically a ventricular run.

A long–short sequence, a recognised bundle-branch morphology and lack of a typical post-ectopic pause can support aberrancy, but no one feature is an absolute discriminator. Atrial fibrillation, ventricular ectopy and pre-excitation can coexist. Use multiple leads, consistent timing evidence and a sufficiently long segment, and state the limitation if the origin of broad complexes remains uncertain.

steps.title: Find the trigger
steps.text: Identify a premature P wave or a long–short RR sequence.

steps.title: Compare activation
steps.text: Assess the QRS onset and bundle-branch-like terminal change.

steps.title: Keep a differential
steps.text: Do not use a single timing sign to exclude ventricular ectopy or pre-excitation.

example.question: Teaching example: AF contains a long RR interval followed by a short one and a broad RBBB-shaped QRS. Other beats are narrow.
working: The long–short sequence is compatible with cycle-dependent refractoriness.
The bundle-branch-like morphology supports aberrant conduction.
Additional evidence is needed before excluding a ventricular premature beat.
example.answer: An Ashman-type aberrant beat is a plausible interpretation, qualified by the available evidence.

pitfalls: Calling every broad beat in AF a ventricular premature beat.
Assuming a long–short RR sequence proves aberrancy.

practice.prompt: The classic Ashman sequence is:
options: A relatively long RR followed by a short RR and aberrant conduction
A long PR followed by atrial standstill
A pacing spike followed by no QRS
practice.explanation: Cycle-dependent bundle refractoriness can broaden a supraventricularly initiated QRS after a long–short sequence.
practice.hint: Compare neighbouring RR intervals.

practice.prompt: Can consecutive broad beats always be called VT?
options: No; aberrantly conducted supraventricular sequences are also possible
Only when there are exactly three
practice.explanation: Runs require mechanism assessment rather than classification by QRS width alone.
practice.hint: Origin and conduction are distinct.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Abnormal ventricular conduction of a supraventricular impulse.
Cycle-length-dependent aberrant conduction classically associated with a long–short RR sequence in AF.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia

deepDive.title: Trace the atrial trigger before interpreting a broad beat
deepDive.text: A supraventricular impulse can activate the ventricles with an unusual QRS if part of the ventricular conduction system is still refractory or has a fixed conduction abnormality. An early P wave followed by a broad QRS can therefore represent aberrantly conducted atrial ectopy. Look for a change in the preceding T-wave contour, a reproducible atrial deflection in another lead and a plausible P-to-QRS relationship. A broad complex with no obvious P is not automatically ventricular, because the atrial event may be concealed. Conversely, a coincident small deflection should not be promoted to a proven trigger without timing evidence.

deepDive.title: Connect cycle-length history with refractoriness
deepDive.text: The Ashman examples link a relatively long ventricular cycle followed by a short cycle with aberrant conduction of the early response. The concept is that the conduction system’s recovery depends on the preceding timing, so a short-coupled impulse may encounter incomplete recovery after a longer cycle. The course shows that more than one consecutive aberrantly conducted complex can occur. A run of broad events in AF is therefore not classified solely by its length. Inspect the initiating long–short relation, the initial and terminal QRS portions, and the variability of the underlying rhythm.

deepDive.title: Combine clues rather than treating them as proof
deepDive.text: The lecture notes familiar clues such as relatively narrow initial activation with later broadening and the absence of a conspicuous post-event pause. They support an aberrancy interpretation but should not become absolute rules excluding ventricular ectopy or tachycardia. Compare multiple events, available leads and any previous ECG. An irregular broad run can have more than one possible mechanism, including pre-excitation in the appropriate context. State which features make aberrancy plausible and which missing information prevents a definitive mechanism. That approach is more defensible than deciding that any long–short sequence settles the diagnosis.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: during an irregular rhythm, a 1.2-second RR interval is followed by a 0.45-second RR interval ending in a broad QRS. The broad complex begins similarly to neighbouring narrow complexes but has an altered terminal portion. What is the reasoning?
steps: Identify the long–short sequence.
Compare the initial and terminal activation rather than overall width alone.
Consider rate-dependent aberrancy in the context of the atrial rhythm.
Retain ventricular ectopy and other mechanisms if supporting atrial or multi-lead evidence is incomplete.
guidedExercise.answer: The timing and morphology support an Ashman-type aberrantly conducted response, but do not independently exclude every ventricular-origin event.
guidedExercise.explanation: The mechanism is inferred from cycle history and activation features together. A single supportive sign should not be stated as a definitive diagnostic rule.

objectives.coverageNote: All aberrancy/Ashman lecture text reviewed. The newly constructed timing example does not replace the multi-beat original strips.

objectives.title: Distinguish blocked atrial ectopy from sinus pauses and 2:1 block
objectives.why: A hidden premature P wave can create a pause or apparent bradycardia without sinus arrest or true alternate sinus block.
know: A premature atrial beat can arrive while the AV conduction system is refractory and produce no QRS response. The atrial depolarisation still exists: the diagnostic task is to find its early P wave, often deforming the T wave of the previous beat. Calling the resulting interval a sinus pause without checking for that event loses the mechanism.

In non-conducted atrial bigeminy, each baseline atrial beat is followed by a premature atrial impulse that fails to conduct. The ventricular rhythm can therefore be slow and regular enough to resemble sinus bradycardia or 2:1 AV block. The atrial rhythm contains alternating ordinary and premature events, even if some are difficult to see.

Compare atrial timing and P-wave morphology. In genuine sinus rhythm with 2:1 AV block, the atrial impulses are normally timed and generally share a consistent sinus morphology. With atrial bigeminy, the ectopic P arrives early and may have a different shape, followed by a reset or altered atrial interval. A single lead can hide these differences, making multi-lead examination important.

The distinction is not decided by ventricular rate alone. Mark expected sinus P positions, inspect suspicious T-wave notches and compare the same event across leads. A short or noisy recording may not show enough evidence, in which case “pause associated with a suspected non-conducted premature atrial beat” is more defensible than a falsely precise sinus-node or AV-block diagnosis.

steps.title: Mark expected sinus events
steps.text: Project the baseline PP timing across the apparent pause.

steps.title: Inspect the preceding T wave
steps.text: Look for a premature deflection at a different atrial coupling interval.

steps.title: Compare morphology and intervals
steps.text: Decide whether alternate P waves are normal and on time or ectopic and early.

example.question: Hypothetical slow rhythm contains an early unusual P deforming each preceding T wave, with no QRS after that early P.
working: The extra P is premature rather than a normal sinus impulse.
Its missing ventricular response is compatible with blocked atrial ectopy.
The repeated pattern explains apparent ventricular bradycardia.
example.answer: Non-conducted atrial bigeminy is supported; do not automatically report sinus bradycardia or 2:1 AV block.

pitfalls: Ignoring T-wave deformation during pauses.
Defining 2:1 block only from a ventricular rate that is half an assumed atrial rate.

practice.prompt: What favours a non-conducted atrial premature beat over a sinus pause?
options: An early abnormal P wave distorting the preceding T wave
practice.explanation: The hidden premature atrial activation explains why a ventricular response is absent.
practice.hint: Inspect the T wave before the pause.

practice.prompt: What favours true 2:1 sinus AV block rather than atrial bigeminy?
options: Regular, normally timed P waves of consistent sinus morphology
Alternating early P waves with different morphology
practice.explanation: Atrial timing distinguishes failure of normal impulses from premature ectopic activity.
practice.hint: Use atrial timing, not just ventricular rate.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: An early atrial depolarisation that is not followed by a ventricular QRS response.
A repeating atrial pattern in which baseline atrial beats alternate with premature atrial beats.

deepDive.title: Search for an early atrial event inside the T wave
deepDive.text: A non-conducted premature atrial impulse can create an apparent pause even though the sinus node has not simply stopped producing visible activity. The critical event may be an early P wave superimposed on the preceding T wave. Compare that T wave with adjacent T waves and inspect leads in which atrial activity is clearer. If a notch is reproducible at a plausible early atrial time, it may account for the pause. If the deflection is uncertain, preserve that uncertainty instead of declaring a mechanism from one contour difference.

deepDive.title: Compare atrial timing and morphology in alternating patterns
deepDive.text: Blocked atrial bigeminy can resemble sinus bradycardia because every second atrial event fails to produce a ventricular response. It can also resemble 2:1 AV block if one notices only two atrial deflections per QRS. The course separates these by the behaviour of the atrial sequence: sinus impulses in 2:1 conduction are comparatively regularly scheduled, whereas atrial bigeminy introduces an early atrial event, often with a different morphology. Measure PP timing, identify whether the second event is premature and compare P-wave shapes. The ventricular ratio alone does not distinguish these mechanisms.

deepDive.title: Explain why this matters to the report
deepDive.text: The same ventricular count can arise from very different atrial sequences. A report that says only “sinus bradycardia” loses the possibility of concealed ectopy; a report that says only “2:1 block” may imply failure of normally scheduled sinus impulses that has not been demonstrated. The evidence should specify the atrial event that is early, whether it conducts, and how the subsequent rhythm resumes. The lecture also shows normally conducted, aberrantly conducted and non-conducted atrial premature beats, illustrating that one atrial ectopic mechanism can produce several ventricular appearances depending on conduction timing.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: each sinus P is followed 420 ms later by a differently shaped small atrial deflection on the T wave. That early deflection has no QRS response. The next sinus P then resumes. Compare blocked atrial bigeminy with 2:1 AV block.
steps: Establish the early timing of the second atrial deflection.
Compare its morphology with the sinus P wave.
Separate the atrial event from its absent ventricular response.
Ask whether the atrial pattern is alternating prematurity rather than a regular sinus train.
guidedExercise.answer: The description favours non-conducted premature atrial activity in a bigeminal pattern rather than a regularly timed sinus sequence with 2:1 AV block.
guidedExercise.explanation: The distinction depends on atrial timing and morphology, not simply on counting two atrial events for each ventricular event. The original simultaneous leads can improve confidence when the early P is hidden.

objectives.coverageNote: Source quiz examples are referenced without copying their images or asserting a new diagnosis from an unseen tracing.

objectives.title: Describe atrial tachycardia with partial AV conduction
objectives.why: The ventricular rhythm does not necessarily reveal the atrial rate or mechanism.
know: Atrial tachycardia can continue at a rapid regular atrial rate while only some atrial impulses conduct to the ventricles. The ventricular response may consequently be slower than the atrial rhythm, and may be regular with a fixed conduction ratio or irregular when the degree of conduction changes.

The important first step is to identify repeating atrial activity across the entire trace. The course highlights P waves hidden within T waves and uses V1 as a helpful view in several examples. No lead is guaranteed to show atrial activity best in every patient, so compare several leads instead of limiting the search to one rhythm strip.

If two atrial impulses occur for every QRS, state 2:1 AV conduction. A longer sequence may show progressive PR changes and grouped ventricular responses compatible with Wenckebach conduction. Describe the observed relationship rather than using the ventricular rate to infer the atrial rate or calling every irregular ventricular response atrial fibrillation.

An organised atrial tachycardia with partial conduction should also be distinguished from complete AV block with an unrelated escape rhythm. In partial conduction, conducted atrial impulses retain a demonstrable relation to their QRS complexes. In a sustained interval of complete block, no atrial impulses conduct. Surface recordings may be limited, and the final report should separate the atrial rhythm, conduction pattern and degree of diagnostic confidence.

steps.title: Count the atria
steps.text: Measure repeated P–P intervals independently of the QRS.

steps.title: Count the ventricles
steps.text: Calculate the response rate and establish regularity.

steps.title: Demonstrate the relation
steps.text: Show which P waves conduct and whether the ratio or PR sequence changes.

example.question: Hypothetical atrial tachycardia is 200/min and alternate P waves conduct with a consistent PR interval.
working: The atrial cycle is 0.30 s.
Two atrial impulses occur per ventricular response.
The expected ventricular response is 100/min.
example.answer: Atrial tachycardia with 2:1 AV conduction, giving a ventricular rate of 100/min.

pitfalls: Calling variable ventricular conduction AF without examining atrial organisation.
Assuming the ventricular rate equals the atrial rate.

practice.prompt: An atrial rate of 180/min with fixed 2:1 conduction gives which ventricular rate?
practice.explanation: Only one of every two atrial impulses conducts: 180 ÷ 2 = 90.
practice.hint: Divide by the conduction denominator.

practice.prompt: What distinguishes partial conduction from complete AV block?
options: Some atrial impulses demonstrably activate the ventricles
The atrial rhythm is always sinus
practice.explanation: Demonstrated conducted beats establish that AV conduction is not completely absent during that segment.
practice.hint: Follow an atrial impulse into its QRS.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: A changing proportion of atrial impulses producing ventricular responses.
A tachycardia originating in atrial tissue, often with organised atrial activity distinct from ordinary sinus rhythm.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia

deepDive.title: Distinguish the atrial rate from the displayed ventricular rate
deepDive.text: Atrial tachycardia does not require a ventricular response to every atrial impulse. If the atrial rate is high and conduction is partial, the ventricular rate can be substantially slower and can even appear relatively ordinary. Find the atrial sequence first, measure its intervals and then count the ventricular responses. In a 2:1 relationship the atrial rate is approximately double the ventricular rate. In a varying conduction sequence the ventricular timing can be irregular despite an organised atrial rhythm. This is why the ventricular rate alone cannot identify or exclude an atrial tachycardia.

deepDive.title: Predict hidden atrial activity from visible cycles
deepDive.text: Once a stable atrial interval is identified, project that interval through the QRS and T waves to search for concealed atrial deflections. The course’s 2:1 examples show alternating changes in the T-wave region depending on whether a P falls there. Use several cycles and more than one lead so that a repeated atrial event is not confused with normal repolarisation shape. In a 3:2 sequence, inspect conducted PR intervals for a Wenckebach-like progression. Do not simply call the ventricular irregularity AF when a repeatable atrial clock can be demonstrated.

deepDive.title: Report the atrial mechanism and conduction pattern independently
deepDive.text: The term atrial tachycardia with block combines two claims: an organised fast atrial rhythm and incomplete conduction towards the ventricles. Each needs its own evidence. An abnormal P-wave appearance can support a non-sinus atrial origin, while a repeating conduction relationship describes the ventricular response. If the atrial waveform is inadequately seen, the safest description may be a suspected organised atrial tachyarrhythmia with partial conduction. Avoid inferring a specific anatomical focus, drug effect or mechanism of the AV-conduction limitation from this surface pattern alone. Those are further interpretations requiring additional information.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: discrete atrial events occur every 300 ms. Most QRS responses follow alternate atrial events, but a later segment contains three atrial events for two QRS complexes with progressive PR change. Construct a two-part description.
steps: Calculate the atrial rate as approximately 200/min.
Describe the initial 2:1 AV relationship and approximate 100/min ventricular response.
Analyse the later 3:2 sequence separately.
Assess whether the measured PR behaviour supports Wenckebach conduction in that segment.
guidedExercise.answer: An organised atrial tachycardia-like rhythm near 200/min with changing partial AV conduction, initially 2:1 and later a 3:2 Wenckebach-like sequence if the PR progression is confirmed.
guidedExercise.explanation: A changing ventricular response does not necessarily mean a changing atrial rhythm. The atrial clock and AV-conduction pattern answer separate questions.

title: VT versus supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy
sourceFilename: D2-4 VT vs aberrant SVT DipECG reviewed Mar2026.pdf
summary: Use a structured differential for broad-complex tachycardia, recognising strong signs and important exceptions.

objectives.title: Build the differential for a regular broad-complex tachycardia
objectives.why: Broad complexes identify abnormal ventricular activation, not automatically the anatomical origin of the tachycardia.
know: A regular broad-complex tachycardia can arise from the ventricles or from a supraventricular rhythm conducted abnormally through the ventricles. Pre-existing bundle branch block, rate-related aberrancy, pre-excitation and pacing all affect QRS morphology and belong in the broader mechanism assessment.

The initial interpretation should describe the observable facts: ventricular rate, regularity, QRS width and morphology, frontal axis, atrial activity and recording quality. This allows an unresolved mechanism to be communicated accurately without pretending that a label is certain. A twelve-lead recording generally provides more discriminating information than one short monitor lead.

A prior sinus-rhythm ECG can be valuable. A closely matching pre-existing bundle branch pattern supports supraventricular tachycardia with that conduction pattern, although comparison must be careful because ventricular tachycardia may sometimes resemble familiar bundle morphologies. Conversely, a new and very unusual morphology can support a ventricular origin without serving as absolute proof.

The course emphasises not dismissing ventricular tachycardia simply because a rhythm is tolerated or the patient is young. Clinical stability, age and a visually typical bundle pattern cannot settle the mechanism alone. In real practice, unresolved broad-complex tachycardia warrants prompt qualified assessment. This objective explains interpretation and reporting; it deliberately avoids giving drug, shock or procedural instructions.

steps.title: Describe the recording
steps.text: State the measured rhythm features without choosing the origin prematurely.

steps.title: Compare prior activation
steps.text: Look for a genuine prior sinus ECG with matching or differing QRS morphology.

steps.title: Retain uncertainty
steps.text: Report broad-complex tachycardia of uncertain mechanism when appropriate.

example.question: A hypothetical 160/min regular broad-complex rhythm resembles LBBB. A prior sinus ECG shows a very similar LBBB pattern.
working: The prior tracing supplies a plausible baseline conduction abnormality.
The similarity supports a supraventricular rhythm with pre-existing LBBB.
It is supportive evidence rather than a stand-alone guarantee against VT.
example.answer: SVT with pre-existing LBBB becomes plausible; integrate atrial and morphological evidence before reaching a final mechanism.

pitfalls: Using clinical tolerance as proof of SVT.
Treating a typical BBB shape as an absolute exclusion of VT.

practice.prompt: A stable patient has a broad-complex tachycardia. Does stability exclude VT?
practice.explanation: VT may be haemodynamically tolerated; clinical stability does not establish supraventricular origin.
practice.hint: Mechanism and tolerance are different questions.

practice.prompt: Which additional recording is particularly helpful?
options: A prior twelve-lead ECG during sinus rhythm
A photograph of the paper colour
Only the machine’s final automated label
A blood-pressure number without an ECG
practice.explanation: It allows comparison with known baseline conduction morphology.
practice.hint: Establish a baseline.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: A tachycardia with widened ventricular complexes; it describes activation without alone specifying origin.
A conduction change that emerges at particular cycle lengths or rates.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia
2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death

deepDive.title: Begin with the shared descriptive phenotype
deepDive.text: Regular broad-complex tachycardia is the starting observation, not the final mechanism. VT and supraventricular tachycardia conducted with fixed or functional bundle-branch abnormality can both produce this phenotype. Pre-excited mechanisms and paced rhythms may also need consideration when the complete context supports them. Measure rate and duration, assess regularity over a sufficiently long segment and inspect the quality of the signal. An automatic machine label or a single familiar-looking QRS should not replace these basic observations. The course provides contrasting examples specifically to show how similar appearances can arise by different routes.

deepDive.title: Use baseline comparison as one strand of evidence
deepDive.text: A previous sinus ECG can show whether the person already has a bundle-branch pattern and whether that morphology resembles the tachycardia. The lecture pairs a tachycardia example with a sinus-rhythm ECG from the same person to demonstrate the value of comparison. However, a baseline tracing must genuinely belong to the same patient and be recorded with comparable lead placement. Similarity is informative but should still be integrated with atrial relationships, onset and other morphology clues. Absence of a previous conduction defect does not establish ventricular origin, because aberrancy may be rate-related.

deepDive.title: Keep age, history and morphology in their proper roles
deepDive.text: Context changes how plausible different explanations are, but it does not make a waveform criterion infallible. The source includes both a young person with aberrant SVT and an outflow-tract VT that can resemble a bundle-branch pattern. Therefore neither youth nor a typical-looking BBB morphology is a guarantee. A well-structured interpretation states the differential, identifies the features favouring one mechanism and acknowledges what cannot be resolved from the available recording. It should not quote population proportions as though they were a certainty about the particular tracing being assessed.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: a regular rhythm at 165/min has 150-ms QRS complexes. A prior sinus ECG shows an apparently similar LBBB pattern. No atrial activity is clearly visible during tachycardia. What does the comparison establish?
steps: Confirm the descriptive broad regular tachycardia.
Verify that the comparison ECG is relevant and comparable.
Use morphology similarity as support for SVT with pre-existing conduction abnormality.
Retain the unresolved atrial relationship and ventricular differential.
guidedExercise.answer: The baseline similarity supports SVT with an existing LBBB pattern, but the supplied information does not alone establish the tachycardia mechanism.
guidedExercise.explanation: Comparison contributes evidence; it does not supply absent atrial timing or prove that a ventricular rhythm could not produce a similar pattern.

objectives.coverageNote: The differential lecture text is fully reviewed. Numerical prevalence statements and diagnostic absolutes are not reproduced as individual probabilities.

objectives.title: Use AV dissociation, capture and fusion as high-value evidence
objectives.why: Independent atrial activity and occasional conducted or fused beats can provide stronger evidence than width alone.
know: During ventricular tachycardia, ventricular activation may proceed independently of sinus atrial activation. Visible P waves can therefore march through the ventricular complexes and T waves without a fixed PR interval. Detecting this relationship in several leads is a high-value observation in a broad-complex tachycardia.

A capture beat occurs when a supraventricular impulse reaches the ventricles at a moment when it can activate them, producing an otherwise conducted complex amid ventricular tachycardia. A fusion beat results when supraventricular and ventricular wavefronts both contribute, creating a morphology intermediate between the ordinary conducted complex and the tachycardia complex.

The timing matters as much as the shape. A merely narrow-looking or unusual beat is not automatically capture or fusion: artefact, changing aberrancy, pacing and superimposed atrial activity can mislead. Search for the preceding P wave and compare the candidate complex with baseline and tachycardia morphology before naming it.

Convincing AV dissociation with capture or fusion strongly supports ventricular tachycardia in the appropriate broad-complex-tachycardia setting. Yet these signs are often absent or concealed, so their absence is not a reliable exclusion test. Independence of atria and ventricles can also occur with other ventricular or junctional rhythms; interpretation must remain tied to the rate, context and full activation pattern rather than a decontextualised slogan.

steps.title: Find atrial markers
steps.text: Follow plausible P waves through several ventricular cycles.

steps.title: Validate an unusual beat
steps.text: Check its timing and relation to baseline conducted QRS morphology.

steps.title: State the strength of evidence
steps.text: Explain why convincing capture or fusion supports a ventricular mechanism.

example.question: A hypothetical 170/min broad rhythm contains P waves at 80/min with drifting PR relations; one appropriately timed P is followed by a QRS matching the prior sinus QRS.
working: The atrial and ventricular rates are different.
The varying relation supports AV dissociation.
The isolated baseline-like complex after a plausible conducted P is a convincing capture beat.
example.answer: The combination strongly supports ventricular tachycardia.

pitfalls: Calling any isolated narrow complex a capture beat.
Excluding VT because no P waves are visible.

practice.prompt: What best validates a suspected capture beat?
options: Appropriate atrial timing and a QRS consistent with conducted activation
practice.explanation: Both timing and morphology should support successful supraventricular activation.
practice.hint: Shape alone is not enough.

practice.prompt: Failure to find fusion beats during a broad tachycardia means:
options: The observation is non-exclusionary because fusion is often not visible
practice.explanation: Useful diagnostic signs may be specific but not consistently present.
practice.hint: Absence of a clue is not proof of the opposite.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Successful supraventricular activation of the ventricles during an otherwise ventricular rhythm.
A QRS appearance created by simultaneous contributions from different ventricular activation wavefronts.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia
2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death

deepDive.title: Search for a genuinely independent atrial sequence
deepDive.text: AV dissociation is not equivalent to failing to see P waves. It requires positive evidence that identifiable atrial activity follows a timing sequence independent of the ventricular rhythm. Track several atrial deflections and show that their positions change relative to QRS complexes. A single small deflection can be noise or a repolarisation feature. A convincing independent sequence in a broad-complex tachycardia is a high-value clue to a ventricular mechanism, but its visibility depends on lead choice, rate, recording duration and whether atrial events are obscured by the ventricular waveform.

deepDive.title: Explain a capture event through timing
deepDive.text: A capture-like beat occurs when a supraventricular impulse activates the ventricles during a predominantly ventricular-origin rhythm and produces a complex resembling the usual conducted QRS. To support that interpretation, identify a plausible preceding atrial impulse, compare the complex with a known conducted baseline if available, and examine the timing within the surrounding tachycardia. A relatively narrow beat alone is insufficient: changing aberrancy or recording variation may also alter width. The source uses capture together with atrial independence to demonstrate why an event’s place in a sequence is more informative than its isolated shape.

deepDive.title: Explain fusion as combined contribution, then state the limit
deepDive.text: Fusion describes a QRS generated by contributions from a ventricular-origin wavefront and a conducted supraventricular wavefront. Its morphology can be intermediate between the tachycardia and the normal conducted complex. The surface ECG does not directly display the meeting of those wavefronts, so the interpretation rests on waveform comparison and plausible timing. Capture and fusion may be absent even in VT because the necessary timing opportunity does not occur during the recording. Do not invert a useful positive clue into an exclusion rule. State whether the evidence is convincing, possible or not assessable.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: a broad regular tachycardia contains a sequence of P waves that drifts through QRS and T. One appropriately timed P is followed by a narrow complex matching the person’s baseline QRS. Explain the high-value evidence.
steps: Demonstrate the independent atrial clock over multiple cycles.
Compare the unusual narrow complex with the baseline conducted morphology.
Assess whether the preceding P-to-QRS timing plausibly represents ventricular capture.
Use both observations together when discussing the mechanism.
guidedExercise.answer: The independent atrial sequence and a convincing capture-like event strongly support a ventricular-origin tachycardia.
guidedExercise.explanation: The argument uses positive atrial timing and an event consistent with conducted capture. Merely invisible P waves or one uncontextualised narrow complex would provide weaker evidence.

objectives.coverageNote: Source illustrations inform the mechanism explanation; the exercise does not claim to reproduce their exact timings or to validate every apparent fusion beat.

objectives.title: Combine morphology and axis clues without using absolutes
objectives.why: The same bundle-branch-like appearance can be produced by different mechanisms, so ECG features should be weighed together.
know: QRS morphology reflects where ventricular activation begins and how it propagates. An impulse arriving normally through part of the conduction system may preserve a relatively rapid initial deflection before delayed terminal activation. Ventricular-origin activation may be slower initially, although the relationship is not universal.

The course compares a typical LBBB appearance during supraventricular tachycardia with an outflow-tract ventricular tachycardia that also has a left-bundle-type pattern. This is a useful demonstration that familiar pattern recognition must be combined with timing, atrial activity, axis and comparison with prior ECGs. A typical bundle pattern supports an explanation but is not a mechanism certificate.

Very broad QRS complexes, extreme frontal axis, precordial concordance and an unusual initial activation pattern can increase suspicion of ventricular tachycardia. None should be applied without checking lead placement, baseline conduction disease and signal quality. There are exceptions, and diagnostic algorithms work by combining observations rather than by elevating a single clue to certainty.

When teaching from schematics, state which features were deliberately built into the example and which are not represented. A stylised waveform cannot demonstrate a real patient’s entire twelve-lead morphology or prove an arrhythmia mechanism. In reports, list the observed clues and give an appropriately qualified conclusion; if evidence conflicts or key leads are absent, preserve that uncertainty.

steps.title: Inspect the onset
steps.text: Compare initial versus terminal QRS activation in informative leads.

steps.title: Add frontal and precordial views
steps.text: Assess axis and concordance across the available leads.

steps.title: Combine, do not cherry-pick
steps.text: Integrate features with atrial evidence and prior ECG comparison.

example.question: A teaching case has a broad tachycardia with an inferior axis and a left-bundle-type pattern, but no visible independent P waves.
working: The morphology can occur with an outflow-tract VT.
It can also resemble supraventricular activation with LBBB.
Lack of visible AV dissociation does not settle the question.
example.answer: The pattern alone cannot prove SVT; VT remains in the differential.

pitfalls: Assuming that all ventricular tachycardias have an extreme axis.
Reading an unlabelled synthetic single-lead strip as a full twelve-lead ECG.

practice.prompt: Which statement is safest?
options: A typical BBB morphology excludes VT
An extreme axis is required for VT
Morphology clues should be integrated with atrial timing and context
QRS width alone always decides origin
practice.explanation: The lecture shows overlapping patterns and stresses that absence of characteristic VT signs does not exclude VT.
practice.hint: Use combined evidence.

practice.prompt: What is precordial concordance?
options: Dominant QRS polarity is the same across chest leads
Every lead has the same numerical voltage
Atrial and ventricular rates are equal
practice.explanation: It describes the distribution of ventricular polarity across precordial leads.
practice.hint: Think of polarity across V1–V6.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: The earliest phase of ventricular depolarisation represented at QRS onset.
A markedly abnormal frontal QRS direction; interpret it together with morphology and lead validity.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia
2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death

deepDive.title: Examine the beginning and end of ventricular activation
deepDive.text: The course contrasts a relatively sharp initial deflection followed by delayed terminal activation with a complex that is broad from its onset. This comparison connects morphology with the possible route of activation: a supraventricular impulse may initially recruit normal conduction tissue before delayed activation becomes evident, whereas a ventricular-origin wavefront can have abnormal early spread. These are useful patterns to inspect, not universal exclusions. Measure the whole QRS, inspect more than one lead and avoid drawing the onset from an unclear baseline or a pacing artefact.

deepDive.title: Combine spatial views rather than counting disconnected signs
deepDive.text: Axis and precordial concordance describe different aspects of ventricular activation. An unusual frontal axis concerns net limb-lead direction, while concordance concerns the predominant polarity across chest leads. Their combination may strengthen a ventricular-origin interpretation, but a missing feature does not exclude it. A normal-looking axis or discordant precordial pattern can occur in ventricular tachycardia. Similarly, a bundle-branch-like shape can support aberrancy without proving it. The source explicitly warns that features commonly associated with SVT may also be present in VT, so a checklist should not be treated as a score with guaranteed performance.

deepDive.title: Tie every inference to a measurement or observation
deepDive.text: A stronger report explains what made the axis unusual, which chest leads were concordant and where the initial activation was broad or sharp. This is more auditable than stating “morphology suggests VT” without showing the evidence. Also record contradictions: for example, a familiar BBB pattern may coexist with a strongly abnormal axis. Contradictory clues should prompt a qualified conclusion and consideration of a longer recording or baseline ECG rather than selective reporting. The final confidence should reflect the whole record and its limitations, including lead placement, signal quality and the availability of atrial evidence.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: a broad tachycardia has a BBB-like shape, an extreme frontal axis and predominantly negative QRS complexes across the chest leads. How should the apparently conflicting clues be integrated?
steps: Describe the familiar BBB-like feature without calling it diagnostic.
Confirm the axis calculation from the limb leads.
State which chest leads show concordance.
Integrate the unusual spatial pattern with atrial and baseline evidence.
guidedExercise.answer: A BBB-like appearance alone does not settle the mechanism; the extreme axis and negative precordial concordance add evidence favouring a ventricular-origin interpretation.
guidedExercise.explanation: The exercise demonstrates combination rather than an absolute rule. No single clue is allowed to erase stronger or conflicting information in the rest of the tracing.

objectives.coverageNote: All morphology/axis differential text reviewed. No diagnostic algorithm performance or numeric accuracy is invented for these qualitative teaching clues.

objectives.title: Write a qualified broad-complex-tachycardia conclusion
objectives.why: A useful report conveys what is observed, what mechanism is supported and what remains unresolved.
know: A broad-complex-tachycardia report should begin with the ventricular rate, regularity and QRS duration. Add the leading morphology and axis observations. State whether atrial activity is identifiable and whether a reproducible atrioventricular relationship, dissociation, capture or fusion can be demonstrated.

Separate direct findings from interpretation. “Regular broad-complex tachycardia with AV dissociation and a capture beat, strongly supporting VT” tells the reader why the conclusion is being made. “Regular broad-complex tachycardia; mechanism unresolved on this single-lead recording” is also a valid result when the evidence is genuinely incomplete.

Do not copy population percentages into the probability for an individual teaching case without knowing the relevant population, selection and clinical context. The course’s prevalence-oriented reminders encourage caution about excluding VT; they are not a substitute for measuring and explaining the particular tracing.

Where available, review a prior twelve-lead ECG, onset or termination recording and clinical context. A clear differential can include VT, SVT with pre-existing or rate-related aberrancy, pre-excitation and ventricular pacing as relevant. Real-patient uncertainty should be communicated promptly to a qualified clinician; an educational app should not convert a short ECG description into treatment advice or claim that its assessment replaces clinical evaluation.

steps.title: Write the facts
steps.text: Include rate, regularity, width, morphology and atrial evidence.

steps.title: Explain the inference
steps.text: Name the signs that support the proposed mechanism.

steps.title: Declare the limit
steps.text: Identify absent leads, hidden atrial activity or missing baseline tracings.

example.question: A hypothetical single-lead broad regular tachycardia contains no reliably visible atrial events. Write a conclusion without inventing evidence.
working: A single lead demonstrates a regular broad-complex tachycardia.
No reliable atrial relationship can be assessed.
Additional twelve-lead and prior-rhythm information would help distinguish mechanisms.
example.answer: Regular broad-complex tachycardia of uncertain mechanism; VT cannot be excluded from the available recording.

pitfalls: Writing “SVT proved” from negative evidence alone.
Assigning a published cohort percentage as a patient-specific diagnostic probability.

practice.prompt: Which report best represents missing evidence?
options: No visible P waves, therefore SVT
Mechanism uncertain on this recording; VT is not excluded
VT impossible because the patient is awake
Normal rhythm because it is regular
practice.explanation: It accurately states the observation and limitation without false reassurance.
practice.hint: Uncertainty can be an accurate conclusion.

practice.prompt: Why avoid assigning a course prevalence figure directly to an individual case?
options: The relevant population and clinical setting may differ
Every case has identical prior probability
practice.explanation: Population frequencies depend on case selection and cannot replace case-specific evidence.
practice.hint: Check the denominator and setting.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: A set of plausible mechanisms considered against the available evidence.
The degree of support for an interpretation, distinct from whether a label is technically possible.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia
2022 ESC Guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death

deepDive.title: Separate observations, favoured explanation and confidence
deepDive.text: A clear conclusion can contain three layers. First state what is measured: a regular tachycardia, its approximate rate, QRS duration and key morphological features. Next identify the mechanism favoured by the evidence. Finally explain the uncertainty and the additional evidence that could change the interpretation. This structure is useful because broad-complex tachycardia can remain difficult even after systematic review. A confident-sounding label unsupported by the recording is less defensible than a qualified conclusion that specifies the positive clues and the unresolved differential.

deepDive.title: Avoid replacing evidence with epidemiological certainty
deepDive.text: The source emphasises the importance of considering VT in broad-complex tachycardia and gives teaching proportions. Such proportions depend on the population and circumstances from which they were obtained. They should not be applied as exact individual probabilities to an unidentified course tracing. Likewise, a safety-oriented clinical convention is not the same as a proven electrophysiological mechanism. For this learning objective, the task is to describe and reason accurately, not to derive a treatment decision from a synthetic example. Keep any clinical history separate from what is actually supplied.

deepDive.title: Specify the next discriminating evidence
deepDive.text: Useful next information is targeted to the uncertainty. If atrial relationships are unclear, request longer simultaneous leads that may reveal an independent atrial clock. If a BBB-like appearance is the main argument for SVT, compare a verified baseline ECG. If the initial activation is obscured, a higher-quality recording may be more informative than repeatedly applying morphology labels. Avoid asking vaguely for “more tests” without stating what question they address. A good educational report also distinguishes absent evidence from unassessable evidence: not seeing capture in a short strip is not proof that capture cannot occur.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original reporting exercise: a noisy single-lead synthetic strip shows a regular broad tachycardia. Atrial activity, frontal axis and chest-lead concordance cannot be assessed. Write a conclusion that is useful without overstating the evidence.
steps: State regular broad-complex tachycardia and the quality limitation.
List VT and SVT with aberrant conduction as unresolved mechanisms.
Do not claim a diagnostic morphology from a schematic single lead.
Specify a clear 12-lead recording, longer rhythm strip and verified baseline comparison as evidence that would address the uncertainty.
guidedExercise.answer: Regular broad-complex tachycardia; the mechanism remains unresolved on this limited recording, with ventricular tachycardia and supraventricular tachycardia with abnormal conduction requiring distinction.
guidedExercise.explanation: The wording preserves the important observation and the differential while refusing unsupported certainty. It also tells the next reader exactly why the present evidence is insufficient.
