title: Recognising cardiac pacing on the ECG
sourceFilename: D2-5 Basic pacing ECGs DipECG amended Mar2026.pdf
summary: Relate pacing artefacts to atrial and ventricular depolarisation and distinguish normal device behaviour from possible malfunction.

objectives.title: Identify atrial and ventricular pacing without relying on spike size
objectives.why: Modern bipolar pacing artefacts can be tiny or invisible, so absence of an obvious spike does not prove absence of pacing.
know: A pacing artefact is the surface representation of an electrical stimulus from an implanted device. In unipolar pacing the current path extends between the lead tip and the generator, often producing a large surface artefact. In bipolar pacing the relevant electrodes are close together, so the visible spike may be much smaller.

An atrial stimulus that captures is followed by atrial depolarisation, usually seen as a P wave. A ventricular stimulus that captures is followed by ventricular depolarisation, usually seen as a paced QRS. The exact morphology depends on the stimulation site, conduction system involvement and any fusion with intrinsic activation; it should not be assumed from the word “paced” alone.

Traditional right-ventricular apical pacing often produces a broad left-bundle-type QRS with secondary ST–T changes. These patterns are useful clues rather than universal rules, because other pacing locations and conduction-system pacing can produce different appearances. A very regular rate can raise suspicion of pacing, but a rate of exactly 60/min is not diagnostic by itself.

Pacing can make underlying atrial arrhythmias less obvious. For example, ventricular pacing can produce a regular ventricular response despite atrial fibrillation. Inspect atrial activity separately, compare device history if available, and avoid relying entirely on an automated ECG interpretation. The ECG is a surface observation; complete device-function assessment may require interrogation and clinical information.

steps.title: Search several leads
steps.text: Small pacing artefacts may be clear in one lead and absent in another.

steps.title: Link stimulus to depolarisation
steps.text: Identify whether the response is atrial, ventricular or both.

steps.title: Check underlying rhythm
steps.text: Do not let ventricular pacing obscure atrial activity.

example.question: A teaching description shows a regular broad-QRS rhythm, tiny preceding artefacts in one lead and fibrillatory atrial activity.
working: Small artefacts are compatible with bipolar pacing.
The broad ventricular responses follow the stimuli.
Fibrillatory activity remains an important independent atrial finding.
example.answer: Ventricular pacing in the presence of AF is plausible; the atrial rhythm should still be reported.

pitfalls: Declaring a device inactive because no large spikes are visible.
Assuming every paced QRS must have an identical classical RV-apical morphology.

practice.prompt: Why can bipolar pacing spikes be hard to see?
options: The current path between closely spaced electrodes produces a small surface artefact
Every ECG machine deletes all atrial activity
The PR interval is always zero
practice.explanation: Artefact amplitude depends on the current path and recording/filtering characteristics.
practice.hint: Small electrode separation matters.

practice.prompt: Which finding still needs assessment during ventricular pacing?
options: Nothing else if rate is regular
practice.explanation: AF or other atrial rhythms can coexist with a regular paced ventricular response.
practice.hint: Keep atrial and ventricular descriptions separate.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: A recorded electrical stimulus from a pacemaker, often called a pacing spike.
Pacing between two nearby electrodes on a lead, often producing a smaller surface artefact than unipolar pacing.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Relate a pacing marker to the tissue response
deepDive.text: A pacing artefact indicates an electrical stimulus, while capture requires a subsequent depolarisation of the intended chamber. Atrial pacing is sought as a stimulus followed by atrial activity; ventricular pacing as a stimulus followed by ventricular activation. The temporal relationship should be repeatable rather than based on one spike-like mark. In dual-chamber systems the two responses need separate assessment. A machine annotation or an apparent thin vertical line is not sufficient by itself, because noise can resemble an artefact and modern pacing markers may be very small.

deepDive.title: Explain why spike visibility varies
deepDive.text: The course contrasts unipolar and bipolar pacing. The stimulus field and the distance through tissue differ, so the surface artefact can be prominent in one configuration and subtle in another. Recording filters, output and lead orientation further affect what the ECG displays. Therefore “no obvious spike” is not equivalent to “no pacing.” A very regular rate near a common programmed lower limit can prompt closer inspection, but rate regularity alone is not proof of a device. Examine the complete pattern, multiple leads and any known device history rather than turning one clue into a diagnosis.

deepDive.title: Continue analysing the underlying atrial rhythm
deepDive.text: Ventricular pacing can produce a regular ventricular sequence while the atria are in a different rhythm. The lecture specifically warns that AF can be overlooked when attention is drawn to paced QRS complexes. Search the baseline for atrial activity and avoid treating regular paced ventricular timing as proof of sinus rhythm. Paced QRS morphology and secondary ST–T changes also reflect the activation route; they should not be interpreted as an ordinary normally conducted complex without qualification. Describe pacing and the underlying atrial process separately whenever the recording allows both to be assessed.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: a patient’s tracing has regular broad QRS complexes at 60/min. Tiny artefacts precede QRS in two leads, and the baseline lacks consistent P waves but has fibrillatory activity. Write the main components of the description.
steps: Inspect several leads for a repeatable stimulus-to-QRS relationship.
Describe the paced-appearing ventricular rhythm and its rate.
Assess atrial activity independently rather than inferring sinus rhythm from regularity.
State uncertainty if the artefacts or atrial baseline are not sufficiently clear.
guidedExercise.answer: A ventricular-pacing pattern at approximately 60/min with fibrillatory atrial activity, if the observed marker-to-QRS relationship is confirmed.
guidedExercise.explanation: The pacing description does not replace the atrial rhythm description. Very small artefacts are compatible with bipolar pacing, but morphology, timing and context should support that inference together.

objectives.coverageNote: All pacing-recognition text reviewed. The synthetic exercise does not identify a specific implanted device or programmed setting.

objectives.title: Explain normal dual-chamber pacing configurations
objectives.why: A device may pace one chamber, both chambers or neither when intrinsic activity is adequate.
know: A dual-chamber pacemaker can interact with both atrial and ventricular activity. In simplified teaching terms, a DDD device can pace and sense in both chambers and can respond to sensed events. Its surface appearance depends on the patient’s intrinsic rhythm, AV conduction, programmed timing and the device’s algorithms.

The course illustrates four normal configurations: atrial pacing with intrinsic AV conduction, sequential atrial and ventricular pacing, sensed sinus activity followed by ventricular pacing, and intrinsic sinus rhythm without delivered pacing. Seeing different configurations during one recording does not by itself establish malfunction.

A demand device can withhold an expected stimulus when it senses a suitable intrinsic depolarisation. Conversely, a device may pace the ventricles after sensed atrial activity when intrinsic AV conduction does not arrive within the relevant programmed interval. A paced ventricular rate above a presumed lower-rate setting can therefore reflect appropriate atrial tracking rather than uncontrolled device activity.

The surface ECG alone does not reveal every programmed setting. Rate response, mode switching, hysteresis and other algorithms can alter timing. A report should describe the observed atrial and ventricular events and their relation instead of guessing the complete device configuration from one beat. Apparent changes should be interpreted alongside device history or interrogation when clinically relevant.

steps.title: Classify atrial activation
steps.text: Is a P wave intrinsic or preceded by an atrial pacing artefact?

steps.title: Classify ventricular activation
steps.text: Does an intrinsic or paced QRS follow?

steps.title: Explain inhibition or tracking
steps.text: Relate absent or delivered stimuli to the sensed intrinsic events.

example.question: A hypothetical DDD-paced patient has sinus P waves at 85/min, each followed by ventricular pacing. The lower programmed rate is reported as 60/min.
working: The lower rate is not necessarily a maximum tracking rate.
The atrial rhythm may be sensed and appropriately followed by ventricular pacing.
The ECG does not supply all relevant programming details.
example.answer: Atrial sensing with ventricular pacing can be normal dual-chamber behaviour; the rate alone does not prove malfunction.

pitfalls: Calling intermittent pacing failure when intrinsic beats appropriately inhibit pacing.
Treating a lower-rate setting as the device’s maximum possible ventricular rate.

practice.prompt: Which can be normal in a patient with a dual-chamber pacemaker?
options: Sinus rhythm with no pacing stimuli when intrinsic activity is adequate
Every absence of pacing is failure
Every paced rate above 60/min is malfunction
Only two spikes before every QRS
practice.explanation: Normal behaviour includes inhibition when suitable intrinsic activity is present.
practice.hint: A device need not pace continuously.

practice.prompt: A DDD device may produce ventricular pacing faster than its lower-rate setting because of:
options: Appropriate atrial tracking within programmed limits
Permanent loss of all sensing in every case
A paper-speed error in every case
practice.explanation: Sensed atrial activity can trigger the ventricular timing sequence.
practice.hint: Distinguish a lower rate from tracking behaviour.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Pacing behaviour in which appropriately sensed intrinsic activity can inhibit an otherwise due stimulus.
A device timing response in which sensed atrial events can be followed by ventricular pacing within programmed rules.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Think in terms of sensing and pacing in each chamber
deepDive.text: The course lists four normal dual-chamber appearances: atrial pacing with native AV conduction, sequential atrial and ventricular pacing, sinus activity with ventricular pacing, and intrinsic sinus conduction without delivered pacing. These are not contradictory findings in someone with a dual-chamber device. They reflect whether intrinsic atrial and ventricular activation occurs in time to be sensed. Analyse the atrial and ventricular rows separately, identify the stimuli that are visible and look for their electrical responses before deciding which configuration is present.

deepDive.title: Understand inhibition when intrinsic activity is adequate
deepDive.text: Demand pacing is designed to avoid delivering an unnecessary stimulus when an appropriate intrinsic event has been sensed. Consequently, a record can contain normal intrinsic beats, paced beats or transitions between them. The lecture shows atrial pacing inhibited when faster sinus activity appears. The absence of a pacing stimulus during an adequate intrinsic rhythm can therefore be expected behaviour. Without knowing the programmed mode and timing, do not describe intermittent pacing as failure simply because the device is not active on every beat. Surface timing supports an interpretation, but interrogation provides the actual programmed information.

deepDive.title: Distinguish atrial tracking from an assumed malfunction
deepDive.text: In a tracking configuration, an increase in atrial rate can be followed by an increase in ventricular paced rate within the programmed behaviour. The source presents this as a common reason for a device appearing to be “going too fast” despite normal function. Identify whether ventricular activation maintains a consistent relationship to sensed atrial activity. Conversely, not every fast paced rhythm is explained by normal tracking, so a short tracing should not be used to certify device function. State the observed configuration and whether it is compatible with expected behaviour, retaining the need for device information when a problem is suspected.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original sequence exercise: the first segment shows an atrial stimulus followed by P and a native narrow QRS. Later, intrinsic sinus P waves occur earlier and are followed by similar native QRS complexes without stimuli. Explain the transition.
steps: Confirm atrial capture in the first segment.
Recognise native AV conduction from P to narrow QRS.
Compare the later intrinsic atrial timing with the earlier paced schedule.
Explain inhibition as a possible normal response to adequate intrinsic activity.
guidedExercise.answer: The sequence is compatible with atrial pacing and native AV conduction followed by inhibition of atrial pacing when faster intrinsic sinus activity is sensed.
guidedExercise.explanation: A change from paced to intrinsic activation is not automatically a malfunction. The surface sequence is compatible with demand behaviour, while the actual mode and programmed intervals remain device data.

objectives.coverageNote: The four source configurations are covered conceptually; this is not a device-programming lesson or an assertion that an individual device is functioning normally.

objectives.title: Recognise possible failure to capture
objectives.why: An electrical stimulus and successful myocardial depolarisation are different observations.
know: Capture means that a pacing stimulus successfully depolarises the intended cardiac chamber. For atrial pacing, this is an atrial depolarisation; for ventricular pacing, it is a ventricular QRS response. The visible stimulus does not itself demonstrate capture, because it records delivered electrical energy rather than the biological response.

Possible failure to capture is suggested when a pacing artefact is not followed by the expected chamber depolarisation. The intended chamber and the expected stimulus-to-response relation must be established first. A ventricular spike followed by no new QRS is different from an atrial spike that is followed by a P wave but not by a ventricular response.

Interpretation requires attention to competing intrinsic activity and timing. A stimulus delivered into already refractory myocardium may not create a new visible response, and a coincident intrinsic beat can make the response difficult to recognise. Lead displacement, output or threshold issues are possible explanations in clinical practice, but a surface tracing alone should not be used to select one cause without additional evidence.

Report the directly observed pattern: for example, recurrent apparent ventricular pacing stimuli without subsequent QRS responses, while intrinsic beats continue independently. Look for accompanying inappropriate stimuli that suggest a sensing issue as well. Because some devices produce very small artefacts and ECG filtering affects visibility, device interrogation and clinical assessment may be required to verify the interpretation.

steps.title: Identify the paced chamber
steps.text: Link earlier successful stimuli to P waves or QRS complexes.

steps.title: Inspect each response
steps.text: Check whether a new depolarisation follows at the expected short interval.

steps.title: Consider timing
steps.text: Distinguish absent response from fusion, intrinsic coincidence or refractoriness.

example.question: In a hypothetical strip, clearly visible ventricular stimuli repeatedly occur without a subsequent QRS, although the patient’s intrinsic QRS complexes remain visible elsewhere.
working: The stimuli are delivered electrical events.
The expected ventricular depolarisation does not follow them.
A specific device or lead cause cannot be established from the strip alone.
example.answer: Possible ventricular failure to capture; describe the stimulus–response evidence and seek device evaluation.

pitfalls: Calling a visible spike successful pacing without checking the response.
Confusing an atrial response with a ventricular response.

practice.prompt: What establishes ventricular capture on the surface ECG?
options: A pacing stimulus followed by an appropriately related ventricular depolarisation
practice.explanation: Capture refers to myocardial depolarisation caused by the stimulus.
practice.hint: Look after the stimulus.

practice.prompt: A spike without a new QRS always proves lead displacement.
options: False; several causes or timing explanations are possible
True only with a narrow intrinsic QRS
practice.explanation: The ECG can demonstrate a possible failure pattern but not necessarily its aetiology.
practice.hint: Observed effect and cause are different levels of certainty.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Successful depolarisation of the intended cardiac chamber by a pacing stimulus.
The minimum stimulus output needed to produce reliable depolarisation under specified conditions.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Separate stimulus delivery from successful capture
deepDive.text: Failure to capture concerns a delivered pacing stimulus not followed by the expected electrical activation. An atrial stimulus should be assessed for an atrial response and a ventricular stimulus for a ventricular response. Do not judge atrial capture merely by whether a QRS follows, because AV conduction can be impaired independently. Compare suspected failed events with neighbouring captured events in the same lead and across other leads. A faint P or QRS may be hidden by noise, and a stimulus delivered when tissue is refractory requires a different interpretation from a routine scheduled stimulus without a response.

deepDive.title: Use event timing to avoid superficial pattern labels
deepDive.text: Mark the preceding intrinsic and paced events, the stimulus time and the expected response. A spike-like artefact that appears after or within a QRS may be difficult to interpret from a filtered surface record. The source includes examples where sensing and capture problems coexist, so identifying a missing response does not answer every device question. Conversely, lack of a visible spike can reflect small bipolar artefacts rather than absence of stimulus delivery. The report should say which chamber response is missing and whether the stimulus is convincingly identified, rather than using “pacemaker failure” as an unexplained umbrella label.

deepDive.title: Distinguish an ECG finding from a device cause
deepDive.text: A surface tracing may suggest failure to capture, but it does not by itself establish why capture failed. The lecture includes a lead-displacement example, yet that particular cause should not be assigned to every similar electrical pattern. Device settings, lead characteristics and additional assessment are separate evidence. Report the frequency and duration of the observed missing responses within the available record and any associated intrinsic activity. A synthetic educational example can illustrate the distinction between stimulus and response without supporting a patient-specific device diagnosis or a treatment recommendation.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: regularly spaced visible ventricular pacing artefacts occur. Most are followed immediately by broad QRS complexes, but two clearly visible artefacts are not followed by ventricular activation in any simultaneous lead. What is the measured finding?
steps: Establish the usual marker-to-QRS relation in neighbouring captured beats.
Check the two suspected missing responses in all available leads.
Consider whether the stimuli occur in a refractory period after intrinsic activity.
Describe the missing ventricular responses without selecting a mechanical cause from the ECG alone.
guidedExercise.answer: Intermittent apparent ventricular non-capture, provided the stimuli and absent responses are confirmed and their timing does not offer another explanation.
guidedExercise.explanation: The phrase identifies the electrical observation. It does not establish lead displacement, a specific output problem or another device-level cause without further evidence.

objectives.coverageNote: All capture-failure source text reviewed; no source treatment algorithm or device-specific programming thresholds are inferred.

objectives.title: Recognise possible sensing problems and avoid pacemaker “non-problems”
objectives.why: Appropriate sensing changes whether a device should deliver a stimulus; missing spikes and unexpected spikes mean different things.
know: Sensing is a device’s detection of intrinsic electrical activity. In a simple inhibited pacing mode, an appropriately sensed intrinsic event prevents or resets an otherwise due stimulus. Failure to sense can therefore produce pacing artefacts occurring despite intrinsic activity that should have affected the timing, including stimuli appearing at inappropriate positions in the cardiac cycle.

The course contrasts possible undersensing and failure to capture with common non-problems. A device that does not pace continuously may be functioning normally because intrinsic rhythm is adequate. Very small bipolar spikes can be hard to see, and atrial tracking may produce a paced ventricular rate faster than a patient expects.

Look for a repeated timing pattern rather than judging a single apparent stimulus. Identify intrinsic P waves and QRS complexes, determine which chamber the device appears to interact with, and check whether sensed events are followed by a plausible inhibition or tracking response. A regular sequence of spikes independent of intrinsic events suggests a different explanation from normal demand behaviour.

Other programmed modes and algorithms can intentionally create appearances that resemble malfunction, and oversensing may inhibit pacing without displaying the signal that triggered it. A surface ECG cannot show the complete sensing channels or programming. The accurate educational outcome is to recognise a possible problem, state the evidence and limitation, and distinguish that from a proven device fault requiring a specific remedy.

steps.title: Mark intrinsic and paced events
steps.text: Create a timeline of P waves, QRS complexes and visible stimuli.

steps.title: Ask what sensing should do
steps.text: Consider whether intrinsic activity should inhibit or trigger the next paced event in the suspected mode.

steps.title: Qualify the concern
steps.text: Use possible undersensing or other dysfunction unless device data confirm the mechanism.

example.question: A hypothetical strip shows ventricular stimuli at fixed intervals despite intervening intrinsic QRS complexes, and several stimuli have no new ventricular response.
working: The stimuli do not appear reset or inhibited by the intervening ventricular events.
Some stimuli also fail to produce a new QRS.
The pattern can suggest both sensing and capture concerns, but programming and device information are needed.
example.answer: Possible ventricular undersensing with apparent failure to capture; describe both observations without assuming a cause.

pitfalls: Declaring malfunction whenever no spikes are visible.
Assigning a device mode or fault solely from a brief trace without programming information.

practice.prompt: Which observation suggests undersensing in an inhibited pacing mode?
options: Stimuli continuing inappropriately despite intrinsic events that should inhibit them
Appropriate inhibition during normal sinus rhythm
practice.explanation: Failure to detect an intrinsic event can leave the stimulus timer unaffected.
practice.hint: Check whether intrinsic events change the timing.

practice.prompt: Which is commonly a normal pacemaker behaviour?
options: No pacing when adequate intrinsic activity is appropriately sensed
Failure of every ventricular stimulus to capture
Random stimuli through all intrinsic QRS complexes
practice.explanation: Intermittent or absent pacing can be the intended effect of demand sensing.
practice.hint: A pacemaker does not necessarily run continuously.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Failure of a device to detect intrinsic activity that should influence its operation.
Detection of signals that should not be treated as the intended intrinsic cardiac event, potentially altering pacing behaviour.

references.label: 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronisation therapy

deepDive.title: Interpret sensing through the timing of delivered stimuli
deepDive.text: Sensing concerns whether the device recognises intrinsic electrical events and changes its behaviour appropriately. A stimulus appearing despite an intrinsic event can raise the possibility of undersensing, but the inference depends on the programmed mode, chamber and timing. Surface ECGs do not directly display the device’s internal event classification. Mark the intrinsic events and visible pacing artefacts separately, then ask whether the delivered sequence is compatible with expected inhibition or tracking. The source’s combined failure example shows why sensing and capture must be evaluated as separate functions even when abnormalities coexist.

deepDive.title: Rule out the common apparent non-problems
deepDive.text: The lecture highlights three misleading complaints: the device is not pacing continuously, no spikes are visible, or the paced rate increases. Each can be compatible with normal behaviour. Intrinsic rhythm may inhibit demand pacing, bipolar artefacts may be inconspicuous, and atrial tracking may increase ventricular pacing. These explanations should be tested against the timing instead of assumed. A recorded rate of exactly 60/min can prompt inspection but is not proof of pacing. Similarly, a period without visible pacing does not prove oversensing; intrinsic activity and the programmed settings may account for it.

deepDive.title: Use qualified language when internal device data are missing
deepDive.text: A surface pattern may suggest inappropriate inhibition or failure to sense, but the device’s markers and interrogation can be needed to distinguish the mechanism. In a report, identify the observable contradiction: for example, pacing artefacts continue at a fixed schedule without a relation to intrinsic ventricular events, or expected output appears absent during a pause. State the chamber and the uncertainty. Avoid declaring that every isolated unusual spike represents a device fault, and avoid certifying normal function from one reassuring interval. The course’s pacing section is a foundation for recognising patterns, not a complete device troubleshooting protocol.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: a person with a known dual-chamber device has intrinsic sinus rhythm at 78/min, normal-looking conducted QRS complexes and no clearly visible pacing artefacts. A colleague calls this “failure to pace.” What should be explained?
steps: Describe the intrinsic rhythm and ventricular response first.
Recognise that adequate intrinsic activity may inhibit demand pacing.
Remember that small bipolar artefacts can also be difficult to see.
Avoid assigning oversensing or device failure without incompatible timing or device data.
guidedExercise.answer: Absence of visible pacing during an adequate intrinsic rhythm is not, by itself, evidence of malfunction; it can be compatible with normal inhibition.
guidedExercise.explanation: The conclusion addresses the actual evidence. Whether the specific device is functioning as programmed requires the appropriate device information rather than an assumption based on spike visibility alone.

title: Ventricular pre-excitation and WPW
sourceFilename: D2-6 pre-excitation & WPW Dip ECG 2025 new.pdf
summary: Connect accessory-pathway conduction to the delta wave, AV re-entry and irregular pre-excited rhythms.

objectives.title: Explain the PR–delta–QRS pattern of ventricular pre-excitation
objectives.why: An early slurred QRS onset reflects competing activation pathways and can alter many other ECG features.
know: A manifest atrioventricular accessory pathway can conduct an atrial impulse to ventricular myocardium without the usual AV nodal delay. Part of the ventricle therefore begins depolarising early. At the same time, the impulse may travel through the AV node and His–Purkinje system to complete activation, producing a combined activation pattern.

The characteristic sinus-rhythm pattern combines a short PR interval, a slurred initial QRS deflection called a delta wave, and a widened overall QRS. The 2019 ESC SVT guideline describes the typical pattern with PR at or below 120 ms and QRS above 120 ms, while degree of pre-excitation and conduction competition can make the surface appearance less obvious.

A delta wave may be positive or negative depending on the lead and activation direction. It can be subtle and present more clearly in some leads than others. Measuring the PR and inspecting the true beginning of the QRS across several leads is therefore more reliable than looking only for a large obvious slur in one lead.

Because ventricular activation is altered, pre-excitation can also change axis, apparent Q waves, QRS voltage, R-wave progression and ST–T appearance. These findings should not be interpreted independently of the activation pattern. A short PR alone is not enough to prove an accessory pathway, and an isolated broad QRS without a delta pattern has many other explanations.

steps.title: Measure the PR
steps.text: Use a lead with a clear P-wave onset and true QRS onset.

steps.title: Inspect the initial QRS
steps.text: Seek consistent initial slurring across suitable leads.

steps.title: Assess the whole pattern
steps.text: Relate QRS width and secondary changes to the proposed early activation.

example.question: Hypothetical sinus ECG has PR 100 ms, a slurred initial QRS in several leads and total QRS duration 135 ms.
working: The PR is short.
The slurred onset supports a delta wave rather than a normal sharp onset.
The widened QRS fits combined early myocardial and normal-system activation.
example.answer: A manifest ventricular pre-excitation pattern is supported.

pitfalls: Diagnosing pre-excitation from a short PR alone.
Ignoring small or negative delta waves.

practice.prompt: What does a delta wave represent?
options: Early ventricular activation through an accessory pathway, producing a slurred QRS onset
Delayed atrial repolarisation in every case
practice.explanation: It reflects altered early ventricular depolarisation rather than an extra atrial event.
practice.hint: Focus on QRS onset.

practice.prompt: Which combination is most supportive?
options: Short PR, delta wave and widened QRS
practice.explanation: The linked activation pattern is more informative than a single component.
practice.hint: Look for the triad.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Slurred initial QRS deflection caused by early ventricular myocardial activation during pre-excitation.
An additional electrical connection that can bypass part of the normal atrioventricular conduction route.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia

deepDive.title: Follow the two routes to ventricular activation
deepDive.text: The course explains manifest ventricular pre-excitation as a contribution from an accessory atrioventricular route alongside the normal AV node–His pathway. An atrial impulse can reach ventricular myocardium early through the accessory route, beginning a relatively slow initial spread through muscle, while the normal conduction route contributes later. This produces a blended activation sequence rather than simply making every part of ventricular activation faster. Relating the waveform to these two contributions helps explain the combination of a short PR interval, a slurred initial QRS component and an increased overall QRS duration.

deepDive.title: Identify the onset carefully across multiple leads
deepDive.text: The PR interval ends at the earliest ventricular activation, including a subtle delta component. If the slow initial deflection is overlooked, the apparent QRS onset may be placed too late and the PR interval may seem less shortened. Conversely, baseline drift or noise should not be mistaken for a delta wave. Inspect several leads and compare repeated beats, because the degree and visibility of pre-excitation can vary. The source emphasises that minimal pre-excitation can produce very small delta waves. A single convenient lead may therefore understate the early component or exaggerate a minor contour change.

deepDive.title: Expect secondary changes without assuming a separate disease
deepDive.text: Because activation begins and spreads differently, QRS amplitude, axis, apparent Q waves, R-wave progression and ST–T appearance may also change. Those secondary findings should be interpreted after recognising the primary pre-excitation pattern. A broad QRS alone is insufficient, and a short PR alone does not establish the complete pattern. A defensible description records the combination and how clearly each component is demonstrated. Surface morphology can suggest the presence of an accessory activation route, but precise localisation and functional properties of that pathway require more evidence than a routine schematic or one lead.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original measurement exercise: the earliest ventricular deflection begins 100 ms after P onset. The first 35 ms of ventricular activation is slurred, and total QRS duration is 135 ms. Explain the three linked observations.
steps: Use the earliest ventricular deflection as the end of PR.
Describe the slurred initial ventricular activation as a delta-like component.
Measure total QRS duration including the slurred onset.
Check that the features repeat across suitable leads and are not recording artefact.
guidedExercise.answer: The combined short PR, delta-like onset and broad QRS supports a manifest ventricular pre-excitation pattern.
guidedExercise.explanation: The three measurements are mechanistically linked by altered initial ventricular activation. The surface pattern does not alone establish symptoms, pathway risk or a precise anatomical location.

objectives.coverageNote: All primary-pattern source text reviewed. The additional numerical example is original and not measured from a supplied patient ECG.

objectives.title: Distinguish a WPW pattern, WPW syndrome and a concealed pathway
objectives.why: A resting ECG pattern is not identical to the clinical arrhythmia syndrome, and a normal resting ECG does not exclude every accessory pathway.
know: A manifest pre-excitation pattern is a surface-ECG observation. WPW syndrome generally refers to manifest accessory-pathway conduction together with associated tachyarrhythmia. An asymptomatic person with the ECG pattern should not automatically be described as having symptomatic WPW syndrome solely on the basis of that recording.

Accessory pathways differ in their direction of conduction. A manifest pathway conducts towards the ventricles during sinus rhythm and can produce a delta wave. A concealed pathway conducts only retrogradely and therefore may not produce pre-excitation on the resting ECG, yet can still participate in orthodromic AV re-entrant tachycardia.

In orthodromic AVRT, conduction travels down the usual AV node/His–Purkinje route and returns towards the atria through an accessory pathway. Ventricular activation may consequently be narrow despite the presence of an accessory pathway. A broad resting pre-excited QRS and a narrow tachycardia are therefore not inherently contradictory observations.

Pre-excitation can be intermittent or become less conspicuous as conduction competition changes. A single normal-looking resting tracing does not establish that a previously observed pathway has disappeared or exclude a concealed pathway. Avoid importing course-level prevalence or risk figures as an individual prognosis. Symptoms, pathway properties and specialist assessment determine clinical interpretation beyond the surface pattern.

steps.title: Separate the observation from the syndrome
steps.text: Record manifest pre-excitation and establish whether relevant tachyarrhythmia is known.

steps.title: Consider conduction direction
steps.text: Ask whether the pathway is manifest or could be retrograde-only.

steps.title: Explain the re-entry circuit
steps.text: Trace the usual orthodromic path down the AV node and back through the accessory connection.

example.question: A hypothetical patient has no resting delta wave but an electrophysiologically established retrograde-only pathway involved in AVRT.
working: A retrograde-only pathway does not pre-excite the ventricles during sinus rhythm.
It can complete the return limb of orthodromic AVRT.
The absence of a resting delta wave is therefore compatible with this pathway.
example.answer: A concealed accessory pathway can support AVRT despite a normal resting pre-excitation assessment.

pitfalls: Equating every pre-excitation ECG with symptomatic WPW syndrome.
Excluding an accessory pathway because a single resting tracing has no delta wave.

practice.prompt: A concealed accessory pathway:
options: May support orthodromic AVRT without a resting delta wave
Always produces a large delta wave
Is the same as complete AV block
practice.explanation: Retrograde-only conduction can participate in re-entry without early antegrade ventricular activation.
practice.hint: Think about the direction of travel.

practice.prompt: What additional information distinguishes WPW syndrome from an isolated manifest pattern?
practice.explanation: The syndrome integrates the manifest pathway pattern with associated arrhythmia rather than the ECG appearance alone.
practice.hint: Pattern and clinical syndrome differ.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: An accessory pathway without manifest antegrade pre-excitation, typically conducting retrogradely.
AV re-entry with antegrade conduction through the usual AV system and retrograde return through an accessory pathway.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia

deepDive.title: Separate a surface pattern from the clinical syndrome
deepDive.text: The course distinguishes manifest pre-excitation on the resting ECG from the syndrome involving the relevant tachyarrhythmia history. A short PR–delta–broad QRS combination describes the electrical pattern at the time of recording. It does not by itself establish the person’s symptom history or demonstrate a documented accessory-pathway-mediated tachycardia. Therefore the report should not add palpitations, syncope or an arrhythmia that has not been supplied. A pattern description is still useful; it is simply a narrower claim than a full clinical syndrome.

deepDive.title: Understand the usual orthodromic circuit
deepDive.text: In the course’s orthodromic AVRT explanation, the impulse travels down the normal AV-conduction route to the ventricles and returns towards the atria through the accessory connection. Because ventricular activation can proceed through the usual His–Purkinje route, the tachycardia may have a narrow QRS even when resting pre-excitation is known. The visibility of a resting delta wave and the ability to participate in a re-entry circuit are related but different questions. The surface tachycardia alone may not distinguish all re-entry mechanisms, so a precise AVRT label needs supporting evidence rather than an assumption based on a fast regular rhythm.

deepDive.title: Explain why a normal resting tracing does not exclude a pathway
deepDive.text: A concealed accessory pathway lacks manifest antegrade pre-excitation on the resting ECG but can still participate in an appropriate re-entry circuit through retrograde conduction. The course also notes that manifest pre-excitation can be intermittent. Consequently, a normal-looking resting PR and QRS on one record does not prove that an accessory pathway is absent. Equally, that possibility should not be used to assert a pathway in every person with a narrow-complex tachycardia. Keep resting appearance, documented tachycardia mechanism and clinical symptoms as separate evidence streams that may or may not have been established.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original comparison: person A has a convincing resting pre-excitation pattern but no supplied tachycardia history. Person B has a normal resting ECG and a documented re-entry mechanism involving a retrogradely conducting accessory pathway. Describe the distinction.
steps: For A, report the demonstrated resting electrical pattern without inventing symptoms.
For B, recognise that a pathway can be concealed during ordinary antegrade conduction.
Explain how retrograde participation can permit re-entry without a resting delta wave.
Avoid using one resting appearance as a complete assessment of pathway function.
guidedExercise.answer: A has a manifest pre-excitation pattern on the supplied evidence. B illustrates a concealed accessory pathway capable of participating in AVRT despite no resting pre-excitation.
guidedExercise.explanation: Resting ventricular activation and re-entry pathway participation are distinct properties. The ECG pattern, syndrome label and mechanism should not be treated as interchangeable terms.

objectives.title: Recognise why pre-excited AF is a distinct irregular broad rhythm
objectives.why: An accessory pathway can carry rapidly varying atrial impulses to the ventricles and produce changing QRS appearance.
know: In atrial fibrillation, atrial impulses are rapid and disorganised. When a manifest accessory pathway can conduct antegradely, some of those impulses may reach the ventricles outside the normal AV nodal route. The result can be a very rapid irregular ventricular rhythm with wide complexes and changing degrees of pre-excitation.

Variable competition between normal conduction and accessory-pathway conduction changes QRS width and morphology from beat to beat. This can resemble ventricular tachycardia or a polymorphic broad-complex rhythm. A markedly irregular rhythm and a prior ECG showing pre-excitation can provide important clues, but the full differential must remain open when evidence is incomplete.

The clinical importance is not simply that the QRS is broad. Rapid antegrade accessory-pathway conduction during AF may be dangerous and can degenerate to ventricular fibrillation. An ECG learning app should teach recognition and urgent communication of the pattern while avoiding a stand-alone treatment algorithm or instructions to try medications from a course case.

The supplied lecture includes a historical case with sequential ECGs and treatment labels. These are source examples for supervised interpretation rather than a recipe to reproduce. Interpret each tracing’s atrial organisation, ventricular regularity and degree of pre-excitation, and use clinical context and specialist assessment. Do not declare every irregular broad tachycardia pre-excited AF or assume that ventricular tachycardia must always be regular.

steps.title: Check irregularity
steps.text: Compare RR intervals across a meaningful rhythm segment.

steps.title: Compare QRS appearance
steps.text: Look for changing width or morphology and seek prior evidence of pre-excitation.

steps.title: Communicate significance
steps.text: State the suspected mechanism and need for urgent qualified clinical assessment in a real case.

example.question: A hypothetical person with a previous delta-wave ECG now has a very rapid, markedly irregular broad-complex rhythm with varying QRS width.
working: Prior manifest pre-excitation provides an accessory-pathway context.
The irregular rhythm and changing activation are compatible with pre-excited AF.
Other causes of irregular broad tachycardia must still be considered.
example.answer: Pre-excited AF is an important concern requiring prompt clinical assessment; this description is not a treatment instruction.

pitfalls: Treating the lecture’s historical medication sequence as an app recommendation.
Assuming irregularity alone rules out every ventricular arrhythmia.

practice.prompt: Which pattern should raise concern for pre-excited AF?
options: Very rapid irregular broad-complex rhythm with varying QRS appearance and prior pre-excitation
Normal sinus rhythm with PR 180 ms
A paced atrial rhythm at 60/min only
A fixed isolated first-degree AV block
practice.explanation: The combination of AF-like irregularity and variable accessory-pathway ventricular activation is important.
practice.hint: Integrate the prior ECG with the current rhythm.

practice.prompt: Why is this potentially dangerous clinically?
options: An accessory pathway may conduct rapidly to the ventricles and permit degeneration to VF
A delta wave always means there is no ventricular activation
A broad QRS guarantees normal AV nodal protection
practice.explanation: The pathway can bypass the usual AV nodal filtering of atrial impulses.
practice.hint: Consider how the impulse reaches the ventricle.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: Atrial fibrillation with antegrade ventricular activation through an accessory pathway.
Electrical conduction from atria towards ventricles.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia

deepDive.title: Analyse irregularity, width and changing activation together
deepDive.text: The course describes pre-excited AF as rapid irregular ventricular activation when atrial impulses can reach the ventricles through an accessory pathway. Because activation can involve differing contributions from the accessory and normal routes, ventricular morphology may vary as well as timing. A short single-lead broad run may not reveal these relationships clearly. Describe irregularity over enough recording, compare the range of QRS appearances and examine any preceding or subsequent resting ECG for manifest pre-excitation. Neither broad complexes nor a very high rate alone establishes this mechanism.

deepDive.title: Keep competing irregular broad-rhythm explanations visible
deepDive.text: AF with ordinary bundle-branch abnormality, intermittent aberrancy and ventricular-origin rhythms can enter the differential of an irregular broad-complex recording. The preceding cycle lengths, the onset of QRS, changing degree of pre-excitation and baseline evidence can help distinguish them. The source’s serial case includes changes between more pre-excited and more normally conducted appearances, showing why one snapshot can be misleading. Do not infer a precise accessory-pathway property or clinical risk from a waveform cartoon. State the pattern that raises suspicion and the additional evidence supporting the proposed route of ventricular activation.

deepDive.title: Treat serial changes as information about visibility, not proof of cure
deepDive.text: A later tracing that lacks an obvious delta wave does not automatically show that the accessory pathway has permanently disappeared. The source includes a sequence in which pre-excitation becomes unapparent and then is visible again. Differences in conduction contribution can change the resting surface appearance. Interpret each recording in relation to timing and the wider history rather than selecting the reassuring-looking segment. The teaching goal is to recognise a distinct possible mechanism and its reporting limits; this exercise does not provide a drug-selection rule or a management algorithm from the ECG alone.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original sequence exercise: an irregular broad tachycardia has changing QRS shapes. A later resting tracing shows a short PR and delta wave. An intermediate record has little obvious delta activity. How should these records be combined?
steps: Describe the irregular broad-complex rhythm without initially fixing its mechanism.
Use the later manifest pre-excitation as relevant pathway evidence.
Consider variable contributions from accessory and normal conduction routes.
Do not interpret the intermediate absence of an obvious delta wave as permanent elimination of the pathway.
guidedExercise.answer: The serial evidence raises a pre-excited atrial fibrillation mechanism, with variable manifest pre-excitation; the mechanism should be confirmed from the actual multi-lead recordings and clinical assessment.
guidedExercise.explanation: Serial surface visibility is not identical to pathway presence or absence. The combination is informative, while the individual snapshot remains limited.

objectives.coverageNote: The serial case is discussed conceptually only; source drug names are not transformed into treatment advice or claims of efficacy.

objectives.title: Avoid pseudo-infarction and hypertrophy diagnoses caused by pre-excitation
objectives.why: Abnormal initial activation can imitate other important ECG diagnoses unless the PR and delta wave are assessed first.
know: Pre-excitation alters the start and direction of ventricular activation. A negative delta wave can resemble an abnormal Q wave, while changes in the overall depolarisation vector can produce a dominant R in V1, axis deviation or increased QRS amplitudes. These appearances can imitate infarction, chamber hypertrophy or bundle branch block.

The course illustrates apparent inferior Q waves produced by negative delta waves, as well as patterns resembling RBBB, LBBB, RVH and LVH. The lesson is not that those diseases can never coexist with pre-excitation. Rather, conventional criteria can lose specificity when the activation sequence is abnormal, and a mimic should be considered before assigning a second diagnosis.

Begin with the PR interval and QRS onset, then decide whether the apparent Q wave or notching is actually part of the delta wave. Compare leads because pre-excitation may be subtle in one region and clearer in another. Interpret the ST and T waves in the context of the altered depolarisation rather than as isolated primary changes.

A careful report can state “manifest ventricular pre-excitation with secondary QRS and ST–T changes; the apparent inferior Q-wave pattern may be due to negative delta waves.” Do not claim that this excludes coexisting coronary or structural disease. Prior ECGs, imaging, symptoms and other clinical information may be necessary to evaluate such possibilities, and the app should distinguish this reasoning exercise from a clinical diagnostic verdict.

steps.title: Check the PR and onset
steps.text: Establish whether early slurring is present before applying other morphology rules.

steps.title: Reinterpret apparent abnormalities
steps.text: Consider whether Q-like deflections and voltages arise from altered activation.

steps.title: Preserve coexistence
steps.text: A mimic explanation does not rule out genuine additional disease.

example.question: Hypothetical ECG has PR 105 ms, clear pre-excitation and broad negative initial deflections in II, III and aVF.
working: The initial negative deflections coincide with the pre-excited QRS onset.
They may be negative delta waves rather than infarction Q waves.
The ECG alone cannot exclude coincident coronary disease.
example.answer: A pre-excitation-related pseudo-infarction pattern is plausible; avoid an unqualified inferior-infarction diagnosis.

pitfalls: Applying standard Q-wave or hypertrophy criteria without checking activation sequence.
Assuming a plausible mimic proves there is no coexisting disease.

practice.prompt: Why can pre-excitation mimic inferior infarction?
options: Negative delta waves can resemble inferior Q waves
It always destroys the inferior wall
practice.explanation: Altered early depolarisation can create a Q-like initial deflection without proving infarction.
practice.hint: Inspect the beginning of the QRS.

practice.prompt: A pre-excitation mimic explanation:
options: Requires qualification and does not exclude coexisting disease
Means the recording is always artefact
practice.explanation: An activation-related explanation can coexist with genuine structural or ischaemic disease.
practice.hint: A mimic is not a universal exclusion test.

objectives.mastery: Explain the mechanism in your own words, apply the observation sequence to the example, and answer both practice questions with a reason for rejecting the distractors.

glossary.definition: An ECG appearance resembling infarction that can arise from another activation or structural mechanism.
A downward slurred initial QRS deflection caused by the direction of pre-excited ventricular activation.

references.label: 2019 ESC Guidelines on supraventricular tachycardia

deepDive.title: Recognise that altered activation changes several diagnostic cues
deepDive.text: Routine ECG interpretation often uses axis, Q waves, precordial R-wave progression, voltage and ST–T patterns as clues to structural or ischaemic disease. Pre-excitation can alter each of these because a different early ventricular wavefront contributes to the recorded signal. The course deliberately presents apparent bundle-branch block, infarction and hypertrophy appearances that are explained by pre-excitation. Therefore assess PR timing and the beginning of QRS before treating the later morphology as an independent disease signature. A primary activation abnormality can reshape several familiar criteria at the same time.

deepDive.title: Distinguish a negative delta component from an infarction inference
deepDive.text: An initially negative accessory-pathway contribution can resemble a Q wave in particular leads. The key question is how that early deflection fits the shortened PR and slurred onset across the tracing, not merely whether the negative component looks broad or deep. Compare other leads and repeated beats, and consider whether the apparent Q-wave pattern changes when pre-excitation changes. This does not mean that pre-excitation excludes coexisting infarction. It means that the usual interpretation of an isolated early negative component is less secure until the altered activation sequence has been accounted for.

deepDive.title: Do not force ordinary voltage or BBB criteria onto a blended QRS
deepDive.text: A dominant R in V1, large QRS amplitudes or a notched broad complex may be produced by the pathway’s activation contribution rather than the structural condition suggested by an unmodified rule. Similarly, ST depression or T-wave inversion can be secondary to the altered depolarisation sequence. Describe the observed changes and the pre-excitation context, then state what additional evidence would be needed to assess a separate structural or ischaemic diagnosis. A resting ECG with minimal delta activity still requires careful onset inspection; the absence of a dramatic slur in one lead does not remove this interpretive issue.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original exercise: a tracing has deep early negative deflections in II, III and aVF, a short PR and a slurred initial ventricular component in other leads. A student reports “definite old inferior infarction.” Explain a more defensible approach.
steps: Identify the combined pre-excitation features before applying a Q-wave label.
Assess whether the inferior initial negative deflections may be negative delta components.
Describe the findings without claiming that pre-excitation excludes coexisting disease.
Specify baseline comparison and independent clinical/imaging evidence if a separate infarction diagnosis is being considered.
guidedExercise.answer: Manifest pre-excitation with inferior negative initial components that can mimic infarction-related Q waves; a definite prior infarction is not established by those components alone.
guidedExercise.explanation: The lesson is to recognise a confounded criterion, not to replace one absolute diagnosis with another. The activation sequence must be considered before assigning a separate disease explanation.

title: Coronary ischaemia and infarction patterns
summary: Connect ST–T and QRS findings with coronary territories, timing and diagnostic uncertainty. ECG criteria support recognition; myocardial infarction requires clinical and biomarker evidence.

objectives.title: Separate ECG evidence of ischaemia from a diagnosis of infarction
objectives.why: Ischaemia changes myocardial electrical behaviour, but an ECG does not directly measure coronary blood flow or cell death.
know: Ischaemia changes myocardial electrical behaviour, but an ECG does not directly measure coronary blood flow or cell death. A tracing may show ST depression, ST elevation or T-wave change, and an early tracing may be unremarkable. Describe what is present before attaching a syndrome label. The course separates stable exertional symptoms, acute coronary syndromes and vasospasm because similar electrical findings can arise in different clinical settings.

Myocardial infarction requires evidence of acute myocardial injury together with evidence supporting acute ischaemia. A rise or fall in cardiac troponin is interpreted against the assay reference limit and the clinical circumstances. An elevated troponin alone is not synonymous with coronary infarction. Conversely, the absence of diagnostic ST elevation does not exclude an acute coronary occlusion or a clinically significant acute coronary syndrome.

For an educational report, combine a precise ECG description with the information that would change its interpretation: symptoms, timing, previous tracings, serial ECGs and biomarkers. Horizontal or downsloping ST depression can support ischaemia, while an isolated shape does not establish its cause. Exercise-test measurements and resting acute-ischaemia criteria are different frameworks. This lesson teaches recognition and defensible wording; assessment and management depend on the clinical setting.

steps.title: Describe
steps.text: Name the leads, direction and magnitude of ST–T abnormalities.

steps.title: Add context
steps.text: Identify symptom timing and whether the tracing is resting, exercise-related or serial.

steps.title: Separate conclusions
steps.text: State the ECG finding separately from the clinical infarction diagnosis.

example.question: Original synthetic educational example — A resting tracing shows horizontal ST depression in V4–V6. No symptom history or troponin result is supplied.
working: The ST changes are described by leads and direction.
Several causes remain possible.
Infarction cannot be inferred from this tracing alone.
example.answer: Lateral ST depression that may reflect ischaemia; correlate with clinical and serial evidence.

pitfalls: Calling all troponin elevations infarction.
Treating a non-diagnostic ECG as exclusion of acute coronary disease.
Using an exercise J+60 ms rule as the resting J-point rule.

practice.prompt: Which statement is most defensible?
options: A normal first ECG excludes an acute coronary syndrome
ECG findings require clinical and biomarker context
Every troponin rise proves plaque rupture
practice.explanation: The ECG contributes evidence; it does not independently determine the mechanism or establish all infarction criteria.
practice.hint: Separate electrical evidence from the clinical diagnosis.

practice.prompt: Does the lead with the deepest ST depression reliably identify the obstructed artery?
options: No; depression has limited territorial specificity
Only when the depression is 1 mm
practice.explanation: ST depression may be widespread or reciprocal and should not be treated as a precise vessel map.
practice.hint: Remember the course warning about depression localisation.

objectives.mastery: Explain the pattern, show the measurements and lead distribution, and state the most important limitation without prompting.

glossary.definition: Insufficient myocardial oxygen supply relative to demand.
Myocardial damage evidenced clinically by troponin above its reference limit; acute injury shows a rise or fall.

references.label: Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2026), EHJ
2023 ESC Guidelines for acute coronary syndromes

deepDive.title: The ECG is an electrical observation, not a coronary image
deepDive.text: Coronary disease, ischaemia, myocardial injury and infarction describe related but different things. The lecture moves between a fixed narrowing, transient vasospasm, plaque disruption and established infarction. Before choosing among them, state the electrical observation: the leads involved, ST direction and shape, T-wave polarity and any Q waves. A surface tracing does not show whether a particular plaque has ruptured or directly demonstrate living versus dead myocardium. Those conclusions require evidence beyond waveform recognition.

deepDive.title: A finding acquires meaning through its setting
deepDive.text: The exercise examples and resting acute-coronary examples belong to different interpretation settings. The course measures exercise ST depression after the J point, whereas its acute ST-elevation framework uses the J point itself. A technically correct number can therefore become a misleading conclusion if it is attached to the wrong setting. Record whether symptoms were occurring, whether the ECG was taken during exertion, and whether the changes are new, resolving or persistent. Context should change the inference, not the measured observation.

deepDive.title: Avoid a one-to-one disease map
deepDive.text: The lecture’s simplified diagrams are useful introductory models, but partial obstruction does not invariably map to one ECG category and complete obstruction does not invariably fulfil standard ST-elevation criteria. Its later slides explicitly challenge that shortcut. Similarly, an elevated troponin supports myocardial injury but does not by itself identify an ischaemic cause. Build a report in layers: measured change, plausible electrical process, supporting clinical evidence, and remaining alternatives. Each layer should be defensible independently.

deepDive.title: Compare evidence over time
deepDive.text: A normal or non-diagnostic first tracing cannot establish that nothing is evolving. Compare serial ECGs with consistent electrode placement and calibration, because both physiology and recording differences can change apparent morphology. If the available record contains only one time point, make that limitation explicit rather than inventing an evolutionary stage. The educational goal is a justified statement about what the ECG contributes, not a confident disease label based on a single suggestive feature.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: resting ECG A shows horizontal ST depression in V4–V6. A later ECG is less abnormal after the discomfort settles. No biomarker result or coronary imaging is supplied. Write a two-sentence interpretation.
steps: Name the regional ST depression and its observed change over time.
Recognise that symptom-linked dynamics increase interest in an ischaemic explanation but do not prove its cause.
Separate possible ischaemia from a confirmed diagnosis of myocardial infarction.
guidedExercise.answer: Lateral ST depression has become less marked on the later tracing. The dynamic findings may support myocardial ischaemia in the appropriate clinical setting, but the ECG record alone does not establish infarction or the coronary lesion.
guidedExercise.explanation: The useful result is not merely a differential list: it is a clear distinction between directly observed serial change and a clinical diagnosis requiring additional evidence.

objectives.coverageNote: Includes stable, vasospastic and acute-coronary teaching; the original case ECGs and final paradigm discussion remain source readings, not independently validated diagnoses.

objectives.title: Measure J-point elevation with contiguous-lead and age/sex rules
objectives.why: ST elevation is a measurement in a lead, whereas an ST-elevation infarction pattern is an interpretation across leads and clinical context.
know: ST elevation is a measurement in a lead, whereas an ST-elevation infarction pattern is an interpretation across leads and clinical context. First check recording calibration and identify the J point where the QRS ends. Compare its level with a suitable baseline, taking care when baseline drift, atrial repolarisation or tachycardia makes the reference uncertain. At standard gain, 1 mm represents 0.1 mV.

The current universal definition uses new J-point elevation in at least two contiguous leads, in the absence of confounding LVH or LBBB. For leads other than V2–V3, the usual threshold is at least 1 mm. In V2–V3 the thresholds are at least 2.5 mm for men under 40 years, 2 mm for men aged 40 years or older, and 1.5 mm for women. These are criteria within an assessment framework, not a guarantee of either coronary occlusion or its absence.

Contiguous means leads viewing neighbouring myocardial regions, rather than simply adjacent printed boxes on the ECG sheet. Evaluate distribution, reciprocal changes, serial evolution and symptoms alongside the numbers. A value just below a threshold can still be important, particularly with a convincing regional pattern. A value above a threshold may have a non-ischaemic explanation. State both the measured result and the assumptions used to interpret it.

steps.title: Check the recording
steps.text: Confirm 10 mm/mV and identify a stable baseline.

steps.title: Measure
steps.text: Measure the J point in two anatomically contiguous leads.

steps.title: Apply the correct rule
steps.text: Use the V2–V3 age/sex rule where relevant and identify conduction or voltage confounding.

example.question: Original synthetic educational example — A 35-year-old man has J-point elevation of 2.0 mm in V2 and 2.2 mm in V3, at 10 mm/mV.
working: Both are below the 2.5 mm threshold for men under 40 in V2–V3.
This numerical result does not exclude clinically significant ischaemia.
example.answer: The specified V2–V3 threshold is not met; interpret the regional pattern and clinical evidence.

pitfalls: Forgetting that women have a separate V2–V3 threshold.
Counting two non-contiguous leads.
Applying the standard rule uncritically during LBBB.

practice.prompt: At 10 mm/mV, 0.2 mV equals how many millimetres?
practice.explanation: Multiply millivolts by the gain: 0.2 × 10 = 2 mm.
practice.hint: Gain converts electrical amplitude to paper height.

practice.prompt: Which V2–V3 threshold applies to a woman?
practice.explanation: The usual V2–V3 threshold is at least 1.5 mm in women, within the stated clinical framework.
practice.hint: V2–V3 differs from the general 1 mm rule.

objectives.mastery: Explain the pattern, show the measurements and lead distribution, and state the most important limitation without prompting.

glossary.definition: The junction between the end of the QRS complex and beginning of the ST segment.
Leads viewing neighbouring anatomical regions.

references.label: Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2026), EHJ
2023 ESC Guidelines for acute coronary syndromes

deepDive.title: Find the measurement landmark first
deepDive.text: Locate the end of ventricular depolarisation before measuring ST displacement. The J point is the transition from the QRS complex into the ST segment; it is not the most visually elevated point reached later by an upward-sloping segment. The course deliberately contrasts J-point and J-plus-60-ms measurements to show how different landmarks can yield different numbers on the same waveform. Choose a suitable reference baseline and describe uncertainty if baseline wander or a broad terminal QRS prevents confident placement.

deepDive.title: Convert paper distance into voltage
deepDive.text: At a gain of 10 mm/mV, 1 mm represents 0.1 mV and 2 mm represents 0.2 mV. That conversion is independent of paper speed, which governs horizontal time measurements. Check the printed gain before translating a vertical box count into an elevation threshold. A change in display magnification does not change the underlying recorded voltage. If a source image has been resized without its calibration mark, describe the morphology but avoid pretending that on-screen millimetres are original ECG millimetres.

deepDive.title: Apply the cited framework to the correct leads
deepDive.text: The source reproduces a 2018 consensus framework requiring new J-point elevation in at least two contiguous leads, with different cut-points in V2–V3 according to age and sex. In that cited framework the V2–V3 values are 2.5 mm for men under 40, 2 mm for men 40 or older, and 1.5 mm for women; other standard leads generally use 1 mm. These are source-specific teaching criteria, not a complete current clinical decision rule.

deepDive.title: Explain what a threshold can and cannot settle
deepDive.text: Contiguous leads represent related anatomical views; two unrelated abnormal leads are not interchangeable with a regional pair. The cited table also states its setting excludes major confounders such as ventricular hypertrophy and bundle branch block. The lecture warns about limited sensitivity: failing a cut-point does not exclude an important acute process. Conversely, passing it does not identify the cause of elevation without considering the entire tracing, earlier recordings and clinical context. State the criterion result and its limitations separately.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: a 35-year-old man has J-point elevation of 2 mm in V2 and V3 at 10 mm/mV. The same segments reach 3 mm at J+60 ms. How does this compare with the source’s cited V2–V3 rule?
steps: Use the J point, not the later 3 mm height.
Choose the source’s age/sex category: men younger than 40.
Compare 2 mm with the cited 2.5 mm cut-point while retaining the limitation of threshold testing.
guidedExercise.answer: The 2 mm J-point elevation does not meet that source’s 2.5 mm V2–V3 cut-point for men under 40. The later 3 mm measurement is not a substitute for the J-point measurement, and the criterion result alone does not exclude acute ischaemia.
guidedExercise.explanation: This exercise tests landmark selection, calibration and correct population category rather than asking the learner to diagnose the supplied person from two measurements.

objectives.coverageNote: Threshold table on source page 39 was visually checked; its 2018 date and stated exclusions are retained as limitations.

objectives.title: Localise regional patterns and recognise posterior and right-sided clues
objectives.why: Lead geography helps describe the distribution of an abnormality.
know: Lead geography helps describe the distribution of an abnormality. Inferior leads are II, III and aVF; I, aVL, V5 and V6 view lateral regions; the precordial leads describe overlapping anterior and septal regions. A regional combination is more informative than a single lead. Electrical territories overlap, and coronary anatomy varies, so report the region confidently only when supported and avoid asserting a particular culprit artery from one clue.

Reciprocal ST depression can strengthen the interpretation of regional ST elevation, but it is neither mandatory nor perfectly specific. Posterior injury can appear as a mirror-image pattern in V1–V3: ST depression with relatively prominent R waves and upright T waves may be suggestive in the appropriate setting. This is different from declaring every anterior ST depression posterior infarction. Additional posterior leads V7–V9 can provide a more direct view.

Inferior patterns can coexist with right ventricular involvement. Right-sided leads, especially V3R and V4R, add information that the standard precordial placement may miss. The course illustrates these relationships; supplemental ESC guidance supports appropriate additional leads. In an interpretation, identify which leads were actually recorded. Do not write that a posterior or right ventricular diagnosis was confirmed when the necessary evidence is absent. Distribution, associated findings and clinical context should be stated together.

steps.title: Map the pattern
steps.text: Group abnormal leads into anatomical regions.

steps.title: Look opposite
steps.text: Check for reciprocal changes without making their absence an exclusion rule.

steps.title: Name missing views
steps.text: Recognise when posterior or right-sided recordings could clarify the pattern.

example.question: Original synthetic educational example — An educational tracing has ST depression and tall R waves in V1–V3 during a chest-pain scenario.
working: The anterior findings may be a mirror image of posterior injury.
Other causes of tall R waves and ST depression remain possible.
V7–V9 would add direct posterior information.
example.answer: Possible posterior ischaemic pattern; additional evidence is needed.

pitfalls: Equating lead territory with a certain culprit artery.
Claiming posterior leads do not exist.
Treating S1Q3T3 or an isolated tall R wave as an infarction diagnosis.

practice.prompt: Which leads provide a posterior view?
options: V1 and V2 in standard positions
practice.explanation: V7–V9 are additional posterior leads.
practice.hint: Think beyond the standard six precordial positions.

practice.prompt: II, III and aVF are conventionally grouped as which region?
practice.explanation: These limb leads view the inferior region.
practice.hint: Use the limb-lead map.

objectives.mastery: Explain the pattern, show the measurements and lead distribution, and state the most important limitation without prompting.

glossary.definition: An opposite-direction ST change in leads viewing a region opposite the principal pattern.
Additional leads V7–V9 placed to view the posterior left ventricular region.
