Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2026), EHJ

deepDive.title: Localise a pattern before naming an artery
deepDive.text: Lead groups offer different electrical views of the heart. The source groups II, III and aVF as inferior and I, aVL, V5 and V6 as lateral, then builds anterior patterns across the precordium. Describe the actual affected leads before assigning a territorial shorthand. Territorial names summarise the recording; they are not images of a coronary lesion. Coronary branching and myocardial distribution vary, so a familiar lead group cannot prove the identity or exact position of an obstructed vessel.

deepDive.title: Use reciprocal findings as a consistency check
deepDive.text: An injury-related electrical vector may appear positive in one view and negative in an opposing view. This explains why regional elevation and reciprocal depression can form one coherent pattern rather than necessarily representing two separate lesions. The source’s limb-lead discussion emphasises this geometric relationship. Check whether the opposing changes fit the same overall distribution. Do not turn all ST depression into a reciprocal sign: its interpretation still depends on which leads are involved and what the other leads show.

deepDive.title: Recognise the limitations of the standard lead set
deepDive.text: The standard anterior chest leads do not directly cover every relevant surface. The lecture teaches posterior-pattern clues through anterior reciprocal changes: ST depression with relatively prominent R waves in V1–V3 can prompt consideration of a posterior or related regional process. It also introduces right-sided views when inferior changes suggest right ventricular involvement. These are reasons to seek appropriate additional recording information, not reasons to convert an isolated dominant R wave or one elevated lead into a definitive territorial diagnosis.

deepDive.title: Keep anatomical terminology and uncertainty visible
deepDive.text: The course itself notes that traditional posterior-wall language does not map perfectly onto later imaging-based descriptions. Use the conventional term when needed to discuss the teaching pattern, while reporting the observable anterior changes precisely. Poor R-wave progression is another clue requiring alternatives: placement, conduction and non-ischaemic myocardial disease can affect it. A strong interpretation explains why the complete distribution supports a proposed regional process and identifies what additional leads or comparison recordings would test that explanation.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: II, III and aVF show ST elevation; aVL shows depression. V1–V3 also show depression with relatively prominent R waves. Describe the combined pattern without claiming an angiographic result.
steps: Identify the inferior lead-group elevation.
Recognise the opposing aVL change as compatible with a reciprocal relationship.
Describe the anterior depression and R-wave prominence as clues to additional posterior-pattern involvement.
guidedExercise.answer: Inferior ST elevation with opposing change in aVL and anterior changes that raise consideration of a posterior-pattern extension. The affected coronary vessel and full anatomical extent cannot be established from these features alone.
guidedExercise.explanation: Combining distributions produces a more useful interpretation than assigning a diagnosis separately to each abnormal lead, while avoiding an unjustified artery-level claim.

objectives.coverageNote: Expands the lead-group, reciprocal, posterior/right-sided and anatomical-language slides; original territory examples remain essential private-viewer practice.

objectives.title: Recognise dynamic T-wave warning patterns without overcalling a single tracing
objectives.why: T waves can change before a tracing meets conventional ST-elevation thresholds.
know: T waves can change before a tracing meets conventional ST-elevation thresholds. Hyperacute ischaemic T waves may be broad and disproportionate to the preceding QRS complex, often in a regional distribution. Their significance comes from comparison with the surrounding leads, prior tracings and clinical timing. A tall T wave alone has many explanations, including normal variation and potassium disturbance; absolute height is an inadequate definition of acute coronary occlusion.

The course introduces a Wellens pattern: characteristic biphasic or deeply inverted anterior T waves, classically in V2–V3, in a suitable clinical setting. Preserved R progression and little ST elevation can coexist. This is a warning pattern associated with important anterior coronary disease, rather than a standalone anatomical diagnosis. Symptoms may have settled when the changes are recorded. Do not treat apparent improvement in pain as proof that a concerning tracing is benign.

A de Winter pattern combines upsloping ST depression near the J point in precordial leads with prominent T waves in the appropriate setting. It illustrates why the statement that all upsloping depression is normal is unsafe. Compare serial recordings carefully: changing morphology can provide evidence unavailable from one snapshot. Report the pattern and uncertainty explicitly. These educational recognition tasks do not provide a provocative-test or treatment instruction; real clinical decisions require prompt qualified assessment.

steps.title: Compare proportions
steps.text: Judge T-wave size and shape relative to its QRS, not only millimetres.

steps.title: Assess distribution
steps.text: Look for a coherent anterior or other regional pattern.

steps.title: Use time
steps.text: Compare symptoms and serial tracings rather than assigning a diagnosis from shape alone.

example.question: Original synthetic educational example — A synthetic case has recent chest discomfort followed by biphasic T waves in V2–V3 with little ST elevation.
working: The distribution and morphology resemble a Wellens warning pattern.
Clinical timing and alternative causes must be assessed.
example.answer: Describe a possible Wellens pattern, rather than diagnosing a specific stenosis from the ECG alone.

pitfalls: Calling all upright tall T waves hyperacute.
Declaring all upsloping ST depression normal.
Assuming resolved pain rules out a high-risk pattern.

practice.prompt: Which feature is most useful when assessing a potentially hyperacute T wave?
options: Its size relative to QRS, distribution and serial change
Whether it is upright in any lead
practice.explanation: Proportion, regionality and evolution improve interpretation beyond a single amplitude cutoff.
practice.hint: Use relationships and context.

practice.prompt: Which pattern may include biphasic T waves in V2–V3?
practice.explanation: Biphasic or deep anterior T-wave inversion can form a Wellens pattern in the appropriate context.

deepDive.title: Look at proportions and shape, not height alone
deepDive.text: The lecture compares tall T waves in several settings. A potentially hyperacute T wave is assessed relative to the preceding QRS, its breadth, symmetry and relationship to the ST segment, rather than by a single absolute amplitude. A narrow, pointed appearance can suggest a different process from a broad-based change, but morphology alone cannot determine an electrolyte concentration or coronary finding. Compare several neighbouring leads and, when available, a previous tracing from the same person.

deepDive.title: Tie a dynamic pattern to its recording time
deepDive.text: The Wellens teaching examples show that appearances may change as discomfort changes. Biphasic or deeply inverted anterior T waves, preserved R waves and little ST displacement form a pattern worth recognising in the appropriate setting. The temporal relationship matters: the appearance during pain may differ from the appearance after pain settles. Do not treat the name as a replacement for describing the actual waveforms, the symptom timing and whether the entire expected pattern is present.

deepDive.title: Recognise why a narrow threshold screen can miss a pattern
deepDive.text: The later coronary slides introduce patterns in which a major acute coronary process may not satisfy conventional ST-elevation cut-points. Their educational role is to prevent a false reassurance rule based solely on millimetres. A combination of precordial J-point depression and prominent T waves, for example, should be described as a combination rather than dismissed because elevation is absent. Named patterns are interpretive aids; their recognition requires the complete ECG and a suitable clinical context.

deepDive.title: Describe change without inventing a sequence
deepDive.text: Serial comparison is particularly valuable when abnormalities are subtle or transient. Confirm that electrodes and calibration are comparable before interpreting a new T-wave contour as physiological evolution. If only one image is available, list plausible alternatives and state that dynamic behaviour cannot be assessed. Source case outcomes demonstrate possibilities, not the predictive accuracy of the app’s teaching examples. A learner should be able to say both why a pattern deserves attention and why its exact cause remains uncertain from a single tracing.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: ECG A has modest anterior T-wave changes. ECG B, recorded when pain has settled, shows deeper symmetrical inversion in V2–V4 with preserved R waves and little ST elevation. What information should a careful report retain?
steps: Record the serial anterior T-wave change and the symptom relationship.
Describe the preserved R waves and limited ST displacement rather than reporting inversion alone.
State that the combination may resemble a recognised ischaemic warning pattern, while clinical and complete-ECG evidence remain necessary.
guidedExercise.answer: The report should retain the dynamic anterior T-wave morphology, the recording’s relationship to pain, and the accompanying R-wave/ST features. It should not claim that T-wave inversion alone proves a particular coronary lesion.
guidedExercise.explanation: The exercise makes the temporal and morphological reasoning explicit instead of testing recall of a name without its defining context.

objectives.coverageNote: Broadens hyperacute, Wellens and non-standard occlusion-pattern teaching without reproducing case tracings or presenting historical case percentages as current performance estimates.

objectives.title: Describe Q waves and evolving ST–T changes without dating infarction precisely
objectives.why: Q waves represent initial ventricular activation directed away from a lead.
know: Q waves represent initial ventricular activation directed away from a lead. Small septal Q waves are normal in some leads, whereas unusual duration, depth and distribution may raise concern for myocardial disease. The course uses simplified size rules to introduce the idea. In practice, pathological Q-wave criteria depend on lead and context, and abnormal Q waves can have causes other than infarction. Interpret a pattern across leads rather than labelling every negative initial deflection as a scar.

Infarction-related ECGs may evolve through changing ST levels, QRS morphology and T waves, but there is no universal timetable visible on a single tracing. Some infarctions do not produce persistent Q waves; some Q waves regress; pre-existing Q waves can coexist with a new event. A Q wave does not independently establish that myocardium is irreversibly non-viable. An ECG also cannot reliably determine an exact infarct age without clinical and serial evidence.

Poor precordial R-wave progression is similarly descriptive rather than diagnostic. Lead placement, body habitus, conduction disturbance and myocardial disease can all contribute. Confirm technical factors and compare previous recordings before inferring an old anterior infarction. A defensible report distinguishes an observed QRS feature, a possible explanation and the evidence needed to resolve it. This approach preserves useful information while avoiding a falsely certain history generated from electrical morphology alone.

steps.text: Identify unusual Q waves or R progression and their lead distribution.

steps.title: Check alternatives
steps.text: Consider placement, conduction and non-ischaemic myocardial causes.

steps.title: Qualify timing
steps.text: Use prior ECGs and clinical history rather than assigning a fixed age.

example.question: Original synthetic educational example — A synthetic asymptomatic case has Q waves in inferior leads, with no previous ECG or biomarker data.
working: The inferior Q-wave pattern is an observation.
Its mechanism and timing are not established by this record.
example.answer: Inferior Q waves requiring clinical and previous-ECG correlation; do not label an exact old infarct date.

pitfalls: Equating Q waves with certain irreversible necrosis.
Dating an infarction from a textbook sequence alone.
Calling poor R progression proof of previous anterior infarction.

practice.prompt: What does poor R-wave progression establish by itself?
practice.explanation: Several technical and biological explanations exist.
practice.hint: Description is stronger than an unsupported diagnosis.

practice.prompt: Can Q waves alone date an infarction precisely?
practice.explanation: Q waves may persist, regress or have another cause; timing requires additional evidence.
practice.hint: Morphology is not a clock.

glossary.definition: The first negative QRS deflection before any positive R wave.
The pattern of changing R-wave amplitude across precordial leads.

deepDive.title: Define the waveform before interpreting its cause
deepDive.text: A Q wave is an initial negative ventricular deflection before any positive R wave in that lead. A QS complex remains negative without a subsequent positive R. Duration, depth relative to the following R wave, affected lead and distribution all influence interpretation. Small initial septal q waves in appropriate leads can be normal, while an isolated large Q in a lead with a variable normal orientation may be less specific. Measure before choosing the adjective pathological.

deepDive.title: The same loss of initial positivity has several explanations
deepDive.text: The lecture uses infarction to explain reduced early positive forces and abnormal Q waves, but this is not a one-to-one mechanism map. Its other course modules show Q-wave or QS patterns in cardiomyopathy, infiltration and altered activation. Lead placement can also change apparent R progression. Therefore, state the abnormal morphology and distribution first, then integrate corroborating changes and history. An isolated Q wave does not by itself establish necrosis, its aetiology or the date on which it occurred.

deepDive.title: Treat evolutionary diagrams as models, not clocks
deepDive.text: The source’s sequence from T-wave change through ST elevation and later Q-wave/T-wave patterns is an organising model. Real recordings vary with timing, infarct extent, reperfusion, previous disease and the available comparison. Features can coexist or be absent, and a later-looking appearance cannot provide an exact age from a single ECG. Serial recordings can establish that a change developed between two observations; they do not justify assigning a precise biological timetable without other evidence.

deepDive.title: Use a descriptive conclusion that can be audited
deepDive.text: A useful report names the leads with abnormal initial negative forces, records whether ST displacement or T inversion accompanies them, and states whether earlier ECGs show the same pattern. Poor R-wave progression should be described with the same discipline rather than automatically treated as equivalent proof of a previous anterior infarct. Where the source labels a case as recent or old, distinguish that case’s supplied clinical information from what you could conclude if shown the tracing alone.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: a single tracing has QS complexes in V1–V3 and no substantial ST elevation. No previous tracing, electrode-placement check or imaging is provided. Can it be dated as an old anterior infarct?
steps: Describe the QS distribution without assuming its mechanism.
Look for corroborating or conflicting ST–T and conduction findings.
Identify the absent comparison and technical information that prevent confident dating and attribution.
guidedExercise.answer: No. Report the anterior QS pattern and its differential interpretation. Previous infarction is a possibility in the appropriate setting, but the supplied ECG information does not establish the cause or age of the pattern.
guidedExercise.explanation: The interpretation remains useful because it identifies the finding and the missing evidence, rather than replacing uncertainty with an unsupported date.

objectives.coverageNote: Includes normal/abnormal Q-wave distinctions and evolution diagrams; simplifies none of these into a universal necrosis or infarct-dating rule.

objectives.title: Interpret ST changes when LBBB alters ventricular activation
objectives.why: Left bundle branch block changes ventricular activation and therefore alters repolarisation.
know: Left bundle branch block changes ventricular activation and therefore alters repolarisation. ST segments and T waves often point opposite the main QRS direction, creating expected discordance. Standard ST-elevation thresholds cannot simply be applied as though the QRS were narrow and normally conducted. Start by recognising the conduction pattern, then assess whether the ST deviation is concordant or disproportionate to the underlying QRS.

The course introduces Sgarbossa criteria and a proportional modification. Concordant ST elevation and certain concordant ST depression patterns can be important clues in LBBB. Excessive discordant elevation is assessed relative to the preceding negative QRS, rather than only by a fixed absolute number. In the modified approach, an elevated ST segment at least one quarter of the depth of its preceding S wave is a concerning proportional finding when the complete criterion and clinical context are satisfied.

Keep the signed and absolute conventions separate. For a 2 mm positive ST displacement above a 6 mm negative S wave, the signed ST/S ratio is −0.33 and the magnitude ratio is 0.33. Both describe the same relationship. A ratio is not an independent diagnosis, and negative criteria cannot exclude all infarctions. The source slide occasionally labels this relationship ST/T; the intended denominator in this proportional assessment is the S-wave amplitude. Show your measurements so that another reader can audit the conclusion.

steps.text: Establish LBBB and expected discordant repolarisation.

steps.title: Assess concordance
steps.text: Compare ST direction with the principal QRS direction in each relevant lead.

steps.title: Measure proportion
steps.text: Record ST displacement and S-wave depth using an explicit sign convention.

example.question: Original synthetic educational example — A synthetic LBBB lead has an S wave of −8 mm and ST elevation of +3 mm.
working: Absolute magnitude ratio = 3/8 = 0.375.
The proportion exceeds one quarter.
example.answer: Disproportionate discordant ST elevation is a concerning finding; integrate the full ECG and clinical evidence.

pitfalls: Using T-wave height as the denominator.
Mixing a negative signed ratio with a positive magnitude threshold.
Treating a negative criterion as an infarction exclusion test.

practice.prompt: For ST elevation 2 mm above an S wave 10 mm deep, what is the magnitude ratio?
practice.explanation: The magnitude ratio is 2/10 = 0.2.
practice.hint: Divide amplitudes measured in the same units.

deepDive.title: Start with the altered activation sequence
deepDive.text: Left bundle branch block changes ventricular depolarisation and normally produces secondary ST–T changes. This means an ST segment cannot be interpreted with the same expectation as in an otherwise narrow, normally activated QRS. Identify the dominant QRS direction in each relevant lead before describing the ST segment. A secondary repolarisation pattern often points opposite to the dominant ventricular deflection; that relationship provides the background against which a potentially unexpected ST finding is assessed.

deepDive.title: Concordance and discordance are relationships
deepDive.text: Concordant elevation is elevation in a lead whose dominant QRS is positive. Concordant depression is depression in a lead whose QRS is negative; the original framework particularly examines V1–V3 depression. Discordant elevation accompanies a predominantly negative QRS and may be expected to some extent in LBBB. These terms do not mean normal or abnormal by themselves. Specify the waveform relationship and its magnitude, because the distinction depends on both parts of the complex rather than ST height alone.

deepDive.title: Why proportionality matters
deepDive.text: The lecture contrasts an absolute discordant-elevation cut-point with a proportional comparison to the preceding S-wave depth. The same 2 mm elevation has a different relationship to a 3 mm S wave than to a 20 mm S wave. In the source’s signed convention, ST elevation is positive and S-wave depth negative, so their quotient is negative. An implementation must keep that convention explicit; otherwise an apparently correct calculation may be compared with a threshold having the opposite sign.

deepDive.title: A structured criterion is not a complete exclusion test
deepDive.text: The source presents original and modified Sgarbossa approaches to help interpret the difficult LBBB setting. Use the correct framework, its stated measurement definitions and the full tracing rather than combining selected rules into an invented score. A criterion-positive pattern increases concern in context, while a negative result does not establish that acute ischaemia is absent. Record the LBBB, the unexpected ST–QRS relationship, the actual measurements and the need for serial or clinical correlation without claiming a stand-alone ECG diagnosis.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: a lead with a negative QRS has an S-wave depth of −4 mm and J-point ST elevation of +1.5 mm. Calculate the signed ST/S quotient and explain why reporting only the 1.5 mm height loses information.
steps: Use the same baseline and voltage calibration for both measurements.
Divide +1.5 by −4 to obtain −0.375.
Compare the magnitude relative to QRS depth, using the source’s signed convention rather than treating 1.5 mm as inherently small.
guidedExercise.answer: ST/S = −0.375. The elevation is substantial relative to the shallow S wave even though its absolute height is below 5 mm; this is the proportional reasoning illustrated in the lecture.
guidedExercise.explanation: The calculation illustrates the modified criterion’s rationale. It does not independently establish infarction, and a real interpretation must assess all relevant leads and clinical evidence.

title: Pulmonary embolism, pericardial and myocardial inflammation
summary: Recognise supportive ECG patterns while preserving the distinction between an electrical clue and a clinical diagnosis.

objectives.title: Recognise right ventricular strain clues without diagnosing pulmonary embolism
objectives.why: Acute pulmonary embolism can increase right ventricular pressure and alter both activation and repolarisation.
know: Acute pulmonary embolism can increase right ventricular pressure and alter both activation and repolarisation. The course illustrates sinus tachycardia, rightward axis, right bundle branch block and right precordial T-wave inversion. These findings become more informative when they form a coherent right ventricular strain pattern. None directly displays a pulmonary arterial clot, and several occur in other cardiopulmonary conditions.

S1Q3T3 describes an S wave in lead I together with a Q wave and inverted T wave in lead III. It is a memorable pattern, but it has limited sensitivity and specificity for pulmonary embolism. Its absence is common and cannot exclude the condition. Its presence may indicate right-heart loading in an appropriate setting, rather than proving a particular cause. A normal or non-specific ECG also does not rule out pulmonary embolism.

Begin with rate, rhythm, QRS duration and axis, then inspect V1–V4 and inferior leads for repolarisation abnormalities. Compare with a previous tracing if available, because chronic right-heart disease can resemble acute strain. Clinical probability and appropriate non-ECG investigations establish the diagnostic pathway. In this course, practise reporting the pattern and its limitations. Do not use an ECG pattern score as a substitute for clinical probability or laboratory and imaging evidence.

steps.text: Assess rhythm, rate, axis, QRS width and right precordial T waves.

steps.title: Group clues
steps.text: Describe a possible right ventricular strain pattern when findings agree.

steps.title: State uncertainty
steps.text: Explain that the ECG cannot independently confirm or exclude PE.

working: The combination can accompany right ventricular strain.
PE is one possible explanation among others.
example.answer: Right ventricular strain features; determine their cause from the clinical assessment.

pitfalls: Treating S1Q3T3 as diagnostic.
Excluding PE after a normal ECG.
Assuming every right precordial T inversion is acute.

practice.prompt: A normal ECG in suspected PE means what?
options: The ECG has not demonstrated a specific pattern
practice.explanation: The ECG may be normal or non-specific in PE.
practice.hint: Consider sensitivity.

practice.prompt: What is the best interpretation of S1Q3T3?
practice.explanation: The pattern is supportive in context but not specific to PE.
practice.hint: It describes electrical morphology, not clot imaging.

glossary.definition: An ECG pattern that can reflect right ventricular pressure or load, with characteristic repolarisation and sometimes conduction changes.

deepDive.title: Think in terms of a right-heart electrical pattern
deepDive.text: The source gathers sinus tachycardia, rightward axis, right precordial T inversion, right bundle branch block appearances and the S1Q3T3 combination as possible clues in pulmonary embolism. Their common educational theme is a changed right-heart electrical pattern in the appropriate clinical setting. They are not a direct recording of a clot. Begin by describing rate, conduction, axis and repolarisation separately, then ask whether those observations form a coherent pattern rather than searching only for one memorable sign.

deepDive.title: Deconstruct S1Q3T3 instead of using it as a password
deepDive.text: The label describes an S wave in lead I, an initial negative ventricular deflection in lead III, and T-wave inversion in lead III. Check each component on the actual tracing. A Q wave in III alone can occur with normal variation, and T inversion has many possible causes. Even the complete combination is not specific enough to diagnose pulmonary embolism. The source cases also demonstrate that some people with the supplied diagnosis do not show the complete named combination.

deepDive.title: Do not equate absence of a clue with absence of disease
deepDive.text: An ECG can be normal or nonspecific in pulmonary embolism. Its value here is to contribute to assessment, reveal rhythm or strain-related findings, and suggest alternatives; it is not an exclusion test. Equally, the presence of right ventricular strain-like changes does not quantify obstruction or haemodynamic severity. Avoid repeating the lecture’s simplified wording as a rule that a particular appearance proves a massive embolus. The clinical probability and other diagnostic evidence lie outside the waveform alone.

deepDive.title: Use the source cases to compare overlap
deepDive.text: The lecture shows anterior ST changes that can resemble an acute coronary presentation. Compare these examples with the coronary module by asking what is directly recorded, which distribution supports each possibility, and which history would matter. A troponin elevation does not automatically settle that differential, because myocardial injury is not unique to coronary infarction. A careful learning report should name the electrical pattern and the relevant clinical question while retaining uncertainty about its cause.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: an ECG shows sinus tachycardia, right precordial T inversion and an incomplete RBBB-like pattern, but no clear S1Q3T3. Can either presence or absence of pulmonary embolism be established?
steps: Describe the rate, conduction appearance and T-wave distribution.
Recognise that absence of the complete named pattern does not exclude the condition.
Recognise that the remaining findings also occur in other settings.
guidedExercise.answer: Neither conclusion is justified from the ECG alone. The tracing shows a right-heart strain-like electrical pattern that may contribute to assessment in the appropriate clinical context.
guidedExercise.explanation: This exercise rejects both the positive shortcut and the negative shortcut: a recognisable ECG clue is neither a clot detector nor a reliable rule-out test.

objectives.title: Compare pericarditis, regional ischaemia and early repolarisation
objectives.why: Acute pericardial inflammation may produce widespread ST elevation and PR-segment depression.
know: Acute pericardial inflammation may produce widespread ST elevation and PR-segment depression. The distribution can extend beyond a single coronary territory, while aVR and sometimes V1 may show opposite changes. A downsloping TP segment is another supportive observation described in the course. These are tendencies rather than compulsory findings; an ECG alone does not establish the entire clinical diagnosis.

ST-segment shape is not a dependable binary test. Concave elevation can occur in pericarditis or early repolarisation and also during acute infarction. Pericarditis can be regional, and myocardial inflammation can produce a focal infarct-like pattern. Assess reciprocal changes, PR shifts, symptoms, prior tracings, biomarkers and imaging context together. A normal tracing does not exclude pericardial inflammation. New regional changes in a concerning clinical setting require an appropriately cautious interpretation.

The source compares ST elevation with T-wave height as an aid to distinguishing early repolarisation and pericarditis. A relatively large ST/T ratio in an appropriate lateral lead may support pericarditis, but it is not a universal diagnostic threshold and cannot safely decide among all causes of ST elevation. Learn the relationship as one supporting feature. A defensible answer explains why one possibility fits better, names an important alternative and identifies missing clinical information.

steps.text: Decide whether the changes are widespread or regional.

steps.title: Inspect atrial baseline
steps.text: Look for PR shifts and distinguish PR from TP segments.

steps.title: Compare competing explanations
steps.text: Combine distribution, serial change and context rather than using concavity alone.

working: The combined pattern supports pericardial inflammation.
Concavity alone would be insufficient.
Regional coronary disease and myocardial inflammation remain clinical considerations.
example.answer: ECG pattern compatible with pericarditis; clinical diagnostic evidence is still required.

pitfalls: Declaring concave ST elevation non-ischaemic.
Calling an ST/T ratio diagnostic by itself.
Assuming pericarditis must always be diffuse.

practice.explanation: Multiple coherent features outperform a single morphological shortcut.
practice.hint: Use the whole pattern.

practice.explanation: Concavity does not exclude infarction.

deepDive.title: Compare distributions, not just curvature
deepDive.text: The source introduces widespread ST elevation and PR depression as a pericarditis-associated pattern, then explicitly warns that pericarditis is often overdiagnosed. A concave upward ST segment is not sufficient to distinguish inflammation from a coronary process or early repolarisation. Inspect which leads are affected, whether changes are regional or widespread, and whether there are opposing changes or other features that make one explanation more coherent. Describe those observations before giving the pattern a cause.

deepDive.title: Choose a baseline that does not hide the clue
deepDive.text: PR depression is assessed relative to an appropriate baseline; a sloping TP segment or unstable baseline can complicate that judgement. If the PR segment is itself displaced, using it uncritically as the ST reference can change the apparent elevation. Examine several beats and leads, check recording quality and state uncertainty where the baseline is ambiguous. The aim is not to find a required sign at any cost, but to recognise a consistent relationship in a technically interpretable tracing.

deepDive.title: Use a supporting ratio with its limitations
deepDive.text: The lecture illustrates the ratio of ST displacement to T-wave amplitude in selected leads as one aid when comparing pericarditis-associated appearances and early repolarisation. Both quantities must come from the same lead and use consistent units, so millimetres may be divided by millimetres or millivolts by millivolts. A ratio from one illustrative study is supporting evidence, not a universal discriminator. It cannot compensate for an unsuitable lead, uncertain baseline, altered T morphology or a conflicting clinical presentation.

deepDive.title: Understand the sequence without demanding it
deepDive.text: The course describes ST changes resolving before later T inversion in a typical inflammatory evolution. This is a useful comparison with some coronary evolutionary patterns, but not every tracing follows a complete textbook series. Earlier ECGs and symptom timing may be more informative than the shape of one isolated segment. A defensible interpretation explains why inflammation is plausible, which competing patterns remain possible, and what the ECG cannot determine about the pericardium or myocardium on its own.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: a selected lead has ST displacement 0.2 mV and T amplitude 1.0 mV. Other leads show widespread elevation, but the baseline is somewhat variable. Calculate the ratio and state how much weight it should carry.
steps: Divide 0.2 mV by 1.0 mV to obtain a unitless ratio of 0.20.
Recognise the measurement uncertainty caused by the baseline.
Use the ratio as supporting pattern evidence alongside distribution and context, not as a diagnosis.
guidedExercise.answer: The ratio is 0.20. Its value is limited by baseline uncertainty and by the fact that a supporting ST/T ratio cannot independently distinguish all causes of elevation.
guidedExercise.explanation: The exercise tests calculation and appropriate evidential weight; it deliberately avoids a rigid rule that would overrule the rest of the ECG.

objectives.coverageNote: Pericarditis/early-repolarisation comparisons and the original source ratio are contextualised; concavity is not taught as an exclusion of coronary ischaemia.

objectives.title: Explain low voltage and electrical alternans in pericardial effusion
objectives.why: A large pericardial effusion can reduce the recorded amplitude of cardiac electrical activity.
know: A large pericardial effusion can reduce the recorded amplitude of cardiac electrical activity. The source illustrates low QRS voltage and electrical alternans, sometimes with sinus tachycardia. Low voltage means small measured QRS amplitudes in a defined lead set at a known gain; it is not simply a tracing that looks small on a resized screen. First check calibration and recording quality.

Electrical alternans is beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude or axis. In a large effusion, movement of the heart within fluid can change its relationship to the recording electrodes. However, alternating complexes can also arise from other mechanisms, including rate-related changes. Do not confuse true alternation with intermittent ectopy, noise, respiratory amplitude change or an irregular sequence of different conducted beats.

Neither low voltage nor alternans proves tamponade. Tamponade is a clinical and haemodynamic syndrome, assessed with the examination and appropriate imaging. Effusion may exist without either ECG finding, and low voltage has several non-effusion causes, including body habitus, lung disease and myocardial disorders. The educational task is to recognise the clue, describe its regularity and state the limits. An interpretation should not convert an illustrative association into an unsupported definitive diagnosis.

steps.title: Confirm scale
steps.text: Verify gain and assess QRS amplitude consistently.

steps.title: Track consecutive beats
steps.text: Decide whether the amplitude alternates regularly or varies for another reason.

steps.title: Link cautiously
steps.text: Explain the effusion association and the need for clinical/imaging evidence.

working: The pattern may represent electrical alternans.
Effusion is a relevant association but is not established.
example.answer: Describe electrical alternans and low voltage; assess cause and haemodynamic significance clinically.

pitfalls: Diagnosing tamponade from ECG alone.
Measuring a screenshot without calibration.
Confusing ectopic beats with alternans.

practice.explanation: The defining observation is beat-to-beat variation, often in amplitude or axis.
practice.hint: Focus on consecutive complexes.

options: Only when the rate is normal
practice.explanation: ECG sensitivity is limited, and many effusions do not produce low voltage.

deepDive.title: Electrical amplitude is influenced by more than myocardial activity
deepDive.text: The potential recorded at the body surface depends on the generator, its direction and the surrounding volume conductor. Fluid around the heart can contribute to smaller surface waveforms, but low voltage has multiple technical and biological explanations. Check recording gain, lead contact and whether small amplitude is present in limb leads, precordial leads or both. A low-voltage description is an ECG finding; it does not directly measure fluid volume or establish the presence of an effusion.

deepDive.title: Recognise true beat-to-beat alternation
deepDive.text: Electrical alternans describes a repeating change in amplitude, direction or morphology between successive beats. The source illustrates a large-effusion setting in which cardiac motion changes the recorded electrical orientation. First confirm that the alternation is systematic rather than random baseline noise, movement or a changing lead connection. Also identify the underlying rhythm: alternating QRS appearances due to a rhythm mechanism are not automatically the same phenomenon as the source’s swinging-heart illustration.

deepDive.title: Combine clues without making them mandatory
deepDive.text: Sinus tachycardia, low voltage and alternation can form a suggestive combination in the right circumstances. The source explicitly notes that smaller or moderate effusions may produce little ECG change. Thus, absence of the classic combination cannot exclude fluid, and its presence cannot provide a direct measure of haemodynamic impact. Avoid turning a memorable illustrative triad into a requirement that every effusion must satisfy, or a stand-alone diagnosis that replaces other assessment.

deepDive.title: Separate an electrical report from an imaging conclusion
deepDive.text: A report can state that a low-voltage tracing shows beat-to-beat alternation and explain why a pericardial process is among the possibilities. It should also state which recording checks were made and whether there are relevant previous ECGs. Structural information such as the presence and extent of fluid requires another source of evidence. This separation makes the reasoning auditable: the ECG supports a question about the pericardium rather than purporting to display its anatomy directly.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: at standard gain, consecutive sinus beats alternate between larger and smaller QRS complexes in several leads. Limb-lead amplitudes are low. Write an observation and a separate inference.
steps: Confirm that the underlying rhythm is sinus-like and that the alternation repeats across beats.
Record low voltage only after checking gain and lead quality.
Keep the possible pericardial explanation separate from the directly observed electrical findings.
guidedExercise.answer: Observation: low-amplitude complexes with repeating beat-to-beat QRS alternation. Inference: the combination may support consideration of a pericardial process in context, but the ECG alone does not confirm an effusion or its physiological effect.
guidedExercise.explanation: Writing two distinct statements prevents a visible electrical sign from being mistaken for direct structural or haemodynamic evidence.

objectives.coverageNote: Expands the three effusion slides; no ultrasound anatomy or clinical severity is inferred from the ECG alone.

objectives.title: Report inflammatory myocardial patterns and their diagnostic limits
objectives.why: Myocardial inflammation can affect ventricular repolarisation, conduction and rhythm.
know: Myocardial inflammation can affect ventricular repolarisation, conduction and rhythm. The course shows that myocarditis may produce ST–T abnormalities, ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block, and can mimic a coronary presentation. The electrical pattern varies with the distribution and severity of the process. There is no single ECG appearance that confirms myocarditis in all patients, and a normal ECG cannot exclude it.

Pericarditis and myocarditis may overlap, so a tidy distinction based solely on whether ST elevation is diffuse or focal is unreliable. Interpret symptoms, biomarkers and imaging information alongside the tracing. Troponin can identify myocardial injury without by itself specifying whether the cause is inflammatory, ischaemic or another mechanism. Similarly, an arrhythmia is an important finding but not a label for the underlying disease.

A useful integrated interpretation has three parts: the actual electrical abnormalities, the plausible disease categories, and the missing evidence that prevents certainty. For example, focal ST elevation plus a ventricular arrhythmia supports concern for myocardial disease but does not settle its aetiology. Use original synthetic cases to practise this reasoning without presenting them as patient evidence. The 2025 ESC guideline adds a contemporary multimodal context; this ECG course remains a recognition resource rather than a complete myocarditis investigation protocol.

steps.text: Record ST–T changes, conduction abnormalities and rhythm disturbance separately.

steps.title: Generate a differential

steps.title: Identify missing evidence
steps.text: Specify the clinical, biomarker and imaging information that would discriminate causes.

working: The ECG establishes electrical abnormalities.
Both inflammatory and ischaemic explanations remain possible.
example.answer: Report the pattern and need for clinical evaluation rather than declaring myocarditis.

pitfalls: Diagnosing myocarditis from a troponin result alone.
Assuming diffuse changes are obligatory.
Calling a normal ECG an exclusion test.

deepDive.title: Myocardial inflammation has several electrical expressions
deepDive.text: The source states that no ECG abnormality is specific for myocarditis. It illustrates ST–T changes, ventricular arrhythmias and AV conduction abnormalities because myocardial involvement can affect both working muscle and specialised conduction tissue. A learner should therefore retain the complete systematic reading rather than stopping after noticing ST elevation. Rate, rhythm, PR, QRS duration and repolarisation findings can each contribute to the description, even when none identifies the underlying inflammatory cause.

deepDive.title: Understand why a coronary-like tracing can have another cause
deepDive.text: The myocarditis examples deliberately resemble regional acute coronary patterns. Electrical injury patterns do not uniquely identify plaque disruption or obstruction. Conversely, normal coronary imaging in a supplied case does not mean every similar future ECG has myocarditis. The source’s confirmed outcomes depend on clinical and imaging information provided with those cases. When that supporting information is absent, use broader descriptive language and retain plausible alternatives rather than transferring a case caption directly onto a new tracing.

deepDive.title: Integrate conduction and repolarisation findings
deepDive.text: One source example combines high-grade AV conduction disturbance with ST and Q-wave abnormalities. Analyse the atrial and ventricular timing independently before interpreting the ST pattern. Counting P waves, identifying which conduct, and measuring the QRS can prevent a visually dramatic repolarisation change from concealing an important rhythm feature. The combination may make diffuse myocardial involvement a relevant consideration, but still does not prove its aetiology. A multi-component electrical report is more informative than a single disease name.

deepDive.title: Use comparison as an exercise in evidential boundaries
deepDive.text: The final chest-pain set is well suited to comparing similar appearances with different supplied clinical labels. For each image, write the findings before reading its caption; then identify which parts of the case history or additional tests are needed to support the named diagnosis. This practice exposes overconfident shortcuts and builds a reproducible reporting habit. It also preserves the distinction between recognising a pattern, explaining a plausible mechanism, and establishing an inflammatory myocardial diagnosis.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: a hypothetical record has regional ST elevation, T-wave inversion and a newly observed AV conduction disturbance. An inflammatory illness is mentioned, but no imaging or biomarker details are supplied. What should the ECG report contain?
steps: Describe the affected leads and the ST–T findings.
Analyse and report the atrial–ventricular relationship separately.
State that inflammatory myocardial involvement is one contextual possibility while retaining other causes of injury and conduction change.
guidedExercise.answer: A complete electrical description should report both the repolarisation pattern and the conduction abnormality. The context may raise consideration of myocardial inflammation, but it is not confirmed by those ECG findings alone.
guidedExercise.explanation: The exercise discourages premature closure on a young age, an illness history or a regional ST pattern, while showing how the ECG can still contribute useful structured information.

objectives.title: Apply LVH voltage criteria without claiming anatomical hypertrophy
objectives.why: High QRS voltage can be a clue to increased left ventricular mass, but voltage is influenced by age, body habitus, electrode placement and training.
know: High QRS voltage can be a clue to increased left ventricular mass, but voltage is influenced by age, body habitus, electrode placement and training. The course introduces Sokolow–Lyon voltage as a practical measurement: add the depth of S in V1 to the larger R amplitude in V5 or V6. At standard 10 mm/mV gain, a sum greater than 35 mm meets this particular voltage criterion.

The result is an ECG criterion, not a direct measurement of ventricular wall thickness. Some people with anatomical LVH do not meet voltage criteria, while healthy young or trained individuals may have high voltage. Associated lateral ST depression and T-wave inversion can strengthen concern for an abnormal repolarisation pattern, but normal ST–T segments do not exclude structural hypertrophy. Do not use a single voltage rule as either a universal diagnostic or exclusion test.

For transparent reporting, give the recorded amplitudes, gain, selected criterion and relevant accompanying findings. Different named criteria use different leads and sometimes age- or sex-specific thresholds, so do not mix their components. Clinical history and imaging clarify whether an electrical voltage pattern corresponds to anatomical disease. This distinction also helps an athlete ECG interpretation: isolated high voltage can have a different significance from high voltage accompanied by pathological repolarisation, symptoms or a concerning family history.

steps.text: Record SV1 and the larger RV5/RV6 at the stated gain.

steps.title: Calculate

working: Use the larger lateral R wave, 18 mm.
example.answer: This meets Sokolow–Lyon voltage criteria; anatomical LVH is not established by this sum alone.

pitfalls: Adding both RV5 and RV6.
Ignoring gain.
Equating isolated voltage with disease in every athlete.

practice.explanation: The measured amplitudes are added: 16 + 15 = 31 mm.
practice.hint: Use the same amplitude units.

deepDive.title: Electrical voltage and anatomical mass are different measurements
deepDive.text: The lecture begins with increased ventricular muscle mass but later emphasises that ECG voltage schemes do not perfectly identify anatomical hypertrophy. The recording reflects the direction and timing of activation as well as body build, electrode position and conduction. A thin young person may have large QRS amplitudes without increased ventricular mass. Equally, an anatomical abnormality may not satisfy a particular voltage rule. Keep the measured electrical criterion and any structural conclusion as separate statements.

deepDive.title: Calculate the named criterion reproducibly
deepDive.text: For the source’s Sokolow–Lyon example, measure the S depth in V1 and the larger relevant R height in V5 or V6, using the same gain. At 10 mm/mV, a total of 35 mm is 3.5 mV, not 35 mV. Record both components and their sum so another reader can check the calculation. Do not add amplitudes from arbitrarily selected leads or switch between millimetres and millivolts without conversion. The precise named rule determines which measurements belong together.

deepDive.title: Look beyond an amplitude sum
deepDive.text: The source also considers lateral ST depression and T-wave inversion, atrial abnormalities, and different named voltage schemes. These may change the coherence and significance of an electrical pattern, but absence of a particular ST–T appearance does not prove that anatomical hypertrophy is absent. Bundle branch block changes activation and reduces the reliability of some standard voltage approaches. State the conduction setting before applying a rule derived for a different activation pattern.

deepDive.title: Explain a positive or negative result honestly
deepDive.text: A useful learning report says that a particular voltage criterion is met or not met and describes accompanying repolarisation findings. Structural confirmation belongs to imaging and broader clinical assessment, rather than to a box count alone. The lecture further distinguishes electrical LVH from anatomical LVH as potentially different constructs. Do not collapse that distinction into either extreme: voltage is not a direct wall-thickness measurement, but a reproducible electrical finding is not meaningless simply because it is imperfect anatomically.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: S in V1 is 18 mm and R in V5 is 20 mm at 10 mm/mV. QRS duration is not prolonged and lateral ST–T morphology is unremarkable. Calculate the total and write a qualified interpretation.
steps: Add the specified amplitudes: 18 + 20 = 38 mm.
Convert to 3.8 mV at standard gain.
Report the criterion result while keeping anatomical hypertrophy and the absence of secondary ST–T findings separate.
guidedExercise.answer: The Sokolow–Lyon voltage sum is 38 mm, or 3.8 mV, meeting the source’s voltage threshold. This is an electrical voltage finding; the supplied ECG information does not establish anatomical LV hypertrophy.
guidedExercise.explanation: The example specifically avoids the source’s over-strong shortcut that normal ST–T findings would make structural hypertrophy impossible.

objectives.coverageNote: All LVH text slides reviewed; simplified categorical source statements are qualified, and numerical voltage units are corrected where necessary.

objectives.title: Recognise a right ventricular pattern using axis and precordial balance
objectives.why: The normal adult left ventricle dominates the surface QRS because of its greater muscle mass.
know: The normal adult left ventricle dominates the surface QRS because of its greater muscle mass. Right ventricular enlargement or pressure loading can shift the balance of forces. The course illustrates a relatively dominant R wave in V1, deep lateral S waves and rightward axis as potential clues. The combination matters more than any one feature, because individual findings have several alternative explanations.

A tall R wave in V1 can also reflect right bundle branch block, posterior myocardial injury, pre-excitation, lead position or a normal variant. Begin by checking QRS duration, initial activation and technical placement before attributing the pattern to RVH. Right precordial ST depression or T-wave inversion may reflect repolarisation changes, but should be interpreted with age and clinical context. A normal ECG does not rule out right ventricular structural disease.

It is more accurate to report an ECG pattern suggesting right ventricular dominance or strain than to declare a specific anatomical measurement. Use history, prior records and imaging to assess the cause. The source contains a wording slip defining RVH in terms of the left ventricle; the intended chamber is the right ventricle. This lesson corrects that wording while preserving the useful lead-based reasoning. Avoid making pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary embolism or a congenital lesion synonymous with one morphology.

steps.text: Assess QRS duration and exclude an obvious activation explanation for tall RV1.

steps.title: Combine leads

example.question: Original synthetic educational example — A synthetic tracing shows rightward axis, dominant RV1 and deep SV6 with a narrow QRS.
working: The findings collectively suggest right ventricular electrical dominance.
Structural and non-structural alternatives remain.
example.answer: Possible right ventricular hypertrophy/strain pattern requiring clinical correlation.

pitfalls: Using tall RV1 alone as proof of RVH.
Ignoring RBBB or pre-excitation.
Confusing right ventricular dominance with a specific cause.

practice.prompt: Which combination better supports a right ventricular pattern?
options: Dominant RV1 with rightward axis and deep lateral S waves
practice.explanation: The combined distribution suggests a shift in ventricular forces.
practice.hint: Look for agreement between axis and precordial findings.

practice.prompt: Which can also produce a prominent R in V1?
practice.explanation: Conduction delay can change the right precordial QRS.
practice.hint: Exclude competing activation patterns.

deepDive.title: Recognise an altered balance of ventricular forces
deepDive.text: The standard adult ECG often reflects a larger net left ventricular contribution. The source’s right ventricular pattern combines a rightward frontal axis, greater initial positivity in V1 and persistent terminal negativity in the left precordium. The educational value lies in the consistency of these views: more than one lead group suggests a changed ventricular balance. Do not interpret the dominant R in V1 in isolation or assume that any rightward axis directly measures right ventricular wall thickness.

deepDive.title: Measure the specified voltages at the recorded gain
deepDive.text: The source presents an R-in-V1 plus S-in-V5-or-V6 sum of at least 1.1 mV as one voltage approach. At 10 mm/mV this equals 11 mm. Measure the appropriate deflection from baseline and keep the selected left-precordial lead explicit. Check whether a broad QRS, unusual lead placement or a different activation sequence could make the voltage comparison inappropriate. A precise sum remains a criterion result, not a stand-alone structural diagnosis.

deepDive.title: Test alternatives to a prominent anterior R wave
deepDive.text: A relatively prominent R wave in V1 can also arise in other course contexts, including altered conduction, a reciprocal posterior-pattern presentation or anatomical/technical differences. Use QRS width and morphology, the frontal axis, ST–T distribution and the remainder of precordial progression to compare explanations. A source case with known congenital disease demonstrates one possible setting; it does not mean every superficially similar ECG has the same congenital anatomy or pressure-loading mechanism.

deepDive.title: Report the pattern and the unresolved anatomy separately
deepDive.text: A strong report describes the rightward axis and precordial balance, then states whether the combination supports a right ventricular electrical pattern. The source lists pulmonary and congenital associations as contexts, not as an exhaustive aetiological diagnosis. Clarify what imaging or historical evidence would be needed to identify the structure involved. The RVH source slide that inadvertently refers to increased LV mass should not be learned literally: the topic concerns right ventricular adaptation, and the ECG remains indirect evidence.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: an ECG has a rightward QRS axis, a narrow dominant R in V1 and a deep S in V6. What makes a right ventricular electrical pattern more plausible than relying on V1 alone?
steps: Combine the frontal axis with the precordial distribution.
Confirm whether QRS width and morphology suggest another activation explanation.
Describe the internally consistent pattern while withholding an unsupported anatomical cause.
guidedExercise.answer: The axis and opposing right/left precordial forces reinforce each other. They may support a right ventricular electrical pattern, but neither the pattern nor a voltage sum alone proves hypertrophy or identifies its cause.
guidedExercise.explanation: The reasoning is based on agreement across independent views, not on a single tall R wave or a disease association remembered from a slide.

objectives.coverageNote: RVH voltage and distribution slides used; source page 12’s LV-mass wording is treated as a label error rather than repeated as right-ventricular physiology.

objectives.title: Describe atrial electrical abnormalities using P-wave width and components
objectives.why: The P wave combines right and left atrial activation.
know: The P wave combines right and left atrial activation. Its early part predominantly reflects right atrial depolarisation, while later activity includes the left atrium. The course uses lead II and V1 to show how changes in timing or direction can alter the total waveform. These are electrical observations; terms such as left atrial abnormality are often more defensible than claiming anatomical enlargement from morphology alone.

A broad P wave, often at least 120 ms, or a distinctly bifid appearance in lead II can support left atrial electrical abnormality. An enlarged terminal negative component in V1 is another clue; both its duration and depth matter. A tall peaked P wave in inferior leads may suggest right atrial abnormality, with a conventional lead-II amplitude threshold around 2.5 mm at standard gain. These criteria are not perfectly sensitive or specific.

First ensure that the deflection really is a sinus P wave and that calibration and lead placement are appropriate. Ectopic atrial origin, conduction delay and overlapping repolarisation can alter P morphology without directly representing chamber size. Assess several consecutive beats rather than measuring one distorted complex. Report the feature and its lead, then state the atrial interpretation as a suggestion. Clinical history and imaging are needed when the anatomical size or pressure of an atrium matters.

steps.title: Identify sinus P waves
steps.text: Check consistency and separation from T waves.

steps.title: Measure dimensions
steps.text: Use duration and amplitude with known speed/gain.

steps.text: Compare lead II and terminal P activity in V1 before concluding.

example.question: Original synthetic educational example — A synthetic sinus tracing has P duration 130 ms in II and a prominent terminal negative P component in V1.
working: The duration is prolonged.
The V1 component provides a second supporting clue.
example.answer: Left atrial electrical abnormality is suggested; chamber size is not measured by the ECG.

pitfalls: Calling atrial enlargement certain from one P wave.
Measuring a fused P/T complex.
Ignoring paper speed when measuring width.

practice.prompt: P-wave width primarily measures what?
practice.explanation: It reflects the timing of atrial depolarisation.
practice.hint: Distinguish an electrical interval from anatomy.

practice.hint: Use language matched to the evidence.

deepDive.title: Why atrial abnormality is a careful term
deepDive.text: The source explicitly moves away from equating P-wave appearances with atrial enlargement. The P wave reflects atrial activation, so its morphology can change with anatomy, conduction or both. Calling it left or right atrial electrical abnormality preserves that distinction. A wide, notched waveform does not directly measure chamber volume, and a tall P wave does not identify a valve lesion. Begin with what is visible and measured before proposing a chamber-associated interpretation.

deepDive.title: Separate duration, amplitude and component polarity
deepDive.text: In lead II, inspect P width, notching and height rather than using one visual impression. In V1, examine the initial positive and terminal negative components separately. The source links increased terminal negativity with more posteriorly directed late atrial forces and shows tall initial positivity in a right-atrial-associated pattern. These components are affected by the lead’s view, so keep their location explicit; a component measured in V1 is not interchangeable with a total P-wave height measured in II.

deepDive.title: Convert units before applying a criterion
deepDive.text: At 25 mm/s, 1 mm horizontally is 40 ms, making 3 mm equal to 120 ms. At 10 mm/mV, 1 mm vertically is 0.1 mV. A source description of a terminal negative component at least 1 mm deep and 1 mm wide therefore combines amplitude and duration, not two amplitudes. Check speed and gain first, then state the actual measurements. Ambiguous P-wave boundaries, overlap with preceding T/U waves and baseline noise should reduce confidence rather than encourage rounding into a criterion.

deepDive.title: Integrate, but do not over-attribute, the pattern
deepDive.text: Mitral or tricuspid disease, ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary pressure-related conditions and cardiomyopathy appear in the source as possible clinical settings. The ECG cannot choose among them solely from P morphology. More than one atrial abnormality may coexist, and a rhythm without consistent discrete P waves may prevent applying sinus-P criteria at all. A useful report describes the measured components and their likely atrial association, while leaving chamber size, pressure and cause to corroborating assessment.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: at 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV, a notched P in II spans 3.5 small squares. V1 has a terminal negative component 1.5 mm deep and 1.2 mm wide. Convert the timings and describe the findings.
steps: Calculate total P duration: 3.5 × 40 = 140 ms.
Calculate terminal-negative duration: 1.2 × 40 = 48 ms, while retaining 1.5 mm as an amplitude.
Describe a prolonged/notched P and a prominent terminal negative component rather than asserting an imaged chamber size.
guidedExercise.answer: The P duration is 140 ms and the terminal-negative V1 component lasts approximately 48 ms. The combination supports a left-atrial electrical abnormality pattern in the appropriate rhythm and recording setting.
guidedExercise.explanation: The exercise separates two measurement dimensions and preserves the source’s distinction between electrical abnormality and anatomical enlargement.

objectives.coverageNote: All atrial morphology and comparison slides included; ambiguous wording on P width is resolved through explicit paper-speed conversion.

objectives.title: Identify cardiomyopathy and infiltration clues without disease-specific certainty
objectives.why: Myocardial disease can alter conduction, QRS amplitude and repolarisation without producing a unique ECG signature.
know: Myocardial disease can alter conduction, QRS amplitude and repolarisation without producing a unique ECG signature. The source describes dilated cardiomyopathy with possible bundle branch block, atrial or ventricular arrhythmias, abnormal R-wave progression and non-specific ST–T changes. These observations are useful clues to a substrate, but the ECG cannot establish ventricular dimensions or systolic function by itself.

An infiltrative process such as cardiac amyloidosis may produce low voltage or a pseudo-infarction Q-wave pattern. A mismatch between increased wall thickness on imaging and relatively small QRS amplitudes can be informative. However, low voltage is not present in every case, particularly across different amyloid subtypes. Conversely, low voltage has many other explanations, so it is neither a universal screening rule nor a standalone diagnosis of infiltration.

Interpret electrical findings alongside the structural information actually supplied. If there is no imaging, do not imply that a voltage–mass discrepancy has been demonstrated. Note conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias separately because they may be clinically meaningful regardless of the final cause. Compare previous records for progression. A careful synthesis can suggest further evaluation of myocardial disease while keeping alternative explanations visible; it should not turn an illustrative pattern into a specific histological diagnosis.

practice.explanation: Not every case has low voltage; phenotype varies.

deepDive.title: A non-specific ECG can still carry useful information
deepDive.text: The dilated-cardiomyopathy section deliberately lists several abnormalities rather than one diagnostic pattern. Conduction delay, axis change, atrial abnormalities, arrhythmias and ST–T changes may coexist. Analyse each component systematically instead of expecting a single signature that proves chamber dilatation or reduced function. A tracing may be substantially abnormal yet remain aetiologically non-specific. Distinguish its diagnostic limits from its usefulness in documenting activation, rhythm and changes over time.

deepDive.title: Compare limb and chest-lead amplitudes
deepDive.text: The source highlights that limb-lead voltage can be low even when precordial voltage is not. This distribution is more informative than a vague statement that the whole ECG is small. Check gain and recording quality in both lead groups and report the actual pattern. Surface amplitude does not directly equal myocardial mass: orientation, conduction and surrounding tissue influence it. The apparently counterintuitive combination of thick walls on supplied imaging and low ECG voltage is therefore an important comparison, not a measurement contradiction.

deepDive.title: Recognise pseudo-infarction appearances
deepDive.text: The amyloidosis examples show Q or QS patterns that can resemble prior infarction. The purpose is to widen interpretation of lost initial forces, especially when low voltage or other non-ischaemic clues coexist. An abnormal Q wave is still described precisely, but its cause is not settled by that description. The source’s supplied diagnosis depends on information beyond the ECG. Avoid reversing the shortcut and calling every low-voltage Q-wave tracing amyloidosis; several other settings can produce overlapping features.

deepDive.title: Keep structural and aetiological claims proportional
deepDive.text: A report can explain why a combination raises consideration of a myocardial or infiltrative process while acknowledging that the ECG cannot identify the deposited substance, measure wall thickness or establish systolic function. Conduction abnormalities and atrial rhythms should remain explicit because they can affect waveform interpretation. Compare previous recordings when available and identify which corroborating information would discriminate between hypotheses. This approach uses the full source case set while preserving the boundary between pattern recognition and a confirmed cardiomyopathy diagnosis.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: limb-lead QRS amplitudes are small, precordial voltage is better preserved, and QS complexes appear in V1–V3. Is anterior infarction the only defensible interpretation?
steps: Describe the voltage distribution and initial ventricular forces separately.
Check gain, electrode placement and conduction before assigning a disease cause.
Use the source’s non-ischaemic examples to retain alternatives without claiming a specific infiltrative diagnosis.
guidedExercise.answer: No. The ECG has a low-limb-voltage and anterior QS pattern with several possible explanations. Prior infarction is one contextual possibility, but a myocardial or infiltrative process and technical/activation factors must not be excluded solely by the QS appearance.
guidedExercise.explanation: The exercise makes differential reasoning symmetrical: a familiar infarction-like feature should neither force infarction nor automatically identify an alternative disease.

objectives.coverageNote: Dilated and restrictive/infiltrative case-caption text reviewed; the original imaging and ECG figures require private-source inspection and are not reproduced.

objectives.title: Use congenital and systemic associations as differential clues
objectives.why: The course links some congenital and systemic conditions with recognisable ECG combinations.
know: The course links some congenital and systemic conditions with recognisable ECG combinations. An atrial septal defect may be associated with right-sided loading and an rSr′ pattern in V1. Axis can differ with the anatomical subtype; a secundum lesion often has rightward forces, while a primum lesion may have a leftward axis. These associations help generate a differential, but they do not establish a defect or determine its size.

Systemic neurological events may produce striking repolarisation changes, including deep T-wave inversion and QT changes. Neuromuscular disease can also affect myocardial conduction and produce unusual Q waves or ST–T patterns. These examples show why a dramatic electrical appearance need not be coronary in origin. Equally, a known systemic condition must not be used to dismiss possible concurrent cardiac disease. Interpretation still requires the symptoms, temporal sequence and clinical investigations.

The purpose of learning associations is to ask better questions, rather than to memorise a disease label for every waveform. Describe whether the finding concerns activation, repolarisation or chamber loading, then explain which supplied contextual detail makes a particular association plausible. If the clinical history is missing, keep the differential broad. Imaging and specialist assessment provide information the ECG cannot supply. This disciplined approach prevents an attractive pattern match from becoming an unsupported structural or systemic diagnosis.

steps.text: Separate loading, conduction and repolarisation observations.

steps.title: Use the supplied context
steps.text: Connect a known congenital or systemic condition only when evidence supports it.

steps.title: Avoid diagnostic leaps
steps.text: State which anatomy or cause remains unconfirmed.

rSr′ also has other explanations.

Assuming neurological T waves exclude coronary disease.
Treating an association as a sensitive screening test.

practice.explanation: Anatomical confirmation requires appropriate imaging.
practice.hint: The ECG describes electrical consequences.

practice.prompt: Deep T inversion can have which origin?

practice.explanation: The differential includes multiple myocardial and systemic processes.
practice.hint: Avoid a one-waveform, one-disease rule.

glossary.definition: A small initial R, intervening S and terminal positive deflection in a right precordial lead.
A relationship between ECG changes and a disease outside the primary electrical system.

deepDive.title: Use associations to ask a better question
deepDive.text: The source links combinations of axis and right-precordial conduction appearances with particular atrial septal defect examples. These are useful associations, not sufficient anatomical diagnoses. An rSr′ appearance in V1 must be assessed with QRS width, axis, precordial placement and the remaining tracing. A notched inferior R wave can be described without claiming that it proves an atrial communication. The learning task is to connect an observed pattern to a clinical question that needs corroboration.

deepDive.title: Neurological illness can alter the ECG interpretation context
deepDive.text: The neurological examples contain marked repolarisation abnormalities that can resemble coronary patterns. A wide or deeply inverted T wave, prolonged QT or ST change remains an electrical finding even when the supplied case has an intracranial diagnosis. History matters because similar appearances do not all arise from the same process. Do not infer an intracranial event from a tracing, and do not dismiss a potentially relevant cardiac process merely because a neurological explanation is mentioned.

deepDive.title: Systemic disease may involve several electrical domains
deepDive.text: The neuromuscular examples include initial-force changes, conduction delay, altered PR or QT timing, and ectopic ventricular activity. This diversity explains why one remembered pattern is not a reliable disease fingerprint. Analyse the whole ECG and state which features are measured, which are rhythm findings and which require comparison. In an individual with a known systemic condition, a new electrical change can be important without being specific. In an individual without that history, the same change cannot establish the systemic diagnosis.

deepDive.title: Avoid false certainty from memorable case captions
deepDive.text: The course’s associations work best as comparison exercises. First describe a case image without its title, then consider how the supplied history changes the differential. Retain the distinction between an association reported in selected teaching cases and a validated diagnostic test with known accuracy. Prevalence figures or strong categorical statements in an older slide should not be repeated as universal contemporary evidence. The app’s report should show the reasoning chain, including the alternative explanations that the available data cannot distinguish.

guidedExercise.prompt: Original guided exercise: a person with a known neuromuscular disorder has lateral Q waves and a dominant R in V1. No coronary history, imaging or earlier ECG is supplied. How should the association influence reporting?
steps: Record the lateral initial negative forces and prominent V1 positivity.
Recognise that the known systemic condition provides a relevant alternative setting for the pattern.
Avoid using either the ECG or the history alone to prove the cause of the electrical changes.
guidedExercise.answer: Describe the abnormalities and note that a non-ischaemic systemic/myocardial association is relevant in this context. Neither prior infarction nor a specific systemic cardiac manifestation is confirmed by the supplied ECG information alone.
guidedExercise.explanation: The exercise encourages contextual interpretation while avoiding the equally misleading extremes of ignoring a known systemic condition or attributing every abnormality to it.

objectives.coverageNote: Congenital, cerebrovascular and neuromuscular material is explicitly incorporated; source associations are not converted into stand-alone anatomical or systemic diagnoses.

objectives.title: Distinguish dextrocardia clues from limb-lead reversal
objectives.why: A globally negative lead I can be a technical clue or reflect unusual cardiac orientation.
know: A globally negative lead I can be a technical clue or reflect unusual cardiac orientation. Right–left arm electrode reversal typically inverts lead I and exchanges other limb-lead relationships, while the precordial leads retain their usual placement and progression. Inspect the entire tracing rather than treating one negative complex as a diagnosis. Non-sinus atrial activation and other technical issues can also complicate the pattern.

In dextrocardia, both limb-lead orientation and precordial progression may be altered. The source contrasts negative P, QRS and T in lead I with poor or reversed progression across standard left-sided chest leads. This differs from simple arm-electrode reversal, where the precordial sequence is usually preserved. The distinction is especially useful when a surprising axis or global inversion otherwise tempts a disease diagnosis.

Check recording labels and the actual electrode positions before interpreting anatomy. If placement is uncertain, the educational conclusion is that technical clarification is needed, not that a rare anatomical condition has been established. A repeat correctly labelled recording and clinical confirmation can resolve uncertainty. Do not teach the source shorthand that only two causes of negative lead I exist as an exhaustive rule. The broader lesson is to test a technical explanation before constructing a complex pathological narrative.

steps.title: Inspect lead I
steps.text: Look at P, QRS and T polarity together.

steps.title: Check precordials
steps.text: Assess whether the usual R progression is preserved or reversed.

steps.title: Verify recording
steps.text: Clarify electrodes and labels before inferring anatomy.

example.question: Original synthetic educational example — A synthetic tracing has negative P/QRS/T in I but preserved normal precordial progression.
working: The limb-lead pattern is unusual.
Preserved chest-lead progression favours an arm-electrode issue over typical dextrocardia.
example.answer: Suspect limb-lead reversal and verify recording placement.

pitfalls: Diagnosing dextrocardia from lead I alone.
Ignoring precordial progression.
Treating a technical differential as an exhaustive list.

practice.prompt: Which finding favours simple arm-lead reversal over typical dextrocardia?
practice.explanation: The chest electrodes are unaffected by an arm swap, so their progression is generally preserved.
practice.hint: Compare the limb and chest leads.

practice.prompt: The first response to suspected technical reversal should be what?
practice.explanation: Technical verification prevents a false disease interpretation.
practice.hint: Check the recording before the diagnosis.
